speechtext:
I enjoy the Hon. Member's rhetoric. I am glad I finally got his attention.
What it really boils down to in terms of the grain industry is this. Is there a possibility, if the pressures are international, to get what I think of as subsidy programs by the EEC and as a result of the U.S. Farm Bill turned around? What have we done? What we have done is this. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has taken the lead, both nationally and internationally. That work has been very closely co-ordinated with the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. What have they done? They have visited countries that are involved in grain production to try to discuss the issue and to try to come up with some modus operandi whereby we will not all drown in subsidies. That is what they have tried to do.
There is not only that. The Prime Minister in negotiations at the summit has been able to bring forward agriculture as Canada's number one issue. It is the first time that a Prime Minister, a leader, has made agriculture the number one issue on a country's agenda. Happily, it is being accepted by other

April 30, 1987
countries as being sufficiently important internationally to examine at the summit. I think almost all Governments know that we cannot continue to drive down prices artificially by subsidy and then somehow have a viable agricultural community.
Farmers do not want to have subsidies. They do not want to come cap-in-hand to the Parliament of Canada for money for a commodity which they are producing and for which they should receive a fair return every time there is a crisis. Those are the realities. The NDP can argue all it wants. Those are the facts.
Let us now consider the moratorium. It is interesting when we consider the moratorium and farm financing to consider also a Bill passed by the NDP Government of Manitoba which would remove, for example, chattels against any loans taken for farm purposes. The Government there wanted support for such a proposition. However, a great many farmers were against it. It is quite evident why they were against it. It is because farmers see very clearly that they need a consistent line of credit with banking institutions in order to keep their operations going. They are in the business of agriculture. So what they were saying in Manitoba is that it might be a well-intentioned Bill, it might even be a Bill which is seen to be "against the banks", which is popular from time to time on the Prairies, but upon closer analysis they were concerned because the last thing they want is the cutting off or a reduction of that credit or the ability to obtain credit.
That is why the federal Government came in with a farm debt review board to see if we could not work out a common position, not only on the Prairies, but a common position by which all farmers could continue to operate while not jeopardizing their ability to obtain credit and the loans of the banking institutions could be repaid.
I would now like to talk about a press release put out by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association yesterday in which it is agreed that the moratorium had to be lifted. It points out that there has to be caution taken, obviously, so that people are not put into a situation whereby they will lose their farms. The Ministers have very clearly stated that that will not be the case.
What was involved was two types of payments. There were payments to financial institutions, including banks, credit unions and the FCC on the one hand, while on the other hand there were those who had the ability to pay at least something who chose not to pay in the hope that, perhaps, there would be an amnesty or whatever. It was not fair. It was not making the credit situation any better. Those are the situations, and I do not think we should put it any other way.
I am absolutely convinced, Mr. Speaker, that this Government's support for agriculture is very sound. I have already given examples of that, such as the FCC, the capital gains tax
exemption, the fuels tax credit, the Special Grains Program, the Western Grain Stabilization Act amendments, and others.
The Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board announced just a week ago that there would be another S705 million allocated for payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
I was in Manitoba during that period of time and had occasion to speak to the grain farmers. They knew what the situation was, and they also knew about the payments under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. They were pleased that the two announcements came in and around the same time. It provided them with some form of assurance in respect of their crops.
I am pleased with the way in which our farmers have been reacting to the situation. Quite frankly, trying to create an even larger crisis than all of us recognize already exists because of world pressures is not doing anything at all to help the farming community.
I remain convinced that we must come to an international agreement, an international consensus, an international recognition that the kinds of subsidy programs now in place internationally are going to continue hurting our farmers, our economies, our international relations. It is for that reason that it is critical that the Prime Minister and others take this issue to the summit table. It is absolutely critical.
I am not using that argument to deflect what the Government should do, what the Government is doing, what farmers are doing; but, we all recognize that that is the absolute requirement.
I do not know whether or not Hon. Members recognize it, but 80 per cent of Manitoba's agricultural production must find a market outside Manitoba. Without access to the American markets, all of the subsidies in the world, all of the agreements in the world will be of absolutely no value. If we do not have access to international markets, the agricultural industry will suffer.
Of course there has to be protection in terms of supply-management and commodity prices-and we all recognize that. Everyone understands that. No one is blind to that. But, I wish, once and for all, that the Opposition, who can be as critical as they wish, would at least base their criticisms on fact. They can be as critical as they wish, but their criticism should be based on a recognition of the world situation. They should at least on occasion tip their hats to the reality that exists on the Prairies.
We hear a lot about western alienation. I think this debate on the western grain situation should demonstrate for all of us exactly how much Canadians of one region need Canadians of other regions.
Today it is the west. With the dairy policy, it was primarily Quebec. Both policies were right.
It is time that Canadians, no matter what the pressures, no matter where their region, recognized that we are one country,
April 30, 1987

and they do. While we will fight for our regional positions, there is an over-riding larger consideration, that being the ability of Canadians from one region, as the tugs and pulls and pressures come, to help Canadians in trouble in another region. That is how this country has been built.
If this debate teaches us anything, it is that we are only strong when we recognize the need to work together.
I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, that my colleagues in government from other than the prairie region have gained an appreciation of what is happening on the Prairies, and I am particularly pleased that they have shown a willingness to approve costly measures to assist in the situation.
All we on the government side ask is that there be a recognition of those facts and that there be a critical analysis of what else could be done, rather than making politics more important than the health of the grain business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been roughly thirty-seven and one half hours since I entered the Chamber to participate in this debate. With a short break that allowed some of us to catch a reasonable night's sleep, we now have the opportunity to continue the debate.
It is a very important debate. Quite frankly, it is a debate about the future of the Canadian farmer; it is a debate about the Canadian grain situation, about the family farm. It is not a debate, as some in this House would have us believe, particularly those on the government side, solely about the western Canada situation. There are farmers in Atlantic Canada; there are farmers in Quebec and Ontario; there are farmers on the Prairies; and there are farmers in British Columbia-and all are impacted by the decision of this Government to lift the moratorium on foreclosures.
It reaches out to those who are not directly tied in with the Farm Credit Corporation, that institution being the key element in this debate because of the decision to lift the moratorium on any foreclosures by it. But, as we all know, Mr. Speaker, in this market-place environment, if there are restrictions on one element, then, ipso facto, there are restrictions on the other sectors as well, the banks and the credit unions.
I wish to commence my contribution to this debate by reminding the House and those who have followed it of the steps taken to trigger the debate.
The first step was taken by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), that step coming in the form of a letter to the Speaker of the House of Commons, dated April 27 last.
I should like to take a few moments to read that letter into the record. Over the course of the debate, it has become apparent that there is a misconception on the part of some as to what the intent in requesting this emergency debate was.
The letter reads:
April 27, 1987
The Hon. John Fraser P.C., M.P.
Speaker of the House of Commons Room 222-N House of Commons Dear Mr. Speaker:
I am writing this letter to notify you that tomorrow I intend to rise under the provisions of Standing Order 29 to seek leave to adjourn the House for the purpose of considering a question of urgent and pressing necessity. That issue is the current crisis facing Canadian grain producers.
At the moment there does not appear to be any opportunity in the immediate future to have these issues brought before Parliament for a full and open discussion. Recent developments have however brought an urgency to this issue that might not have existed before. These include the following;
(1)	Last week the Canadian Wheat Board announced that the initial price for Number 1 Canadian wheat would be 18 per cent lower than last year's price. This follows on last year's price which was about 20 per cent less than the year before. Taken together this is a very substantial drop in the price that grain farmers will be guaranteed for their crop and it will mean hardship for many farm families across Canada.
(2)	It was announced today that the Farm Credit Corporation moratorium on farm foreclosures was being brought to an end as a result of a decision of the Minister of Agriculture. This will mean that for those families who cannot absorb the fall in the price of grain announced last week, bankruptcy will be the only option left open to them. This is indeed a sad situation and a direct attack on the viability of the family farm, particularly in Western Canada.
(3)	At this time of year when prairie grain farmers are engaged in planting this year's crop it is extremely important that they have an idea as to whether or not they can expect a deficiency payment this year. So far the government has refused to give them its assurance.
Mr. Speaker I believe that these are sufficient reasons for granting a request for an emergency debate. The problems in the economy of Western Canada are severe and growing worse. The situation facing the prairie grain farmer needs immediate attention and I believe that granting an emergency debate so that Members of Parliament have an opportunity to discuss these issues would be wholly appropriate at this time.
And the letter is signed by Mr. Hovdebo, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert.
Mr. Speaker, as you know, and as others in this country will be aware, the Speaker did deem the issue to be of an emergency nature and granted the request to hold an emergency debate on it. That debate started at 8 p.m. on April 27 last and went around the clock some 21 hours, to a point yesterday afternoon. This morning, the debate was resumed.
We feel very strongly that this is not just an opportunity to get up in the House to talk about farm issues, the survival of the family farm and various crops. It is not just a reason so we can have something to mail out to our farm constituents. We believe the fundamental purpose of this debate is to focus public attention and, therefore, government attention on the very serious situation that exists in rural Canada.
The moratorium is supposed to come off tomorrow, Friday, May 1, and we are hoping through this combined pressure, through the Members of the House of Commons and through farm groups and citizens across Canada that the Government will reconsider its decision. We hope it will announce some

April 30, 1987
time today during the debate that, in fact, taking the moratorium off is wrong, and that it will stay in place for a period necessary to ensure that the appropriate mechanism is put in place for debt review and to allow farmers to get rid of their debts. They will not then be under the gun of the Farm Credit Corporation, the bank or the credit union. We are getting that support, Mr. Speaker.
I have two letters here, one which actually came before the debate. It is addressed to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney). It is from a very important agricultural group in Manitoba, namely the Keystone Agricultural Producers. Mr. Jack Penner, President, wrote the letter with copies to the Minister of State for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). I have had the opportunity of meeting with Mr. Penner on a couple of occasions at grain related conferences or Seaway conferences which he and I have attended. I have grown to respect the man. I also know that he has a direct involvement in the politics in western Canada. He has worked from time to time for the Minister of State for the Wheat Board in terms of his own political career. I want to read into the record the plea from the Keystone Agricultural Producers of last week:
On behalf of grain producers in Manitoba, we call on your Government to announce, as soon as possible, intention to introduce a similar program for the 1987-88 crop year, with support levels at least equivalent to those under the 1986 program.
We feel strongly that any such additional program should be based simply on acreages to keep it production neutral. The farm financial crisis is so serious that we feel action must be taken prior to the end of April to ensure grain farmers and the business community that the Federal Government is supportive.
What did the Government do? It pulled out the rug from underneath those who were able to keep the FCC at bay because of foreclosure. Mr. Penner's letter continues:
A second important step should be a bold new initiative through the Farm Credit Corporation to save thousands of commercial farms from insolvency. In addition to new loan funds at affordable rates, the FCC should become a full service lender to the farm community. This we feel would provide the assurances required now by the farm community, in times when other lending institutions are threatening to withdraw services.
What does the Government do, Mr. Speaker? It joins in with the threats and pulls the plug. The letter continues:
The CAP supports the initiative of your government in attempting to persuade the European Economic Community, the United States and Japan to discontinue the current trade war, which is seriously affecting the economies of other grain producing countries. Unfortunately, even positive results from these efforts will be too late to save many thousands of young farmers, with serious detrimental effects for rural towns.
Your immediate and urgent attention to this matter is sought by the farmers of Manitoba.
As history will show, they did not get that support. In fact the opposite occurred.
I have another letter from the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool dated April 28, 1987. It is again written to the Prime Minister. It concerns the emergency debate on the farm economic crisis. Remember, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of the largest pool elevator groups in western Canada, one that has major holdings in Thunder Bay where a lot of the grains it
handles are moved through my community. Mr. Stevenson writes:
Saskatchewan Wheat Pool believes that the rural way of life and related service industries are in jeopardy.
The Pool asks that all Members of Parliament recognize the very critical economic situation confronting Western Canadian families and communities. This crisis has far-reaching social and economic implications for the national economy, as well as for the West.
We specifically recommend:
1.	That programs be immediately developed through federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in productive capacities.
2.	That early consideration be given to the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year.
3.	That government continue its efforts to restore sanity in the international grain market.
Saskatchewan Wheat Pool continues to be prepared to work with government to achieve short and long-term solutions in the interests of the farmers and communities of Saskatchewan and Western Canada.
Those are two comments from two diverse farm groups in western Canada. Both clearly plead to this Parliament, and to the Government of Canada, to do something positive to protect their existence.
What are we talking about in terms of numbers when we talk about farm foreclosures? We have had a number of them quoted in this House. During the Standing Committee on Agriculture meeting on March 24 of this year the following information was given. Eight per cent of our farmers are insolvent. Based on 171,000 farmers that means over 13,500 farmers are considered insolvent. Some 23 per cent have major cash flow problems; that is in the magnitude of 53,000 farmers. Of the Farm Credit Corporation borrowers, 6,000 are more than two years in arrears. Can you imagine if that were one of us and it was a car or a house? It would be gone a long time ago.
There has been some compassion. The powers that have said no, that we should not be pulling the rug out from under these people. Give them a chance to continue to survive. The family farm is part of Canada. Farming is part of Canada. It is part of the reason we exist as a country.
As we developed the CPR west of Thunder Bay we were opening up more and more acres of farmland encouraging people to move out there to develop a sound economic basis to feed our country, to feed North America and finally to feed the world.
It is not just the western producer. It is not just the grain producer. First, in terms of the moratorium it is any farmer in Canada whether in Atlantic Canada, Quebec, Ontario, northern Ontario, New Liskeard, the Sault Ste. Marie area, the Thunder Bay area, the Slate River Valley, in Rainy River, or in British Columbia. All farmers are affected and all farmers are nervous. It is creating a lot of stress in the family, and I will come back to that.
I want to mention that it is not just grain per se or wheat per se, it is the corn producer, the soybean producer, the small grain producers in central and Atlantic Canada. They are
April 30, 1987

affected by the deficiency payments. They need to know that when they put their seeds in the ground over the next couple of weeks that they will get enough money for the produce when they harvest it so they can pay the bills for planting and maintaining that crop. They would even like it if there was a little left over to put food on the table. They are not asking for the moon. They are asking for a decent opportunity to make a living in farming. They know the world markets are working against us. They know, whether we have the biggest crop in our history, that because of the international price that that price alone will not allow them to recover the cost of producing that grain.
We know it is a world situation and we have seen the response of the other countries. The European Economic Community is one of the biggest supporters of its agricultural sector in the world. In 1985, it provided support of $2.60 per bushel. That support jumped to $3.13 per bushel in 1986, an increase of 53 cents per bushel. The United States, in its effort to catch up with the EEC, has gone from support of $1.49 per bushel to $3.13 per bushel in 1986, an increase of $1.14. What was Canada's response? Two nickels a bushel is all we upped the ante. How can we help keep our producers producing if that is the kind of nickel and dime commitment we give to them? We are not asking that those figures be matched. We are just asking for sufficient funds for the producers to have confidence enough to survive.
I am not a farmer. I am not much good at even growing a garden other than to do the digging but my roots are in farming. My grandfather and his brothers homesteaded in rural Manitoba in a community now called Angusville which, I am proud to say, is named after them. My father was a farmer until he went off to war.
Many of the people in the community of Thunder Bay and the surrounding area moved to Thunder Bay from western Canada. They followed the grain to the Lakehead. There are literally thousands who work and live in Thunder Bay whose livelihoods depend on the viability of the western Canadian farmer. The fewer farmers there are, ultimately the less grain there is to move through the Port of Thunder Bay. The less grain that moves through the Port of Thunder Bay, the less grain that moves through the St. Lawrence and all the communities along it.
I would like to give the House an idea of the number of communities in eastern Canada that are touched directly by the resourcefulness and skills of producers in western Canada. In Thunder Bay, 2,000 people are involved in the grainhandling sector. Up to 2,000 people work on the lakers taking the grain from Thunder Bay to points along the Seaway. In Montreal, 175 people work in the elevators and their livelihoods depend on western grain. In Sorel, there are 43 people who depend on grain. In Trois-Rivieres, there are 50. In Quebec City, there are 105 and in Saint John there are 50. In Halifax, there are 60 people who depend on grain. Here is the
rub. In the riding of Manicouagan, there are 194 people, some in Port Cartier, some in Baie Comeau, whose livelihoods depend on grain being produced and sold at a decent price or at the very least sold somewhere in the world.
Yesterday morning at approximately 8 a.m., the Prime Minister spoke in the House. A number of us were quite surprised to see him here. However, we felt good that he was here because it meant the message was getting out. The Government was feeling the pressure and it had to have the Prime Minister respond. He reminded us that he is only a phone call away. Mind you, that was a phone call during an election in which there was a chance there would be a change in Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister wanted to do his best to help out his friends.
Today, yesterday and the day before we have been asking for some very specific assistance for Canadian farmers and the Prime Minister seems to be ignoring those pleas. Perhaps he will get an earful this afternoon when he meets with the premiers. We know that they too have been feeling the pressure. Although their meeting is not to deal with agriculture but with the Constitution, we would be very shocked to learn that they did not raise this extremely important matter with the Prime Minister.
We should not have to rely on phone calls. We should have a Government that is prepared to examine a sector like agriculture in the context of the world market and in terms of the Canadian need and say: "We have to do something, here is our plan. Let us protect those farmers who have loans with the Farm Credit Corporation and by doing so send a signal to the banks". Can you imagine what signal the banks are receiving today, Mr. Speaker? As soon as the foreclosure moratorium stops tomorrow, it will be open season on farmers. There are a lot of them who are in jeopardy.
Once again, it seems that the banks will get their way. Not so long ago, this broke Government that is so concerned about the deficit found $ 1 billion over a week-end. Now it cannot even say to the Canadian farmers who are under pressure from those very same banks that it will keep the wolf away from their doors and put in place a program that will allow them to get rid of their debt in a realistic way. The Government will not say that it will provide the supports that would ensure at the very least that farmers could get as much out of their products as they put into them.
I appreciate having the opportunity finally to speak in this debate. I had hoped to be the wrap-up speaker, Mr. Speaker, but I am sure you will be disappointed to know that I am not and that there are many more to come.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that I was able to return from western Canada this morning to offer a few comments on this critical situation. I was in Winnipeg last night and at the meeting 1 attended there were many members of the farming community.

April 30, 1987
1 notice a few of my Tory friends across the way snickering at the fact that the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-West-mount would rise to speak on a farming issue. I would like to register for the record as probably many people in the House can that I in fact grew up on a farm only a few miles from this city. I spent all the formative years of my life on a small family farm in the Ottawa Valley between Cumberland and Orleans. I do not say that to add credibility to the remarks I will make because they will stand on their own merits. I simply say that many of us in Canada come either from farming backgrounds or have roots in farming backgrounds. I believe that fact reminds all of us of the importance of the Canadian farming sector, the backbone of every nation.
Often we tend to be somewhat complacent about farmers. Over the years, Canadians have grown rather accustomed to having good quality food at reasonable prices with little thought given to where that food comes from. The trials and tribulations of the farming sector, when it encounters them, are often forgotten. I hope that if this debate accomplishes anything, and I am not sure it will accomplish much to change the obdurate attitude of the Government, it will raise the consciousness of Canadians as they sit in their living rooms and at their dinner tables across the country reflecting somewhat upon the critical situation currently faced by western grain farmers and likely to be faced by farmers in other sectors as well.
Not many of us know a lot of rich and wealthy farmers. We know a lot of hard-working, dedicated people who love both the land and their occupation. In many cases farms have been in their families for generations. Others had dreams to be farmers and now find those dreams in jeopardy.
When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) spoke some weeks ago in this House he said: "We will spare no effort". He was referring of course to the resolution of the farming crisis in western Canada. You will find at page 5450 of Hansard where our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), in response to his own question of whether the Government of Canada would help the farmers of western Canada, that being the content of telephone calls he was allegedly receiving, said firmly: "Yes, we will help the farmers of western Canada". I ask him: What is the help? Where is the help?
We have grown rather accustomed, as has the Canadian public since the Prime Minister assumed office, to great noble declarations, but we have seen little action to give concrete expression to those declarations. At the risk of sounding cynical, it almost looks as though the way the Government and Prime Minister intend to provide that help is to drive many farmers from their farms. It is rather like the Spanish Inquisition where heretics were burned at the stake so they could move on to a better afterlife. More recently you will recall in the Vietnam War that famous declaration of an Army commander who said that he had to destroy a village in order to save it. Is what we are seeing today the destroying of the
western farming sector in order to save it? That effectively is all we have seen so far.
It is not fair, and I am the first to acknowledge it, simply to criticize a very difficult situation.

It is not fair to criticize without offering alternative and concrete policies to remedy a situation that I, Mr. Speaker, can only describe as disastrous.

What are the problems in the farming sector in western Canada? In fact many of the problems are the same in the rest of the farming community. However, what are the problems that the Government can and should correct? Personally I believe the Government can do a great deal more. The Minister says that no effort will be spared. Let him live up to his word. I have a few suggestions to make.
First, the fundamental problem in the farming sector is the unhappy fact of falling revenue. Revenue has been in a disastrous downward curve. It is falling because of declining grain prices. We then have the convergence of those declining prices on the one hand with increasing input costs on the other. We know that the costs of fertilizer, fuel and labour have increased. An infinite number of costs have increased so as to make that convergence a reality. Most importantly, perhaps, in this current situation, are the financing costs. One of the questions the Government must immediately ask itself if it intends to spare no effort is simply this: How does the Government cushion those input costs, especially financing costs?
I listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) today, a Minister for whom I have considerable respect. He comes out of Manitoba and should know the situation well. I heard him making some declarations about the uninformed rhetoric in this Chamber. He then went on to make some of the most uninformed and stupid comments I have heard in this House from someone who should know better. He focused, for example, on the question of interest rates and went back to 1982.

Yet here we have members of the Government bragging about the fact that the FCC rate is now something in the order of 10 per cent, and it was 11 per cent in the first quarter.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

The Minister of Agriculture says he will spare no effort. I think one effort he should not spare is to walk over and have a word with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). That is not too difficult. There is no reason why the Government should be profiting in its loans to grain farmers during a period when grain prices were slashed 15 per cent to 25 per cent this year after an incredible 19 per cent to 26 per cent drop last year.
Exceptional and critical circumstances require an exceptional response from a Government that accepts its responsibilities. Yet we have had no response. We have had people bragging about the level of the FCC rate, which is absolutely outrageous.
I want to pick up the Minister of National Health and Welfare on another point he made. When we talk about costs and interest rates the real issue is the real interest rate. What is the real interest rate? What is the difference between the Consumer Price Index and the interest rate that anyone is obliged to pay? If we look at the situation in Canada we will find that when the FCC was lending at 11 per cent, the CPI annual rate was 3.9 per cent. That means the real interest rate for farmers was 7.1 per cent. The spread was never that high
during the most critical periods of the recession in the early 1980s.

speechtext: Let me ask a question which I hope the next Tory speaker, if the Government has the courage to put one up, will respond to. Is it an outrageous proposition to suggest that the Farm Credit Corporation, during this critical period, should lend to farmers at the same rate as it borrowed from the Canadian public on Canada Savings Bonds? Is that an outrageous suggestion? I do not think it is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Did you ever do that?

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I am quite prepared to answer those questions in due course, but I ask the next Tory speaker who has the courage to stand to tell me whether that is an outrageous proposition. We are not impotent.
I referred a moment ago to the circumstances of grain farmers in western Canada who have seen their guaranteed prices fall 15 per cent to 20 per cent in the current year, 19 per cent to 26 per cent last year, and who are faced with interest rates at the level about which we are talking. Not one Member on the other side of this House would have to pay such interest rates on a five-year home mortgage yet our farmers are being obliged by the Farm Credit Corporation to pay interest at this level.
You know a lot about business, Mr. Speaker. Do you know any business which does not have an incredible equity base that could survive a 15 per cent to 20 per cent cut in its prices this year and a 19 per cent to 26 per cent cut in its prices last year? Farms which have a very substantial equity base and those which were inherited through generations and have had

April 30, 1987
their capital costs amortized may be able to stagger through this period, but they will not get rich. All of the others that have any loans which they have been encouraged to take over the years by the credit corporation will find themselves faced with foreclosures.
That brings me to another question. Why in the name of God would the Government, given the circumstances which the farming community faces, lift the moratorium on foreclosures at this time? Only a Conservative could answer that question and I hope some of them will if they dare to stand.
This issue does not affect only Canadian wheat farmers. This is our great Canadian heritage, our great Canadian asset. Even the farms which survive this crisis are going to watch their assets erode because they have no available funding to do the important things which are necessary to preserve the quality of the farmland in western Canada.
You are familiar with the salinization problems which are taking place, Mr. Speaker. You know of the soil erosion problems. You are from the Edmonton area and you see it. You know how much of our western soil is blown away each year, and know of the expense of introducing the farm technology necessary to prevent that from happening and to prevent the saline conditions from increasing. These all cost money. The people who lose their farms are in one situation, but the people who stay on their farms do no have adequate resources to do the things necessary to preserve our great natural heritage, our great natural resource, for generations to come.
On the input cost side the Government can act, should act, must act. It can act quickly on the issue of interest payments and by getting rid of the ridiculous notion of introducing foreclosures at this time. It is admittedly more difficult on the revenue side because of the international situation. No efforts should be spared.
I realize I only have a brief moment left to speak, but I am sure I will get unanimous consent to continue because the Members are learning something which they obviously have not known before.
There is an opportunity here to do something concrete. The United States and the European Economic Community can be associated with our major problems. This crisis is effectively being driven by a price war. We know from this month's releases by the Embassy in Washington that the U.S. Trade Bill is once again introducing more measures that will be damaging to Canadian agriculture. For example, the Export Enhancement Program is being amended to expand the number of countries which will be offered U.S. agricultural products at subsidized prices. This has a direct impact on the health and welfare of Canada.
I know I have little time left and I want to make reference to a letter which my colleague, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), today sent to the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). He said that it has been brought to his attention that the Department of
Agriculture has a new agricultural trade subsidy initiative which will include measures damaging to Canada. They are proposing to include, under the Export Enhancement Program, an offer of 1.25 million metric tonnes of barley to Saudi Arabia. As you know, Saudi Arabia is a traditional Canadian buyer. If this is approved by the trade review committee of the U.S. administration it will mean a loss of $75 million to $85 million to Canadian farmers.
Where will this end? The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has said that this is a battle of national Treasuries but the Government has said it cannot afford this fight between Treasuries. What ground will we fight it on? The ground is surely at the negotiating table between Mr. Murphy and Mr. Reisman. Why is this issue not up front? Why is this not the primary item of concern in those negotiations? This is a critical period and we are not told how-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, millions of Canadians who are accustomed to tuning in just about now, especially the good people of Hamilton-Wentworth, may wonder what an MP from southern Ontario is doing participating in a debate on the grains crisis and the lifting of the moratorium on the FCC. It is a monumentally important debate. The Hon. Member for Saint-Henri- Westmount (Mr. Johnston) who preceded me talked about the courage of Tory MPs in getting up to speak. Since this debate began yesterday seven cabinet Ministers, including the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), and 25 Members of Parliament on this side, I being the twenty-sixth Conservative MP, have entered this debate. The Liberals have put up 12 speakers. That is courage. That shows the commitment we have to Canadian agriculture and to the importance of this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I would like to listen to what the Hon. Member is saying. I will listen to all other Hon. Members when it comes their time to debate.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
This is a monumentally important debate on a national issue. It is not just a western Canadian problem, it affects all of Canada's farmers.
I am delighted to be receiving so much attention from the Opposition because it gives me and other Hon. Members an opportunity to put on the record the importance of this debate.
April 30, 1987

1 repeat that it is not just a western Canadian problem, it affects all of Canada's farmers. There are many small family farms in the 650 square miles of my Hamilton-Wentworth area. That is why Members of Parliament from across Canada feel it is important to participate in this debate so that we can put on the record the Government's commitment to agriculture and to all farmers across Canada.
I cannot help but repeat the reference that the Right Hon. Prime Minister made to one of his predecessors, former Prime Minister Trudeau. We were given an example of his attitude from his famous statement that he made when confronted with not dissimilar circumstances. He said, "Well, why should I sell your wheat?" After the former Prime Minister said that, apparently he was confronted by a number of farm leaders who said his statement was giving them a real headache. Mr. Trudeau then said, "What the hell, it may be a headache for you guys but it is not migraine". That was the attitude that the Prime Minister of the day and the Liberal Government of the day took toward the problems of Canadian farmers.
During the 1984 election campaign we promised a 16-point commitment to the farmers of this country. We have delivered on 14 of them. Since 1984 we have pumped $6 billion in initiatives into Canadian agriculture. The Government has given agriculture a priority that is unprecedented. I believe that our record is second to none. Of course, agriculture means about 1.6 million Canadian jobs.
In the recent Throne Speech we promised to spare no effort in seeking to protect the interests of Canada's farming communities in the face of unfair pricing and subsidy practices conducted beyond our borders. I will return to that question because those pricing practices beyond our borders are instrumental to the whole thrust of this debate.
We are providing the largest farm assistance package ever, with the billion-dollar Special Canadian Grains Program which is putting a billion dollars of new money into the pockets of our farmers. I am delighted that almost without exception every member of the Opposition who has spoken in this debate has recognized the importance of that much needed money to western Canadian farmers.
Our Government, led by the Prime Minister, successfully pushed for agriculture to be included in the negotiations under GATT. For the first time agriculture will be on the table. We are continuing to push for a better mechanism for settling agricultural trade disputes with the United States. Those negotiations are continuing as we speak.
We are seeking secure, reliable access for our farm products. The motion passed in the House of Commons on March 16 supports the negotiation of a trading agreement with the United States which will protect our agricultural marketing systems.
Since we came into office in 1984, we have introduced over 400 agricultural initiatives at a cost of nearly $6 billion. That is over one new initiative for every other working day. I think it is worth putting those initiatives on the record so that the
people of Canada understand our commitment to agriculture in general.
We provided $200 billion in drought assistance for the western provinces. We abolished capital gains taxes on the sale of farm land up to $500,000. The House will remember the applause we received across the length and breadth of this country as a result of that move. The NDP voted against it. That iniquitous capital gains tax was imposed on farmers by the previous Liberal Government.
We established farm debt review boards, now operating in every province, assisting financially troubled farmers to come to agreements with their creditors to avoid foreclosure.
Mr. George McLaughlin, chairman of the farm debt review board in Ontario estimates that at least 55 per cent of the cases going to the board are being resolved. That is 55 per cent more cases being resolved, when there had been no hope before.
I think it is important to point out in respect of lifting the moratorium on the FCC that the FCC cannot simply move in and foreclose. The review board gives a stay of proceedings for at least 120 days, which provides some breathing space to farmers who are desperately worried, or worse, when one listens to some of the rhetoric coming from the other side during this debate.
We removed the federal sales tax on farm fuels and exempted farmers from the current excise tax. A rebate program reduced taxes on farm fuel.
A further initiative extended the program to effectively remove all federal sales and excise tax on diesel and gasoline farm fuel until January, 1988. When the excise tax was raised in the 1986 Budget, the exemption was also raised to keep farmers from being affected.
We established an agri-bond program to provide loans at reduced rates to farmers. There was an extension of the small business bond program for two years. Hearings were held on agri-bonds.
A moratorium was placed on FCC foreclosures until programs were operating to assist financially troubled farmers. The lifting of those moratoriums is the subject of this debate, and it is definitely the concern of the Canadian Government to make absolutely certain that through this crisis Canadian farmers are treated with the concern and compassion that any Canadian Government can muster under the circumstances.
An optional shared risk mortgage program through the FCC was announced. A commodity-based loan program was introduced in February, 1986. That rose to $300 million as of April, 1987. The FCC interest rate on five-year fixed term loans is at the lowest level since 1979.
We took action to assist farmers who were locked into high interest FCC loans. A five-year $80-million interest rate conversion program assisting 5,400 FCC borrowers was implemented.

April 30, 1987
Interest rates are at their lowest level in nine years. Every 1 per cent decline saves Canadian farmers $130 million a year.
We moved to expand the PFRA to national farm and forest rehabilitation legislation, to bring new technology into the hands of farmers and rural residents. A Private Members' Motion on the PFRA was referred to a Standing Committee.
National Soil Conservation Week was proclaimed in 1985, 1986, and 1987. Federal-provincial discussions on the PFRA and soil conservation are occurring on a priority basis.
In June last year we established the farm finance boards and the farm debt review boards were functioning by September 1. Many Members have referred to the Canadian Rural Transition Program which was established to assist farmers who choose to leave the farm to seek other vocations. Every eligible applicant has been assisted since September, 1986, and $46.6 million has been spent in the interest of assisting farmers who want to move to other vocations under the CRTP.
Section 31 of the Income Tax Act will be changed to reflect the principles of equity, neutrality, simplicity and certainty.
In applying Section 31, Revenue Canada officials were directed not to limit declared farm losses when farmers, for economic reasons, are forced to take temporary part-time work off the farm. Interpretation and enforcement of the Act has been relaxed to benefit Canadian farmers. We moved to amend the Advance Payments for Crops Act to double cash advance levels. The Act was amended, doubling the size of loans for advance payments back in June of 1985. Legislation was introduced to the PGAPA to enact emergency provisions more quickly and to ensure more equitable treatment.
We moved to amend the WGSA to make it more responsive to the immediate needs of producers. Amendments to the WGSA triggered a spring interim payment of $450 million in 1985, another interim payment of $580 million in 1986 and an even larger payment is expected for 1987.
We moved to establish a National Income Stabilization Program for the red meat sector. Here is where we get to the Canadian Cattlemen's Association news release. It supports tough decisions by agricultural Ministers, and I quote:
The Canadian Cattlemen's Association supports the decision of Agricultural Minister John Wise to end the temporary debt moratorium on debts to the Farm Credit Corporation.
The CCA views debt moratoria as a temporary measure and has never supported its use.
CCA President Stan Wilson emphasized, "Our concern is that the distortions caused by debt moratoria do more damage to the farm credit system than any possible benefit to individual farmers".
Mr. Wilson concluded, "As responsible farm leaders, we must do more than continually criticize these actions and decisions of our Ministers".
I hope members of the Opposition are listening. This fellow makes sense. Mr. Wilson continues:
We need to take more responsibility for contributing to farm policy formation in Canada. It took great courage for both Mr. Wise and Mr. Mayer to make these decisions.
He concludes:
As producers, we recognize that courage, and support the measures taken.
I can point out to my Liberal friends that that is another kind of courage which the Ministers have and which we as a Government are demonstrating.
In the very few moments that I have left let me point out that in establishing the Income Stabilization Program for the red meat sector, we asked that participating provinces engage in tripartite stabilization and produce between two thirds and the three quarters of Canada's hogs, fed beef and lambs. We are working with producers to establish the marketing system they desire. Tobacco producers asked for, and received, enabling legislation paving the way for a national supply management system. A broiler hatching egg agency was proclaimed in December of 1986.
Potato producers are working with the Government on a proposal for the Potato Marketing Agency. Public hearings are being held. A Government motion was passed in March of 1986 that:
This House supports the negotiation of a bilateral trading arrangement with
the United States-while protecting our political sovereignty, social programs,
agricultural marketing systems, the auto industry and our unique cultural
identity.
There it is. The fact is that the Government is on record as protecting Canada's agricultural marketing system.
We are re-establishing a long term dairy policy. A new five-year dairy policy was announced endorsing supply management. That involves $1.5 billion in just over five years. We are protecting producers against injury caused by highly subsidized imports. The Government, as I said earlier, at the initiative of the Right Hon. Prime Minister, has made agriculture its top priority for the upcoming GATT talks. The Prime Minister successfully fought to have agriculture put on the table. The Meat Import Act was invoked in 1985 to halt imports of subsidized EEC beef. Legislative action to ensure the Act can be invoked will be taken if necessary.
Corn countervailing duties were made permanent. Grain corn imported from the United States will have a duty of 84.9 cents U.S. per bushel assessed against it.
Let me conclude by saying I have been around this House, either on the third floor in the Parliamentary Press Gallery, or on the second floor of the House of Commons, since 1959. Unless one goes back to the days of the distinguished former Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) back in 1959, when I came here and watched the Hon. Member in action as the Minister of Agriculture under the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker I do not think one has ever seen Government which has been more committed to Canada's agricultural sector than this Progressive Conservative Government. There is no Ministerial expertise anyone can name in any Government which I have watched since 1959 that can match the concern and confidence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr Mayer). There is no
April 30, 1987

Prime Minister who has demonstrated as much compassion toward farmers or is more dedicated to helping preserve the family farm than the present Prime Minister and the Leader of this country.
This crucial agricultural sector, this sector of the economy, does face difficulties from time to time, just as the energy sector faces bumps as a result of world prices, just as every other sector of the Canadian economy every once in awhile has to ride the roller-coaster of international pricing. However, these crises ride themselves out and I have the utmost faith in the efforts of Canada's farmers, their traditional dedication to the preservation of the family farm, and utmost faith in the realization of this Government that we must be determined to see the family farm through this crisis. We are proud of our record and we intend to build on it.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I listen to the Conservatives speaking, I think of the movie "Back to the Future". All they ever do is refer to the golden years of 1959, the Diefenbaker era and the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) who was Minister of Agriculture. I think they should get Michael J. Fox to be their Minister of Agriculture then they could really go back to the future.
We have been told by the previous speaker that the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is dedicated to agriculture. All I know is that he does pay for his own groceries, although perhaps not for his expenses for renovations to his house or his Gucci shoes. He does pay for his own food and I suppose that is a step forward.
I suppose Hon. Members are wondering why a Member of Parliament from a working class riding in central Vancouver is rising to speak on an agricultural debate. I pose that question before some Conservative Members start heckling me about it. The answer is that my constituents do have to eat so they are concerned about what is happening on the family farm. Second, my constituents consider farmers as fellow working Canadians, and when one kind of working Canadian is in trouble, all kinds of working Canadians are in trouble.
I suppose our audience today and those people watching us here and on television, must be wondering what is going on? Where is Question Period? Where is the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent)? Where is all the action? What is this debate on farming? I was hoping that before he leaves the House the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott), who is the most skilled Member of this House-perhaps not when it comes to debating farm issues but when it comes to imitating politicians-he would entertain us a little with some of his imitations. He is well known for it. He did a good imitation of Mr. Trudeau when he said "Why should I sell your wheat?" Actually, it was a rhetorical question asked by Mr. Trudeau. He said "Why should I sell your wheat?" He then responded "The reason why I should sell your wheat is because ..." I say that to be
fair to Mr. Trudeau, not that we have been in the past or have any intention to be in the future.
I thought that the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth might have entertained us. He mentioned that his Government had done a great deal in the area of farming, and I followed his remarks closely. He mentioned different agencies, red meat agencies and so on. I got lost, I must admit, although I am sure other people were able to follow. I did write down that a broiler hatching egg agency was set up. I give credit for that being done. I thought that the present Prime Minister just laid eggs. However, 1 understand this agency was more sophisticated, it was a broiler hatching egg agency.
I would like to return to the present to indicate why we are having this debate today and why there is not a Question Period taking place. I am a neophyte farmer, although I did have a farm once on Mount Lehman Road, in the Fraser Valley. I see the Hon. Member who represents that region is in his place across the way. It was a 20-acre farm on which we had some-

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Marijuana plants.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
My friend suggests we farmed marijuana plants, which is not true, although I understand that crop is booming where the Hon. Member comes from. We farmed cows and eggs, if one can farm cows. We also had some experience with the tax system as well, which is why we know where it should be reformed.
I want to say where we are at here. As I understand it, and I will try to make this simple so that even a thick-headed person like myself can understand, we have a deepening crisis developing on the Canadian farm, especially over the last two years. There is a grain export subsidy war going on. In other words, the European Common Market, with a market of 312 million people, is subsidizing like mad by giving grants to its farmers. The United States has also started that up. The Reagan administration gave a great many grants to American farmers. Of course, philosophically, the Americans would like the market to handle everything, they being conservatives, but when push came to shove they gave their farmers a heck of a lot of money.
That has caused the price of Canadian grain to drop dramatically. In fact, it dropped 20 per cent in price last year and will drop a further 18 per cent in the 1987-88 crop year. Those figures were announced by the Canadian Wheat Board last week. This is part of the reason we have an emergency debate here in the House of Commons today.
Yesterday, the Government announced that on May 1 the Farm Credit Corporation will begin to foreclose on family farms. The Farm Credit Corporation lends money to farmers. As we all know, farmers in Canada are constantly in debt, borrowing to buy machinery and seed in order to plant their crops. They receive money later when they sell their crops. A

April 30, 1987
moratorium was placed on the corporation by the Government some 18 months ago which prevented the corporation from foreclosing on farmers; that is to say, that the corporation would not go around grabbing family farms. So what does the Government do at a time when grain prices will drop another 18 per cent? True to form, the Government hatches another egg. It got rid of the moratorium on the Farm Credit Corporation thus putting many farmers in a panic.
We in the NDP are calling for, at the very least, an immediate commitment by the Government to provide Canadian grain farmers with a guarantee that total grain receipts for crops being planted now in the 1987-88 crop year will equal those of the 1986-87 crop year. That commitment will cost in the neighbourhood of $1.5 billion to $2 billion.
Members opposite say that the Government is working hard on the international front to bring about peace. Hon. Members will recall that I talked about the European Economic Community and the United States subsidizing their farmers, thus forcing down the price of grain. That creates a problem for our farmers. However, I say this to the Government. Be careful. You may be working hard in this area, but it would be wrong to assume that you are really going to get somewhere by trying to wait out the Reagan administration, which will be gone in 1988, or to wait out the European Economic Community. That is a fallacy because measures have to be taken now.
The view of members of the New Democratic Party, unlike the view of members of the Government who think that it is all a problem with the international community, is that as Canadians we can take measures to do things here in Canada.
I remember well Tommy Douglas, whom I had the pleasure of knowing. He once told me here in the House, where he was a Member of Parliament since 1935, that he stood up in the House day after day and said, "Look, we can put people back to work on the Prairies during the Great Depression. We can do things. We can help the farmers and the workers". Day after day the Government would get up and respond, "Sorry, we cannot do anything". Then Tommy Douglas told me that within 18 hours of war being declared Parliament sat all night and into the next day and enacted a series of measures that helped farmers and the workers to get back to work and so on.
We are not in a war today. That was an extraordinary situation then. The fact is something can be done if one has the will. We in the NDP believe that we can do things here in Canada. We do not have to rely on Ronnie Reagan or on the European Community. We acknowledge that we live in a global village, but we should still try to do some things here at home.
The Government has provided some assistance to prairie farmers. It gave them $1 billion, but look at the way it was done. This is the problem the Prime Minister has. A previous Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, looked smug for saying, "Why should I sell your wheat?" But the present Prime Minister looks smarmy and opportunistic. He gave $1 billion to farmers. Why did he give it? Because the Premier of Saskatchewan
phoned and said, "I have an election going on in which the Conservative Government will be defeated. Please send the money right away". How did he give money to oil producers? By getting rid of the petroleum gas revenue tax. He did not do it right away, as promised. He waited until there was a byelection in Pembina when it looked as if the NDP would win the by-election and, bang, the grant came. Such actions catch up to those who take them. People see this as an opportunistic Government, which is why the Prime Minister's Party is at 24 per cent in the Gallup polls.
The Government has consulted farm organizations. Members opposite have said that. But it does not seem to listen to them. The Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth mentioned the Canadian Cattlemen's Association. Everyone knows that those cattlemen are big ranchers. What about the little guy who owns a small mixed farm and a few head of cattle? He is not represented by that big organization. He does not want to see the end of the moratorium.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Cattle people are all in good shape.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
They are getting money, but not some of the smaller ones. I used to be a cattleman, my friend, as I said, in a minor way, and we used to always complain. Government assistance, though significant, was inadequate. It also came at an opportunistic and awkward time.
We know that the Government says it is fighting the deficit, but there are other ways of dealing with it. It could put in place a fair system of taxation so that it could collect more money, therefore having more to redistribute to save the family farm. Even while the Government provides some assistance with one hand it seems to take away money from farmers with the other through the imposition of increased taxes, service fees, freight rates and a whole host of other direct and indirect costs which must be borne by farmers.
The Government should not lift the moratorium until, first, it announces a deficiency program for the upcoming crop year and, second, until it addresses the broad question of the farm debt, which is about $25 billion, most of which is still held at the high interest rates that came in at the time the Liberal Government was in power.
I have heard members of the Conservative Party criticize the previous Liberal Government. We all agree that it had its faults. But why do we not get on and deal with the present? It seems to me that the Government can do something.
On April 1, 1985, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs tabled in this House a unanimous all-Party report, a report that contained several recommendations that could have been put in place to assist the agricultural community.
The first of those recommendations was that the Farm Credit Corporation be encouraged to write down loans. Nothing happened.
April 30, 1987

The second recommendation was that the Minister consider the issue of agri-bonds. Again, nothing happened.
I believe I heard the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Mr. Epp) speak in the House about the Government implementing agri-bonds. But, when and how have they done that? It simply has not taken place. Certainly agri-bonds would be of assistance. It is something that the Government promised at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan during the 1984 election campaign.
Either or both of those suggestions, had they been implemented, would have alleviated the situation somewhat.

I am trying to be positive. I am merely trying to suggest some action that could be taken.
This morning we listened to the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) speak in this debate. He was the lead-off speaker this morning. However, he stayed in his seat yesterday afternoon, leading to the adjournment of the debate. The Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen took the traditional position of the Government side in this debate, that of defending the Government's record.
I managed to search out some material about what was happening in the Okanagan, and according to that material, he takes a different position when in the Okanagan. On one occasion while in the Okanagan he described the situation as being of crisis proportion, and he went on to say, and I quote: "It is the same story on the Prairies. They have the product, but they cannot get the money for it."
This same article goes on to talk about the Jones family. The Jones family bought a farm for $385,000 in my Province of British Columbia, the beautiful Okanagan. That breaks down to a value of $19,000 an acre. Today, that farm is worth $10,000 an acre.
The article points out that there was a federal Government moratorium on farm foreclosures for a year and a half; but that, even with that moratorium, 44 farmers found it impossible, finally giving up their lands to the Farm Credit Corporation.
I listened to my colleagues from the Prairies talking about suicides and depression among members of the farming community. I had not realized how really bad the situation in that regard was.
One of the articles I have here has to do with how the apple growers of the Okanagan were squeezed out of their markets by imports from Great Britain, the Granny Smith apples. We were even serving these apples here in the Parliamentary Dining Room.
When I first became aware of that program through British Columbia television, I made fun of it. It was almost like Mr. Trudeau saying, "Why should we sell your apples?" But in fact I now realize how serious that situation was. The fact is, the British Columbia apple growers had their product
squeezed out of the market. We in Canada could have consumed Okanagan-grown apples rather than importing Granny Smith apples from the United States.
In this article, Mr. Jones, the farmer of whom I spoke earlier, says that while he may be walking away from his land, he refuses to stop farming. He says that he will lease his property from the Farm Credit Corporation if it cannot be sold, or find some other leased land on which to work. He goes on to say:
We have a few options, but we don't know exactly what we will do. The situation will steer the course. If I were to pick up some property, on lease, I would stay farming. I don't have a lot of control over the situation with our debt, so there is not much point in worrying about it. Anyway, if you are a farmer, you get used to disaster.
One can get some glimpse of what it is like for the farmers to have to face these terrible problems, and the determination that they show.
The question I ask, Mr. Speaker, is, why would the Government at this time end the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loan foreclosures? That, it seems to me, is the worst kind of action to take at this time. It is indicative of the worst kind of logic, and it is typical of the Mulroney Government to be so insensitive and inconsistent.
According to my information, FCC loans in British Columbia number 448, of which 249 are more than two years in arrears, with a total value of $12.6 million. Does that mean that 249 farms are going to be seized? Again according to my information, 60 farms will be immediately affected by the lifting of this moratorium.
My concluding remarks, Mr. Speaker, will be on quite a partisan note. As I go through this 1 invite you to guess who wrote this policy. I am about to read the Executive Summary of a report published in May of 1986. This is something that has become the policy of the Government.
It reads as follows:
The (blank) would recommend:-
And I will fill in the blank once I conclude this portion of my remarks. Once again:
The (blank) would recommend:
-government transition programs involving relocation, retraining, and support;
-farm financial review boards be restricted to an advisory capacity with consideration to be given to borrowers of direct lending or provision guarantees to existing lenders where future turnaround of the operations is deemed possible;
-continued improvement in farm management and financial information be promoted by creditors and government;
-proposals involving income supports, target prices, agri-bonds, subsidized loans and interest rebate subsidies should only be adopted where long term benefits clearly outweigh the costs and where the application of such assistance is clearly targeted to specific objectives and a designated user group;
-no consideration should be given to debt moratoriums or compromises.
This is the policy of the Government. And who wrote it, Mr. Speaker? The Canadian Bankers' Association has written the

April 30, 1987
Introduction of Bills
policy of this Progressive Conservative Government, and they are following it. This Government is in bed with the big banks, as it is in bed with the big oil companies in allowing Amoco to take over Dome Petroleum. It ignores the small Canadian oil companies; it ignores the farmers; it ignores ordinary Canadians.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that a government that does that does so at its jeopardy. It is a Government that will be tossed out by the people at the next election. Unfortunately, that is two years away.
I urge this Government to come up with a real farm policy to assist those who are suffering so much. The Government will find support for such a policy in the cities of this country, on the part of those who consume the food and on the part of the working people who sympathize with the farmers.
