subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason Members in increasing numbers are participating in this debate, whether from rural or urban communities, is simply that we cannot understand why two days ago the Government would announce this rather cruel and insensitive measure to lift the moratorium on farm debt by the Farm Credit Corporation. Many Members got upset because one week after initial grain prices were lowered by 18 per cent, by almost one-fifth, 6,000 farmers who were at risk were put into immediate jeopardy as a result of these two announcements.
We cannot understand these developments. As the Leader of our Party put it in this House yesterday, we want a rationalization of them and we want to have a number of questions answered. As the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) put it yesterday, we on this side of the House believe that we need an announcement now of a deficiency payment sufficient to restore this year's prices to last year's prices and so guarantee to Canadian farmers the same returns as they received last year. That was the first point of our Leader.
Second, we on this side believe that not only must cash flow be maintained so that farmers when they seed, know what to seed and whether to seed, we also believe that the growing credit crunch and the avalanche of debt punishing Canadian farmers should be resolved soon in a meaningful way. We do not find it difficult to imagine that if the Farm Credit Corporation begins to go after certain farmers that that phenomenon will also be adopted as a measure by banks from which farmers have received loans. Therefore it is a measure that is not limited to some 50 farmers a month, which the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) made reference to two days ago in Question Period, it is a measure that could snowball and become a real threat at this time to the farming community.
The situation is one that has distressed us in the Opposition to the extent that I have just described. I submit that the roots of this decision can be traced back to November 1984 when the Minister of Finance (Mr.Wilson) made his statement at that time. Since then, systematically, one after the other, the
Government has managed to alienate, irritate and damage a number of sectors in the Canadian society.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of the laughing Progressive Conservative Member who just entered the Chamber, when the Government attempted to deindex the pensions of our senior citizens. That was one of the many measures tried by this Government since November, 1984. That measure was stopped, but there were others that could not be stopped and have been implemented. For instance, the imposition of the federal sales tax, that hidden tax which has been increased three times since the Government was elected.
It is not just a matter of deindexation of pensions or the imposition of federal sales tax; what about the restrictions imposed on workers who are unemployed and whose benefits will not be paid until certain severance pay and certain pension payments are exhausted? It is not only the unemployment insurance measures or the federal sales tax, you will also recall the constant and systematic increases in another tax, namely, the gasoline tax. Or, if you like, a measure that was just announced a few minutes ago by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the systematic reduction in person-years in the federal Civil Service. This is another form of penalizing the public by way of reduced services to people who need federal services, in any daily aspect of life, from the applicants of Canadian citizenship to those who seek guidance and counselling in our employment centres, to those who apply for immigration, landed immigrant status, reunification, or sponsorship of a family member abroad, those who have to wait for weeks and months before they can be given an appointment.
It is these delays and the slowness of the federal machinery in implementing programs that exist and are approved by this Parliament that are the long-term, slow but inevitable result of measures introduced by the Government. We must see this measure that we are debating now for the second day with understandable outrage within the context of a general policy that the Government announced and somehow forewarned us and the public about way back in November, 1984.
In the case of the farming community, having suffered the reduction of 18 per cent in prices and, while attempting to survive despite that, being given this additional kick with the suspension of the moratorium, we see the farming community in a form of crisis that has been exacerbated by these measures we are debating today.
In essence what is emerging in the farming community, east and west, is a crisis that also includes a phenomenon that has been examined and identified in the last five years twice by Ottawa in a variety of ways. I am referring here to a problem which the farming community has to face and would like to resolve, if given the assistance that it requires by Ottawa, namely, soil erosion.

April 30, 1987
The House will recall that five years ago the Senate Committee on soil erosion produced a report entitled Soil at Risk. That was the first indication of awareness at the federal level of an issue that needs attention in order to facilitate a rather difficult transition problem in the farm community. Chaired by Senator Sparrow, the 1984 report brought up a number of interesting facts. One was that lost income to farmers as a result of soil erosion amounted at that time to $1 billion across the nation. That is an amount that has a staggering impact when heard for the first time.
Two years later, the Science Council of Canada followed up on this study and became preoccupied with the same issue. The Council felt that the farming community needed attention from the Government in Ottawa, in a variety of ways, never anticipating that the kind of measures we are debating today would be in store.
In 1986 when the Science Council reported, it estimated that the loss per year to the farming community by way of soil erosion had risen to the staggering figure of $1.3 billion annually. The Council also attempted to estimate the losses associated with soil degradation per hectare and even to define it in terms of net farm income. The figure the Science Council produced is worth tabling. Its conclusion was that the loss to the farmer per acre in 1986 was anywhere between $20 and $25 and the impact of soil erosion on net farm income amounted to some 38 per cent.
An additional refinement of these studies on soil erosion was conducted in southwestern Ontario. Here it turned out that soil erosion caused a 30 per cent to 40 per cent decrease in corn crop yields. We were told that the loss of one inch of soil could reduce wheat yields by 1.5 to 3.4 bushels per acre. We are dealing with a situation-the roots and causes of which would take some time to define-that, if anything, should demand the intervention of the federal Government in order to reverse a trend and help the economy and the income of Canadians whose livelihoods depend on soil and its tillage.
The studies to which I have referred have pointed strongly to the necessity of soil conservation. Last April, the need for a national strategy on soil conservation was defined at a meeting which included farmers, agricultural scientists, business men, policy makers and environmentalists from all provinces and regions of Canada. They met in Saskatoon to develop a so-called framework for a national action plan for soil conservation.
The most pressing issues limiting the effectiveness of current soil conservation efforts were identified at the meeting. One was production or the lack of environmentally sound and economically viable production systems supporting soil conservation. The second was technology transfer or the lack of co-ordination and the negative perception of conservation as an added cost rather than a long-term benefit. The third was marketing or the lack of strategies to decrease uncertainty of product prices and increase efficiency consistent with sound
conservation practices. The fourth was research or the requirement for increased co-ordination and collaboration among federal and provincial Governments, universities, agricultural colleges, industries and farmers, a role that could be played very strongly and centrally by the federal Government. The fifth was education or the need to create an awareness of conservation among the general public and particularly the young and an increased emphasis on conservation practices for students of agriculture. Finally, there were the environmental effects, or the deteriorating quality of surface and ground water by sediments, nutrients and pesticides that are transported from agricultural land because of poor soil conservation. This must be understood, quantified and become the object of alternative policies as early as possible.
I would like to refer the House to a study conducted by Dr. D. A. Rennie which in 1985 estimated the cost of erosion to farmers in western Canada alone. He came to the conclusion that this amount would be some $440 million. To that he added the loss of organic matter amounting to some $326 million per year, and the cost of salinity amounting to some $212 million, for a total loss to western Canada alone of $978 million per year. This has been translated into 16.7 per cent of operating costs or to some 79 per cent of farmers' net income.
When we approach the question of the economic cost of soil degradation on a province-by-province basis, we come up with interesting figures which add up to a different total but, nevertheless, to a figure that has been worked out with great care, I am told. In British Columbia, the estimated annual economic cost of soil degradation amounts to some $45 million, in Alberta to some $429 million, in Saskatchewan to some $560 million, in Manitoba to some $21 million, in Ontario to some $90 million, in Quebec to some $114 million and in Atlantic Canada to some $23 million, for a total of $1,283 billion per year. As I mentioned earlier, this kind of degradation includes erosion, organic matter loss, acidification, salinity, drainage and compaction.
This over-all picture must be defined within the framework of this debate because it is an added economic crisis faced by farmers at the present time. One would have thought that a Government worth its salt would try to come to the aid of the farmer by realizing that when revenue is declining and there are gluts on the market, this could be the appropriate time for Government to provide certain incentives and economic shock absorbers to facilitate the initiatives required to bring the viability of soil back to where it was decades ago before intensive cultivation took place.
I want to reiterate what the Leader of my Party said in this House concerning the Liberal position in this debate. We want the Government to announce a deficiency payment sufficient to raise the return this year to farmers equal to last year's return. We want the Government to do it now so that farmers have some assurance that when they seed they will receive a
April 30, 1987

return that will cover at least the cost of production. That is a very reasonable position.
In addition, we call for a rationalization of farm debt and revocation of the decision by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to lift the FCC moratorium.
Having said that, I would like to conclude by saying that if this debate is proceeding at the rate it is, with interventions from the most unexpected quarters, and I can assure you that there are not many farmers in the riding of Davenport, it is because we are profoundly upset. We do not understand the logic or politics of this decision. That is why we are rising in increasing numbers on this motion. We feel a strong message has to be sent to the Government on the eve of the Prime Minister's visit to western Canada. We hope that this debate will have some effect and register some messages with him so that next week he will have something to say to the farmers, east and west, which is sensible, humane, and takes into account their incredible economic plight.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate on agriculture. The NDP referred to the urgency of this debate. I think it is high time we gave some recognition to the progress this Government has made in two and half years, compared with what the previous Government was able to do in 20. I also think it is high time we reminded opposition Members and the Canadian public that in two and a half years, this Government has fulfilled more than three quarters of its election promises. Earlier, I heard the previous speaker for the Liberal Party talking about the moratorium that was being lifted. Did it ever occur to them that a moratorium was necessary because of the poor administration of the previous Government, when interest rates for farmers went as high as 16 per cent?
When we came to power we had to deal with this problem. The previous Government never had the courage to face up to the banks and deal with the situation, and say they were going to introduce a moratorium until interest rates got back to levels that were reasonable and acceptable to farmers. During the election campaign, we talked about getting back to an average rate of around 10 per cent.
Well, we did it in two and a half years. We got back to an acceptable interest rate, and it is entirely normal we should consider lifting the moratorium. The Government, however, is not abandoning farmers in the process. On the contrary, it has taken steps to ensure that regional panels will examine, on a case by case basis, the situation of farmers who are in difficulty despite a return to normal interest levels. I am surprised that Members of the previous Government should be demanding reinstatement of a moratorium they never had the courage to introduce.
I am also surprised at the comments of the Member of the New Democratic Party who spoke earlier. In concluding his speech, he said that he could see nothing positive in the Government's actions. Since they are so blind to the obvious, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take advantage of the opportunity
I have been given today to speak to this honourable House, and remind the Hon. Member and his colleagues of what the Government has achieved in the past two and a half years. It has been two and a half years since we came to power, after an election campaign in which we produced a document where our objectives were clearly defined. Nearly 75 per cent of those objectives have been met. I may therefore remind him that if he is looking for positive signs, there are plenty among the achievements I am about to mention.
At the same time, I take great pleasure in greeting our farmers in the riding of Richelieu. During the last election campaign, when I was canvassing door to door and at riding meetings, I found they were desperate and depressed because of the crushing pressures of interest rates and also because of the lack of a long-term dairy policy.
There are 800 dairy farmers in my riding who were looking for this kind of stability. There are also pork producers who were absolutely debt-ridden, and who today are all smiles. There are also sheep farmers and grain producers who were suffering again as a result of falling prices, and who were saved by the billion-dollar subsidy. Once again, this Government has acted responsibly.
The farmers I met last week at a meeting to discuss free trade, among other things, told me how pleased they were with everything the Government had been able to do for them in the past few years because, in 1984, the Farm Credit Corporation rate was 16 per cent.
I may also recall the problems farmers were having as a result of oil prices. In fact, it was the previous Liberal Government which brought down the previous Conservative Government during an historic vote in December, leading to an election that cost taxpayers $105 million, and all because of a promise that the 18 cent increase would be scrapped. And lo and behold, less than six months later, we had an increase of over 65 cents. In fact, our Party admitted during the election campaign that the price of oil was having a serious impact on Canadian farmers. Today, thanks to our Government's action, farmers have had some respite as a result of price controls, a drop in the price of oil and fuel tax rebates, either in the form of income tax rebates or direct refunds.
In 1984, Quebec farm producers were hoping to receive compensation for the 1983 drought. The previous Government had flatly refused to make any compensation payments or even listen to these farmers explain the problems they had in 1983 because of the drought. However, thanks to the new Government's awareness of these problems, millions of dollars were set aside for this purpose. In my riding alone, $1,200,000 in compensation payments were paid in connection with the 1983 drought. I think that can be seen as a very positive measure benefitting Canadian farmers, and especially those in Quebec.
Farmers had been waiting five years for a permanent dairy policy. They got one in less than a year with the Conservative Government elected in 1984.

April 30, 1987
The Liberals set up a Crown corporation, Canagrex, which, instead of helping farmers, has been a constant drag on their budget. Our Government has done a great deal for Canadian agriculture, directly contributing to the survival of many farmers.
I would also like to take this opportunity to say what the Opposition is afraid to mention, and I am referring to all the help we have received.
Signing the five-year policy cost the Government $1.5 billion. It was a commitment that was difficult to meet, in the knowledge that we were embarking on free trade discussions, but we nevertheless wanted to provide guarantees for our dairy producers.
The $500,000 capital gains exemption. This program has made it possible for farmers to sell to their sons or neighbours without having most of their profits taxed away. This program has made it possible for farmers to pass on the family farm to the next generation, something they wanted for many years. The capital gains tax exemption has had an extremely positive impact on the number of young farmers which has increased to twice or three times the number noted in the five or six years previous.
The Opposition was against this measure even before it was introduced, but nevertheless, it has been very successful. The Opposition talks a lot about morality. I suggest we call it political morality, and I think that political morality is reflected in acceptable interest rates. It means helping young people who want to take over the family farm. It also means a drop in the unemployment rate and investors who are investing in Canada as never before. Political morality is not the morality of the individual but the morality of a Party that takes charge and defends the interests of all Canadians by increasing their well-being.
For instance, FCC interest rates which were at 16.75 are now below 10 per cent. And we have all the case-by-case studies to help individual farmers.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) introduced 6 per cent programs for farmers in financial difficulty. Is that not an example of the positive factors the previous NDP speaker was looking for?
We introduced a shared-risk mortgage plan at a rate of 9.75 per cent. These measures had been called for by the Opposition, both by the NDP and the Liberal Party. We implemented these measures and today, they tell us we have done nothing positive. We set up a farm debt review board, and in my riding, a dozen cases have already been dealt with successfully, thanks to this board.
Mr. Speaker, we also introduced a diesel fuel tax rebate. Our farmers had been asking for this for years. It means that now they can get a refund, which will help them cope with their debt load and expand their operations. That was another concept people had been talking about for years, but the previous Government never had the courage to put it into practice.
We have compensated Quebec producers for crop losses, as I said earlier. In my riding alone, producers received $1,200,000. We have signed federal-provincial agreements with several provinces, including agreements worth $35 million with Quebec. Under the previous Government, misunderstandings and petty quarrels about protocol and precedence were the order of the day, and while constitutional debates and those same petty quarrels made the headlines, farmers were left to their own devices. All that changed when this Government came to power, and today, farmers are delighted with programs that are bringing in $35 million more for Quebec. I meet these people every week-end and talk to them in my riding. In fact, my riding has the largest number of dairy producers in Canada: 800 farms. These people say they are satisfied and, in fact, delighted with the attention they are getting from the present Government, which listens to them and consults and lives up to their expectations.
We have given $1 billion to help grain producers, and for the first time, the money has not been funnelled into one specific region. Funds have been spread across Canada, so that for the first time, Quebec's grain producers have received $37 million. This is a first, and it is very gratifying. I met with the mayor of Saint-David on the weekend, and he said that for him and his children, $55,000 meant he would be able to save some of his year's production, and he was very pleased.
Yet this man is not a fanatic nor does he support any particular Party. His objective remark to me: the agricultural producers of the Saint-David region are quite satisfied with the wheat output and the deficiency payments they will be getting.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on like this for a long time since the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) have successfully debated the implementation of 414 agricultural initiatives worth in excess of $7 billion. These are concrete achievements which attest to our sense of responsibility towards the Canadian agricultural community and the fact that we believe that agriculture is one of the key sectors of our economy. It goes to show that we intend to continue working along those lines.
Mr. Speaker, for the first time ever agriculture will top the agenda of the GATT negotiations. Thanks to the intervention of our Prime Minister, for once we will be able to give priority to the agricultural sector at the next GATT summit, proof positive that one of our first concerns over the past two and a half years has been agriculture and the farm community because we wanted to help them get out of the slump into which they had been driven by the previous Government.
Yet the Opposition still finds something to criticize. But what exactly is the agricultural program of the Liberal Party of Canada? What specific solutions do they have to propose? What are the solutions of the NDP-and I am talking about realistic solutions, not dream-like solutions which do not even take into account the Canadian Government's ability to pay?
April 30, 1987

Being more realistic, our Government is controlling the state's budget and expenditures and co-ordinating departmental activities to provide the best services possible at the lowest cost to invest billions of dollars in our agriculture to save our western grain producers, to help our Quebec producers and support our potato producers in eastern Canada. I do not share the opinion of the NDP Member who spoke before me, nor that of the Liberal Party Member who was eager to have the moratorium continued, something his own Government had not had the courage to initiate.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me so much time. 1 hope the Government will continue its good work in the area of agriculture.

Every time that one acre of farmland goes out of production in this country a little bit of Canada dies. That debate continued for two days. Meanwhile, farmers who are experiencing these problems and living on the edge were getting notice that the moratorium would be lifted on May 1. I could just see them watching what Parliament was debating on television and asking what Members of Parliament were doing. What is really important, is it the noose or their livelihoods and their farmlands? It was absolutely incredible that when people are faced with these serious problems Parliament engages in a debate on something that had been decided in 1976. I think that the priorities ought to be rethought in this House and by the Government.

Now is not the time to leave the farmers in a quandary.
I want to make a second suggestion to my colleagues opposite on the Government side. Why does the Government not give the assurance that the farmers will receive the same price for their product this year as they received last year? Why does the Government not give them that assurance? That is reasonable.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS

I think that is what they have asked for. If we ran into some difficulty in our nickel industry in the Sudbury Basin, I would be the first one to argue with the Government to extend assistance, even though I have my biases about multinational mining corporations. Because it involves the economy of the community, I would be the first one on my feet. I urged the Government when nickel prices dropped, to stockpile nickel, in other words, to purchase the nickel the workers produced and guarantee the price so they could continue to work. I argued for the workers in the mining industry, so why would I not defend our brothers and sisters in the agricultural industry? It seems to me that that is the whole concept of solidarity. That is what it means. We are all brothers whether we work in the mines or in the fields. It seems to me that that is an investment which Canadians, and all opposition Members who have spoken, have urged the Government to make. It is politically wise and it seems to me it is one thing which would help the Government to raise its profile in the polls.
That brings me to my last argument. The bottom line is this. If the Government will not do it because it is eminently
reasonable, will it at least do it because it is politically expedient? I give a promise that I will not go out and criticize the Government if they did that. I would not say it is because of political expedience. I would not critize the Government for that. I am prepared to give it credit. I am really appealing to the sense of Canadianism on the part of the Government. I am urging the Government to in fact realize that all Canadians want the survival of their agricultural sector.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I represent an urban riding in Winnipeg-St. James there are many people in my riding who are employed either directly or indirectly by the agricultural industry in Manitoba. I was born in the small country town of Morris, Manitoba, which existed primarily because of the agricultural industry around it. I have many relatives who are farmers. So I am quite aware of the importance of the agricultural industry in Manitoba and in Canada. I am very happy to be able to participate in this debate.

April 30, 1987
I am sure that Elon. Members recognize that the farming and agricultural industry is having difficult times at the moment. The Government of Canada is trying to do something about it, to the best of its financial and physical ability. I would like to comment on the importance of the agricultural industry to Manitoba since, according to Statistics Canada, there are some 39,000 Manitobans who are employed in this industry. It is the third largest industry in terms of employment in Manitoba. As well, it is the second largest industry in terms of dollar value in our gross provincial product. In actual fact, it is the fuel that powers the engine of the Manitoba economy.
Why do I raise these particular items with regard to the importance of agriculture to Manitoba in my comments? During my participation in this debate I will attempt to put before the House the record of the present Manitoba NDP Government, as well as its attitude toward agriculture. I will also put forward our Government's record to date since our election back in 1984.
As Hon. Members know, since our Government was elected in 1984, we have initiated 400 different grants and benefits to Canadian agriculture amounting to approximately $5.76 billion. In the two and a half years that the Government has been in power we have assisted agriculture to the tune of $5.76 billion. To me that shows a great deal of effort in terms of trying to preserve this very important industry.
I would like to remind Hon. Members of some of the programs that have been instituted by the Government. First, I would like to mention the special Canadian grains program, which has been mentioned before. Under that program $1 billion was needed to boost the cash flow of grain producers. Over 80 per cent of this money will go to western Canada. Then, there was the new grains deal that my colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), arranged with Russia. It is a five-year agreement that will see the purchase by Russia of at least 25 million tonnes of grain. We also entered into a new long-term agreement with Brazil which guarantees that that county will purchase between 750,000 tonnes and 1.5 million tonnes of wheat annually between 1986-87 and 1988. I would like to compliment the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette for the efforts he is taking on behalf of our farmers to sell their grain in a very difficult world market-place.
There was also the crop and livestock drought assistance which amounted to some $210 million, $150 million of which went to grain farmers hit by last year's drought and grasshopper damage. Then there was $60 million in drought assistance to livestock producers in western Canada. There was also a record interim pay-out under the Western Grain Stabilization Act of $705 million for the 1986-87 crop year. Last year's total pay-out in this regard was $859 million.
We amended the Western Grain Transportation Act. We rolled the rate back to an average of $6 per tonne while the rate projected by the Liberals was going to be $ 11 per tonne. Another very important program which we introduced was the
commodity-based mortgages program. Commodity-based mortgages will be available at a basic interest rate of 6 per cent with a limit of 13 per cent being placed on them should the price of commodities rise again, which we hope will happen. That limit would only be reached if the price of wheat went from $3 per bushel to $6 per bushel. This is a very progressive and forward-thinking program which was introduced by our Government.
We know also that because of our Government's approach to the finances of the country and its determination to bring the deficit under control, and as a result of our economic guidelines, interest rates have dropped. Under the Farm Improvement Loans Act interest rates declined to 11.25 per cent from the level of 14 per cent on election day. In terms of the Farm Credit Corporation, five-year mortgages have fallen by 3.75 percentage points to 10.75 per cent.
What I would now like to comment on is what the Liberal Government did when it had the chance to try to assist agriculture, particularly with respect to interest rates. I direct these comments in particular to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who stated the other day what the Liberals would do and how. I ask the Hon. Member where he was when interest rates on farm improvement loans reached some 23.75 per cent. Where was the Hon. Member then? He was in the Cabinet of the Trudeau Government.
With respect to interest rates in 1987 the prime rate is 9.25 per cent, while the Farm Credit Corporation interest rate is 10 per cent. There is a difference of 0.75 per cent between the two. In 1981 the prime rate was 22.75 per cent while the rate at the Farm Credit Corporation was 16.75 per cent. There is a difference of 6 per cent between the two. Where was the Liberal Government in 1981?
With respect to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, a very important Act for farmers, the interest rate is 10.25 per cent, which is just 1 per cent higher than the prime rate. What was the interest rate when the Liberals were in power? It was 23.75 per cent. There is a difference of 12.5 per cent between 1981 and 1987. Where were the Hon. Members from the Liberal Party who were members of the Trudeau Government then? Where were they when Prime Minister Trudeau said in Saskatchewan, "Why should I sell your wheat?"
We have seen what the Government has done through the Canadian Wheat Board. It has gone out and found new markets and increased markets in these very trying times. Who really believes the Liberals when they stand up today and say what they will do if they formed the Government? Nobody. I tell Hon. Members that nobody in western Canada would believe them because they proved when they were in government that they did not do anything.
I would like to talk about the present Government in Manitoba, the Government formed by the New Democratic Party, and its attitude toward agriculture. As Hon. Members are aware, I am a member of the finance committee. Today we
April 30, 1987

had representatives from the Economic Council of Canada before us who presented us with the Council's activities for the coming year, as well as the issues and reports with which they will be dealing.
One of the studies-and it is probably one of the key studies that we are going to deal with over the next year-is a study dealing with the future of the prairie grain economy.
This was a study requested by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and it is one that is jointly funded by the provincial Governments and private sponsors and the council itself. Those provinces providing funding are eligible to appoint a representative to sit on an advisory committee to this special report and study.
The Government of Saskatchewan contributed $300,000 toward the study and the Government of Alberta contributed $50,000. What did the NDP Government of the Province of Manitoba contribute to the study? Zero dollars.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Shame!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: So much for the socialists.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The Province of Manitoba is not even represented on the advisory committee, Mr. Speaker. Earlier today I asked Ms. Maxwell, the Chairman of the Council, why it is that the Province of Manitoba is not a party to the study, and the answer 1 got was that it wouldn't contribute $50,000.
That is indicative of what the NDP thinks about the agricultural industry in Manitoba. It will not even put up $50,000.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: So much for the NDP commitment.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Why is it important that Manitoba should be represented? In addition to other things, this study will look at the diversification of the agricultural industry in western Canada, the grain industry in western Canada. Manitoba is leading in the field in this respect. Certain lands in Manitoba that had been used for grain production are now being used for other crops. To give some examples, on these lands there is now grown black beans, pinto beans, and peas. In addition, we have two potato plants in Manitoba, Carnation and McCain's, and McCain's wants us to grow peas and carrots. We are growers of grain for ethyl alcohol. We have an ethyl alcohol plant in Minnedosa. And, of course, we have our sugar-beet industry.
The Province of Manitoba should be represented on that advisory committee. It should be part of that study. Those conducting the study itself will be presenting their recommendations to the advisory committee, and that committee will thus have an input in terms of the direction the final report will take and its conclusions.
The Government of the Province of Manitoba has said that it has not got $50,000 to give to that study; that a seat on that advisory committee is not worth $50,000. That tells me that
while the NDP Government makes promises about assisting agriculture, it doesn't do anything about following up on them.
What about our sugar-beet industry in Manitoba? What does the NDP Government of Manitoba think about sugar-beets? There is the opportunity for the Government of the Province of Manitoba to enter into a jointly funded program with the sugar-beet producers that would cost the Government approximately $2 million over five years, or $400,000 per year. This annual funding of $400,000 a year would go a long way toward helping the sugar-beet growers in Manitoba, not to mention the sugar-beet plant that is located in the riding of the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry.
And what is their answer? They refuse to enter into that agreement. If they were to enter into that agreement, thus keeping the sugar-beet industry going in Manitoba, that same Government would receive in taxes from the trucking industry alone $200,000 annually. That is the approximate revenue that would be returned to the Government through fuel taxes and income taxes. In addition, the Manitoba Sugar Company would be paying to the Government $550,000 in taxes. In other words, for an expenditure of $400,000 to save this industry, the Government would be receiving in revenue $750,000. And yet, it has refused to participate.
That attitude prompts me to ask where that Government's policies in support of agriculture are. It is for that reason that I say what we are seeing during the course of this debate is hypocrisy. Who is to say that the federal New Democratic Party would not have the same attitudes toward agriculture as is exhibited by the Manitoba NDP Government. The NDP Government of Manitoba in the last election promised to assist the agricultural industry in Manitoba. We have seen how it has assisted agriculture. It is not doing anything.
We cannot believe the federal New Democratic Party. We know how closely tied it is with its provincial counterparts. How can we believe that it would do anything different if it were to form a federal government-heaven forbid!-than the NDP Government of Manitoba is doing. That Government will not even pay $50,000 to help out the grain farmers of Manitoba or of western Canada. It will not put up $400,000 a year to assist the sugar-beet industry, notwithstanding that it would receive, in return, $750,000 in revenues. It is a Government, Mr. Speaker, that is obviously not interested in agriculture at all.

As is indicated by the number of programs we have instituted since forming the Government, we want to see the agricultural industry thrive and grow. We have indicated, through action, that we do have concerns and that we are prepared to provide assistance, and we shall continue to do so, Mr. Speaker, for however long we form the Government of this country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this emergency debate with regard to the plight of the Canadian farmer. Needless to say, the farmer in Canada is in a desperate situation. Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, the very future of the Canadian farmer is in jeopardy, mainly due to the inaction of this particular Government.
Canadian farmers are in deep trouble, and the response of this Government, this Progressive Conservative Government, has been totally inadequate.
Over the last several weeks, the Government of Canada administered to the farm family in Canada a double whammy. First, the Government, through the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), announced that there would be an 18 per cent decrease in the price of wheat
over last year. As you know, Mr. Speaker, that comes on top of a 20 per cent decrease that occurred last year.
In 1984-85, the price per tonne for Canadian wheat was $170. In 1986-87, the price of that same tonne of Canadian wheat had been reduced to $130. Today, Mr. Speaker, the price is $110 per tonne. The price of barley in 1984-85 was $125 per tonne; in 1986-87, $80 per tonne. This year, Mr. Speaker, it is at $60 per tonne-less than half of what it was two years ago. We have had the price of wheat go from $170 a tonne in 1984-85 to $110 per tonne this year.
The Canadian farmer, the Canadian farm family, is in jeopardy. In effect, the very heart of our nation is being pierced by the inaction of this particular Government.
First it reduced the price of grain. If that isn't enough, on Monday of this week, the Government announced that it would be lifting the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation mortgage foreclosures. A double whammy, Mr. Speaker. The price of grain plummets because of the policies of this Government, and then it turns around and lifts the moratorium on farm foreclosures. As a result of the lifting of the moratorium on FCC mortgages, up to 6,000 farms are immediately subject to foreclosure by the Farm Credit Corporation, and another 10,000 farms are in jeopardy.
One might ask why the Government decided on Monday to lift the moratorium. What message is the Government of Canada, through the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), giving to the farmers of Canada? The message is clear and obvious. The Government of Canada does not care. Is it any wonder, given the inaction of the Prime Minister of Canada and given the inaction of the Government, that the Prime Minister is the Leader of the least popular Government in Canadian history? It is not surprising.
Is it any wonder that the Hon. Member for Edmonton- Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), a Conservative Member of Parliament from Edmonton in western Canada, found it necessary to criticize the Government of Canada? He found it necessary to criticize the integrity of the Prime Minister because of the inaction of the Government regarding the problems existing in western Canada. Notwithstanding the very serious difficulties being faced by farm families in Canada, this Government, for no explicable understandable reason, decided to lift the moratorium and basically drive off the land 6,000 more farm families, with a potential of driving off 16,000.
The Prime Minister, wearing his famous Gucci shoes, blessed the House of Commons with one of his very rare appearances during this debate. What did he say to the House and through the House to the farmers in western Canada? He said precious little, but he did say:
When western Canada asks for help, to the extent humanly possible-
And then his voice deepened:
April 30, 1987

-Brian Mulroney and the Government of Canada will say, "Yes". We are
there to build a stronger western Canada and to build a stronger Canada.
The farmers in western Canada are on their knees begging the Government of Canada to come to their assistance. The Prime Minister says all you have to do is pick up the phone and call.

So, pick up the phone, call 992-4211 and ask for Brian. Tell him, because he does not seem to understand exactly what is happening in western Canada to the family farm. He says that the Government of Canada is acting in the best interests of western Canada and in the best interests of farmers in western Canada. He invites the farmers to call and ask for help. The farmers do not have to call. If this Prime Minister was doing his job, he would understand what is happening on the family farm. How often has the Prime Minister, wearing his $700 silk suits and his Gucci shoes, visited western Canada?

Our Leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), has gone there at least 32 times over the last two and a half years to talk to western farmers to understand what the difficulties are. The Prime Minister says he is going out next week to see exactly what is happening.
One would have thought that the Prime Minister would understand and that his western Members of Parliament would explain the very serious difficulties for the western farmers. We know that the western Conservative Members of Parliament have done absolutely nothing. They sit in the House here as bench warmers. They applaud the Government. They applaud the Prime Minister when the situation back home is desperate. Why have the Conservative Members of Parliament not explained to the Prime Minister the very serious difficulties that exist in western Canada, the very serious difficulties facing farmers?
For example, have western Conservative Members of Parliament explained to the Prime Minister that 9.9 per cent of farmers in Alberta are insolvent as of January 1, 1987? Have they explained to the Prime Minister that 11.4 per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan are insolvent, and that a further 28.3 per cent of the farmers in Saskatchewan are having cash flow difficulties? Have they explained to the Prime Minister that 18.3 per cent of the farmers in Manitoba are having cash flow difficulties? It is obvious, Mr. Speaker,
that they have not. It is obvious that western Canadian Conservative Members of Parliament, with the exception of the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona, have done precious little.
We in the Liberal Party recognize the difficulties facing western Canada and, in particular, the western Canadian farmer. We in the Liberal Party are prepared to take the necessary action to ensure that the farmers in western Canada will be given the opportunity to continue a way of life that has existed since the very birth of our country. Our Leader, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, has made some very basic requests of the Government. First, it is important and incumbent upon the Government of Canada to immediately announce that it will continue the moratorium with respect to FCC mortgages. Now is the time to do it.
I must say at this point that it is somewhat ironic that on Monday the Government should announce that the moratorium would be lifted. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Monday was the day that the Government decided to start debate on the death penalty. What this Government in effect is doing is condemning the Canadian farmer to death. This Government ought to be condemned for its inaction to the plight of western Canada. We have said continue the moratorium. Now is the wrong time to lift the moratorium. It is important that there be some stability, some assurance from the Government of Canada that it will assist the farmer through these difficult times and by lifting the moratorium, the Government is sending the wrong message.
We in the Liberal Party have said, as well that the Government ought to guarantee to farmers immediately, now, as they are about to seed for the upcoming crop year, at a bare minimum the same return that the Canadian farmer received last year in order to assist the farmer to know when to seed, what to seed or whether to seed at all.
The farmers in western Canada are in a state of flux. They do not know what to do with the price of grain as it is today and with ail of the other factors. They do not know whether they should plant a crop at all this year. We know, with the reduction in the price of grain by the Government, that a great number of farmers will be barely recovering the costs involved in carrying on with their farms. First, the Government should continue the moratorium. Number two, it should announce that farmers will be guaranteed the same returns they had last year.
As well, it is important that the Government announce that there will be a deficiency payment this year. We know that last year the Government announced a deficiency payment in the neighbourhood of $1 billion. One must ask, of course, what prompted the Government to provide that assistance to western Canadian farmers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Toronto Member, I am very pleased to be taking part in this emergency debate. I think it is important for those of us who live in cities, do not grow our own food and depend on agriculture to show our support in this real crisis that is being experienced.
I happen to represent a riding in Toronto, Broadview-[DOT] Greenwood, which was in its origin as a European settlement an agricultural area. It was a farming area that supplied food to the City of Toronto, across the Don River. That, of course, was back in the old days when the Don River itself teamed with Atlantic salmon in the appropriate seasons. Now as an industrial and manufacturing centre, we largely depend on the agriculture of the west and the vitality of that agricultural sector is of course extremely important to us as consumers and of course to the entire Canadian economy.
I recently spent a week in western Canada. When I was in Edmonton and Calgary, I saw the plight of the people there who are particularly concerned about the petroleum industry. There is despair, confusion and anxiety as people contemplate their future with falling prices in that sector. From Alberta, I went on to Regina and Winnipeg where I found despair, anxiety and uncertainty about the future that was much more profound. There was a real desperation and a sense of crisis in Regina and Winnipeg over the matter we are debating today.
We know that grain prices are falling. In the case of wheat, there has been an 18 per cent drop on top of a 20 per cent drop, an absolutely staggering drop for farmers to have to face. The question one must ask is why this is and if this has been caused by some fault of the farmers. Are they not being productive? What has gone wrong? Why are farms failing? Of course, we know that it is not due to lack of hard work, effort, skills and productivity. It is simply a question of international markets which are entirely beyond the control of individual farmers.
We know how the political system works and we know that there are massive subsidies for agriculture in the United States and the European Community. The result has been, of course, expanded production there and falling prices on the world markets. This is occurring because those countries see agriculture as being very important and they have ensured that their own farmers will be able to compete and to continue in that way. It is absolutely important for their own economies. Those countries are very clear about the economic, social and political consequences of farm failures. They have massively
subsidized that sector because they want to keep production up. The result, of course, is this enormous instability which our own farmers face, so far without any concrete, adequate solution proposed by the Canadian Government.
Yesterday morning, I listened to the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Of course, it was a speech long on rhetoric. My goodness, I heard such free-flowing phrases of sympathy. The crocodile tears. The commitment in his heart to the west. However, the speech was totally bereft of any practical assistance, as was the Prime Minister's response and that of various Ministers when our Party raised these questions in the House.
One of two particular measures we have advocated, the moratorium on FCC foreclosures, was lifted on Monday. The response from the Government was that a moratorium has to come to an end some time or another. The question is when and why at this time of acute crisis? The moratorium was introduced for a very good reason and the situation remains the same. If you introduce a measure because of need, you should not withdraw the measure until the need has been met. We know that is not yet the case.
The other most pertinent issue is the question of deficiency payments. We have had an important deficiency payment, but we do not have any guarantees concerning what farmers will be given for this crop year. They are seeding without any expectation that they will be able to recover their investment. We call for at the very least an immediate government commitment to provide Canadian grain farmers with a guarantee that total grain receipts for crops being planted now will equal those of the 1986-87 crop year. That is, $1.5 to $2 billion.
Unfortunately, the Government response has been simply to cloud the issue and to suggest that farmers are now getting cheques in the mail. Those cheques are for last year's crop and it was a very poor payment, thanks to falling international prices. One of the purposes of this debate is to put the heat on the Government, remind it of the urgency of the situation, and see if we can get a firm commitment for practical measures.
The Government has not totally ignored this question. It has made some gestures. It seems to be aware up to a point. It is working on the international front to try and bring some stability to grain market prices. It has provided assistance to the farm sector through these payments which have only recently gone out. It has consulted farm organizations. Yet government policy on consultation seems to be, yes, Government listens, Ministers listen, meetings are held and organizations are called in for consultations, but what the organizations say is not translated into action. It is not implemented. So we have a pseudo-consultation, a process of listening, but it does not lead to respect for the proposals or their implementation.
Even while Government has provided some assistance on the one hand, it has been taking it away with the other. The

April 30, 1987
Conservative Government has increased taxes that farmers, as do other Canadians, have to pay. It has increased service charges, freight rates, and of course a host of other direct and indirect taxes. The Government should not lift the moratorium on FCC foreclosures until it announces a deficiency payment program for the upcoming crop year and until it addresses the broad question of farm debt. Of course that is an enormous amount, something in the order of $25 billion across Canada. Much of that debt is still subject to very high interest rates. The Government must let farmers know where they stand now.
The crisis is growing. It has been developing over the last couple of years. Its effect on farmers has been devastating. We are beginning to get a lot of information about what it means for farm families and farm communities. Doctors are telling us that their farmer patients are coming in with more troubles than they have ever had before. We know more are going to psychiatrists. We know there have been more suicides as a result of despair. People are unable to sleep or even relax. They are constantly worried. They have no relief from those worries. The economic burden they bear is tough on the entire family. We as Canadians have to be extremely sensitive to this. We are one family together and when one region of the country is hurting as badly as this, we have to be extremely concerned.
I note that a professor at Brandon University reported to a committee on this issue with some absolutely dire statistics concerning stress. One in two farmers in the sample studied reported feeling chronic fatigue, frequent trouble in relaxing, forgetting things, and losing their tempers. One in three farmers experienced serious disruptions in sleep patterns, increases in family arguments, back pain, trouble in making decisions, frequent headaches, and deteriorating health. They also noticed increasing behavioural problems in their children.
These are the absolutely devastating effects of this situation on the people who have to face it. The suicide rate for farmers in Alberta is going up. A Canadian Mental Health Association study in Saskatchewan found 88 per cent of those surveyed said they experienced stress-related symptoms, including health problems, headaches, fatigue, insomnia, depression, anger and frustration. In some cases there was alcohol abuse. Suicide is the number one cause of death on farms in Ontario after machinery accidents. Suicides are one-third higher for farmers than the rest of the population. We are dealing with a group which has traditionally been considered the most problem-free, the one with a better, healthier life-style without the so-called stresses of urban life. Now we see the situation reversed. People who live on farms and who have to face these enormous financial burdens are under far more stress than city people. I think we should be much more sensitive to that problem and I wish the Government would take this as a real sign of crisis and begin to respond.
We have had communications, representations, proposals and recommendations from numerous people working in the agricultural community. Let me just refer to a couple which I think are particularly significant.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool believes that the rural way of life and related service industries is in jeopardy. They ask Members of Parliament to recognize the critical economic situation confronting western Canadian families and communities. This crisis has far-reaching social and economic implications for the whole national economy as well as for the west. They recommend that programs be immediately developed through federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in a productive capacity, and that early consideration be given to the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for this crop year. Government should continue its efforts to restore sanity in the international grain market. Those are obviously very eminently reasonable proposals to be making. I am sorry that those proposals have not yet been acted on.
Keystone Agricultural Producers from Manitoba is another organization writing on behalf of the farmers of Manitoba with a number of similar very concrete proposals. They call upon the Government to announce, as soon as possible, its intention to introduce a program for this year's crop similar to the Special Canadian Grains Program of last year, with support levels at least equivalent to those under the 1986 program. I will not go into the details, but they are asking that they get at least the same kind of support they got last year in order to sustain them.
A second important step should be bold new initiatives through the Farm Credit Corporation to save thousands of commercial farms from insolvency. There should be new loan funds at affordable rates and the FCC should be a full service lender. I am sorry to say that instead of bold new initiatives, we see the lifting of the moratorium on farm foreclosures.
I am extremely disappointed with the response of the Government which is big on rhetoric, talks about its sympathy, wants to blame other people, previous governments, other governments and markets in the world economy, and yet is not willing to do the things which are within its power to do. There is no doubt that there are long-term solutions to be developed. There must be a long-term solution suitable to the politics of what is happening in Europe and the United States. However, in the meantime there are short-term solutions within the power of the Government. I call upon the Government to act now to deal with the immediate crisis facing agriculture in the west.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Under the legislation introduced by our predecessors and enacted here a few years ago, the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Canadian Transport Commission has to announce by April 30 each year what the freight rates will be for grain in the following crop year. The next crop year, as our western representatives here well know, will commence next August 1. The Canadian Transport Commission must announce the freight rates for the movement of grain in accordance with the formula and stipulations laid down in the Western Grain Transportation Act.
Unfortunately, it therefore announced this afternoon that the grain farmers' share of the rates to be received by the railways for the next crop year will increase from the $5.97 which they are paying in the current year to $8.32 per tonne in the next crop year. The mathematicians among us will realize that that is a 39 per cent increase, a very large increase in the producers' share of the cost.
In 1984-85, which of course was the last year in which our predecessors were in Government for the majority of the year, the total freight rate for the movement of grain was $25.32 of which the Government share was $17.62. At that time the shipper paid $7.70 as the producers' share of that rate. When we came into office three years ago, the producer had to pay $7.70 per tonne of grain moved. In 1985-86 the total freight rate was $28.03 of which the Government paid $22.03 and the shipper paid $6. That, of course, was the year after we came into office.
In the present crop year, 1986-87, the total freight charge is $30.94, of which the Government contributed $24.97 and the shippers contributed $5.97. That rate was calculated last year based on the estimated amount of grain to be moved in the then coming crop year. As it happens, there was an underestimation last year and a great deal more grain has been moved in the present crop year than was anticipated. Approximately 34 million or 35 million tonnes of grain will be moved through the system in the present crop year. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) points out that that is a record.
In June, 1985, the Government amended the original Western Grain Transportation Act to include a ceiling on the producers' share of the freight rate at $7.70 per tonne for the
crop year 1985-86 and the present crop year and replacement of the former rate-setting mechanism with a new tally system.
Action was taken by the Government to ensure that a ceiling of $7.70 would not be exceeded for the last crop year or the present crop year. However, we are now faced with the situation that under the formula in the legislation the producers' share in the forthcoming crop year will be $8.32 per tonne. The Government has acted immediately because the present circumstances of our grain farmers are extremely unfortunate. There has been a decline, as we all know, in the prices they are receiving. The Government has acted in order that this increase will not have to be absorbed by the farmers. We will contribute $2 per tonne in the crop year starting August 1 to that increased cost to the producer.
The over-all cost of that increase in the freight rate was estimated to be approximately $74 million. The government assistance of $2 per tonne based on the estimate of the movement next year of 31.8 million to 32 million tonnes will likely cost the Government $64 million. Therefore, rather than a 39 per cent increase in the producers' freight cost, the actual increase will be in the area of 5 per cent.
It is a disappointment that there are only two people left on the opposition benches, one NDP and one Liberal. I know I am not supposed to comment, but it is so shocking that I cannot forebear to comment on the intense interest being shown in this subject.

April 30, 1987

The Minister of Agriculture, the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board and I certainly deplore the terrible fact that world grain prices are about half what they were five years ago. But certainly the program that we announced today will help the farmers with the cost of moving their grain.
We know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board are doing all they can to initiate discussions among the nations of the world most involved in the export of grain to attempt to get some rational approach to the problems that are facing grain producers around the world.
Discussions are continuing with farmers and provinces about the economic situation facing our grain farmers. I have no doubt that this will not be the last of the measures that will be announced by the Government for the assistance of farmers and agriculture during our term in office.
I have not had the opportunity to listen to the whole of this debate, but I am certain it has been remarked that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) has been very busy in Japan in recent days attempting on behalf of the Prime Minister to get the world grain exporters to deal with their problems. I suggest it must be admitted by anyone who is fair and makes any pretense to fairness or impartiality, that no group of people in the world could be doing more to assist the agricultural area and their own grain farmers than the Government of which I am happy to be a Member.
