subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel somewhat like a jack-in-the-box. I got up and down about six times on these points of order. Shall we try it a few more times?
1 was quite astonished to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) say we cannot control the world price of grain, but he went on to say that we can control the programs which are under our control. That makes a lot of sense, of course. He then listed a whole series of programs the Government has instituted presumably to assist farmers. However, he did not mention science and technology or research and development, which is one of the major failings of the Government. That is something for which the Government could do more for the long-term interests of Canadian agriculture and the Canadian farmer than any one of the other measures the Minister mentioned. I would like to refer to aspects of the question of research and development in my comments. Before I do so, I want to say a few words about the moratorium on farm foreclosures, the question of the Farm Debt Review Board and the possible debt restructuring program.
These measures, as 1 say, I regard in many cases to be temporary palliatives. I think what we have to spend a bit of time on in this House is addressing the long-term solutions, not the band-aids and not the half-baked measures taken by the Government in its two and and a half years in office.
What has precipitated the current debate, of course, is lifting the moratorium on farm foreclosures which has been in effect for the past 19 months. In this period, interest rates have come down, according to the Government, and that is the reason for lifting the moratorium on farm foreclosures. It has been pointed out to me by my colleague, our critic for agriculture, that real interest rates today are higher than they were in 1984. Of course the moratorium itself is nothing but a shortterm solution.
Another short-term solution is the Farm Debt Review Boards. If we look at the statistics and at the facts, we see this mechanism has not been functioning well. In Ontario, I understand there are some 400 cases which have been considered by the Farm Debt Review Board. Agreement was reached in some 195 cases but only two agreements were actually signed. I look with particular interest at the question of the Farm Debt Review Boards because I served on the committee on agriculture two or three years ago in the last Parliament which studied Bill C-653, the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act. You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that this Bill was proposed by a former colleague of mine, the former Member of Parliament for Lambton Middlesex, Mr. Ralph Ferguson.

April 30, 1987
The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act attempted to bring back a procedure that existed in the 1930s and which would allow a farmer to apply to a court for a restructuring of his debt. In the first instance, the farmer would be entitled to apply for a moratorium for a stay of proceedings, if you will, to stop his creditor from proceeding with a foreclosure. The court would be empowered to give the farmer a period of time in which to reorganize his affairs to seek alternative financing. In addition, I believe one of the features of that particular legislation was that the courts in certain extraordinary circumstances had the ability to write down debt.
The Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act was an attempt to come up with a viable permanent solution of which a farmer could avail himself. He would not have to seek a privilege, if you will, or go before a Farm Debt Review Board and try to get the co-operation of the banks. He could actually have a legal recourse which would be binding, of course, if granted by the court.
We got no action from the Government with respect to setting up this type of legally-binding mechanism. Indeed, there has been no action through legislation, specific legislation such as the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act, or through amendments to the Bankruptcy Act. A procedure of this nature would introduce into Canadian law, or bring back into Canadian law, a procedure which exists in the United States. It is not something which is totally unknown or new in the United States.
Under the Bankruptcy Code of the Americans, I believe Chapter 11 of the Code, the owner of a business can ask for the protection of the court and be given a period of time to rearrange his activities, provided, of course, that there is some opportunity to continue a viable business and provided that the owner of the business convinces the court that his plans are viable or have some semblance or hope of success. That is a right under the law; it is not a voluntary arrangement.
1 am sure that most Members of Parliament who have had contacts with businesses which have experienced financial difficulty from time to time understand the importance of having this type of provision in law. I am familiar with a number of businesses which have experienced financial difficulties due to extraordinary circumstances such as market conditions, the 1982 recession, or, say, problems in the steel industry, for argument's sake.
In such cases the creditors, banks in most cases, acted hastily. Bankers panicked. They called the line of credit. They pulled the plug on the company. Very often the owner of the business does not have the opportunity under the law to fight back. I am aware of circumstances in which owners of businesses have had to come up with extraordinary means in order to get the trustees out and in order to maintain a viable business. So it is absolutely crucial that this type of a mechanism be introduced into law, a mechanism which would apply to all businesses and not just to farmers. Of course, the
situation of farmers requires some further assistance, further programs, and I would like to refer to the idea of debt restructuring in particular.
In that respect I am sure that Members of the House are now familiar with the ideas of the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Mr. Garf Stevenson, who in a memo of March 13, 1987, which was sent to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on April 28, suggested that the Government consider a program of debt restructuring. In his memo Mr. Stevenson states that what he has been suggesting is the:
-need to join in developing a method by which farmers with significant debt could temporarily relinquish title to some of their land while perhaps retaining title to the home quarter. The farmer would continue to operate the land under some lease arrangement. The producer hopefully would have the right to retain title at a later date by repurchasing the land or paying out the accumulated debt.
This type of solution obviously merits the immediate consideration of the Government so that some form of debt restructuring program can be introduced in short order.
At this point in my comments I would like to deal with the question of research and development which I do not think has figured too prominently in the debate up to now. In my comments I will try to be positive and appropriately critical. I know that Members of the Government say that opposition Members have nothing to say other than to criticize and, indeed, that we engage in debate for purely dilatory purposes. I would like to inject somewhat of a different tone and respond to those comments by making some remarks which I believe can be taken in a positive light.
As I said earlier, the Minister of Transport threw up his hands and said: "We cannot control the world price of grain". But he did not comment on the promises that were made by the Government prior to the last election in terms of research, promises which have been abandoned by the Government since taking office. We are all familiar with Canada's poor record when it comes to research and development. As the recent round table report of the Canadian Advanced Technology Association reminded us, we do things by halves in Canada. We do half the research and development. We have half the number of scientists and engineers, and I think that is being somewhat generous. We have half the investment and half the jobs. Prior to the last election the Tories promised to double spending on research and development. However, since taking office they have cut practically every form of assistance to research and development.
On a trip to western Canada last November, and I was back again in Manitoba for the high school science symposium in February, I visited a company in Winnipeg by the name of Hi-Qual Manufacturing which has developed a process to treat feed grains with anhydrous ammonia. The company has developed a machine-and I am reluctant to call it a machine, perhaps it might be better to refer to it as a contraption although that would not be doing justice to it either-which will automatically pick up a bale of hay, wrap it in plastic and treat it with anhydrous ammonia. This ammonia treatment swells and breaks down the outer lining or husk of the grain
April 30, 1987

and adds protein to the feed. The purpose of the treatment is to produce a better feed, which in turn produces a healthier animal.
It is calculated that this can lead to a 20 per cent to 40 per cent savings in feedstock costs in an average year. In addition, it increases the digestability of the grain, thus permitting better finishing or fattening, with the result that the cow-calf operator will be able to raise the cattle himself rather than shipping them elsewhere.
This particular procedure costs $250,000 to develop, and its development came with remarkably little assistance from Government. Under the Industrial Research Assistance Program of the National Research Council, the developing company received some $14,000, enabling it to improve its communications and understanding of the technologies in other parts of the world.
It is forecast that this treatment will enable this company to obtain 5 per cent of the total forages market. Just to obtain a 5 per cent market share would require some 3,600 units operating at full capacity. That represents an investment of $60 million-and that is just the cost of manufacturing the equipment.
This kind of development in agriculture only results from an investment at the front end in research and development. There are many other examples I could refer to, such as Export Packers in Winnipeg, a company in the egg processing industry. That is a company that has developed a technology to extract enzyme from eggs, dramatically increasing the value of the ordinary chicken egg.
A study by the Food Sciences Department of the University of Manitoba observes that the potential for similar products is enormous. The problem, of course, is that we are not doing enough research and development in Canada. We are not doing nearly enough. We are only doing half of what our competitors are doing. We will not solve some of the desperate problems facing the agricultural industry, and our other industries, if we do not get more serious about research and development. We have to understand that in research and in science lie the beginnings, if you will, of the answers to some of the economic problems that we face.
I would hope that the Government, in considering the solutions to this crisis, would begin to address the question of research and development, and in doing so I urge it to remember the promises that it made during the 1984 election campaign.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion that we are addressing does indeed reflect a serious situation, not just for Canadian agriculture, and especially the growers of grain and oilseeds, but also for the suppliers of farm equipment, agricultural chemicals, as well as for the transportation sector and even the energy sector. In other words, Mr. Speaker, this debate involves not just one sector of our society
but indeed every Canadian in virtually all areas of this great country. It is a social as well as an economic debate. The future of the Canadian family farm is not something that can be decided solely on economic terms.
Our farm families have come to mean much more to us, and to most Canadians, than simply being the providers of various commodities. These families also represent a way of life which is desirable for many Canadians, and is indeed a way of life which many of our young people aspire to for themselves and for their children.
I am not saying that farming is an easy undertaking. Nothing could be further from the truth. In fact, like many of the Hon. Members of the Progressive Conservative Party, it was my privilege, and my responsibility, to farm in southern Ontario, along with my husband and our two children. And, Mr. Speaker, I can personally assure you that, compared to my experience in the business world, farming is far tougher in its demands. Farming makes it easy to go broke.
I do not know of any other area in small business where one must try to survive by buying retail and selling wholesale. I do not know of many other businesses where the determination of the price of the product is so totally out of the producer's hands, or where the rate of return on equity can fluctuate so dramatically from season to season.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, these incredible Canadian families persevere. They continue against these substantial odds. I say that these families deserve our admiration and our respect, for these families represent the values that we most respect in our society-values that include hard work; values that include determination; values that demonstrate a love for, and respect of, our environment; values that find their reward in benefits that could never be appreciated by those who measure success solely in monetary terms.
In dealing with the farm families of Canada, we are not dealing with people who wish to become rich, with people who wish to make a killing at the expense of the taxpayer; rather, we are dealing with people who want to perpetuate a way of life-and the survival of that way of life may ultimately mean more to those of us who inhabit the urban sprawl than to these farm families themselves.
I have heard statements from all Parties in this House about the need to protect and preserve our Canadian cultural identity. That identity comes from our backgrounds, from our roots, and is reflected by our great Canadian poets, authors, and painters. It is a cultural identity which is forever tied to our land and to the present and former generations who have tamed it and nurtured it. So, when we speak of a crisis in Canadian agriculture, we speak of a crisis which is all-encompassing, one which is manifested in not just financial terms, but also social and cultural terms.
But, Mr. Speaker, to listen to the comments of many of the members of the Opposition, one would believe that this crisis has only suddenly come upon us; that perhaps it crept through the barn door-and who knows when; that it has only just

April 30, 1987
decided that now is its moment to hurl its plague and the pestilence upon the farm families of Canada.
Well, I can assure the Elouse, Mr. Speaker, that that just isn't so. This crisis, as it may in fact be rightly called, has been with us for a long, long time. This crisis was visiting our agricultural communities in various forms long before Confederation, and this crisis will be back on our doorsteps again, awakened by such factors as weather, market prices, world surpluses and interest rates, and by those two indomitable characteristics of the human spirit, greed and fear.
In listening to some of the comments made during this debate, one could easily be deluded into thinking that the problems facing our farm families are the direct result of either government action or government inaction, that is, depending upon your political persuasion. If that were in fact the case, we could cut off foreign aid substantially by offering the services of our colleague in the other place, specifically Senator Davey, to provide rain to those drought stricken areas of our planet that so desperately need the surplus grains that our world has but cannot supply. To all but the most idealistic among us, there are limits to what Governments can do. Our farm families know this. They know that problems created by the European Economic Community cannot be solved through unilateral action in Ottawa. They know that product prices must be affected by a world-wide surplus. They know also that many of the problems they face today could have been avoided by proper planning, by effective marketing and by good management.
Two and a half years is not a long time to spend on the land, but it is the time that so far has been allotted to our Government for proper planning, effective marketing and to implement good management practices.
Our government policies are addressing the challenges of Canadian farm families in effective and substantive ways, ways which offer long-term solutions, ways which meet with the approval of our agricultural community. First, Canada is taking the lead in seeking international solutions to an international problem. Canada played a lead role at the GATT meetings in Uruguay, and agriculture is now part of the main agenda of present and future GATT discussions.
Second, our Government has not been content to sit back and wait for these international negotiations to produce results. Our Government has provided tremendous financial support, support that is unprecedented to Canadian agriculture. This support to the Canadian farming community has been so well articulated by many of my colleagues that there is no need for me to simply duplicate their rhetoric. There is no need for me to mention the special Canadian grains program and the billion dollars it will provide to the cash flow of grain producers. There is no need for me to mention the special Canadian grains program. Everyone knows about the $705 million just announced under the Western Grain Stabilization Act to put money into the hands of farmers when they need it
in time for spring seeding. No one should have to remind this House about the cash advances for unharvested grain that kept many farmers from going under in the fall of 1985 when their fields were wet and snow covered.
Our farm families know about this Government's record in amending the Western Grain Transportation Act and the announcement made by our Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) this afternoon. They know about the new commodity-based mortgages designed to take the heat off when commodity prices plunge around the globe. They know about interest rates and they know the interest rate coin too well. They still remember the other side of that coin, the side where they had to pay 20 per cent or more as a result of the policies and programs of the previous Government.
This debate may be important in emphasizing the problems of the Canadian farm community, but our farm families do not need to be educated about the value of our Government's policies. They recognize the benefits of what we have done and of what we are continuing to do.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, our Government has adopted a policy of marketing and is aggressively pursuing that policy on behalf of the farm families of Canada. This Government believes that it is its responsibility to sell Canadian grain. Through the distinguished efforts of the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), Canada is positioning itself to take advantage of global marketing opportunities as the cycle changes and these markets turn around.
Negotiations have been completed on a new five-year deal with the U.S.S.R., a deal that will see 25 million tonnes of Canadian grains being sold and shipped to that country during the same period. Another 4.5 tonnes will be shipped to Brazil between now and 1988 as part of a new, long-term agreement. In terms of commodities, our Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board may go short on rhetoric but he sure goes long on sales. The agricultural management policies of this Government are clear, clear to anyone who cares to look.
First, the Government is dealing with the causes, not the symptoms. It is demonstrating leadership on an international basis. It is resolving a global problem at its very roots.
Second, this Government is providing interim support, support that is practical, support that is substantive, support that far exceeds that offered by any previous Government.
Finally, this Government is out there in the global marketplace hustling on behalf of the Canadian farmer and hustling successfully, bringing in the orders that are the only thing that will restore our Canadian farm families to vibrancy and economic health.
Our farmers will not be put off by political rhetoric. They will not be satisfied with interventionist programs designed by Government. Our farmers want action, action in dealing with offshore subsidies, action in helping them ride out the current market, action through aggressive marketing. In terms of action, our farmers are giving overwhelming approval to the
April 30, 1987

initiatives and the results that this Government has achieved for them and will continue to achieve in the future.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yes, indeed, I agree with the Hon. Member who has just spoken that the Canadian farmer does want action rather than just words from the Government of the day. Indeed, this is the whole purpose of the motion brought forward by the New Democratic Party that we have been debating now for a great many hours. The two specific actions that seem to us in all fairness that should be taken, if we do not want to see the Canadian farm family destroyed are, first, the action of not removing the moratorium on farm foreclosures tomorrow, of keeping the moratorium in place and, second, of giving grain growers of the West some assurance that the 1987 deficiency payments will at least equal those of last year.
The Hon. Member who has just spoken somehow leaves me with the thought, and I guess I get left with it every time 1 listen to a Conservative, that there has never been any Government involvement in the grain business in Canada, that somehow or other all that is needed is protection against subsidies that other countries are providing and, of course, we all would like to see that, but that no assistance be given to the grain growers themselves.
There have always been prairie farm stabilization Acts. There have always been deficiency payments. There was the Crow rate. There has been a very substantial amount of government involvement in agriculture in Canada's history. 1 do not suppose the Tories want to destroy the Canadian Wheat Board. Therefore, I really do not understand the plea that is made from time to time to have no government involvement when the Canadian economy itself is, as we well know, built on a good deal of government assistance and involvement.
The motion which covers two main points, keeping the moratorium on foreclosures in place and providing deficiency payments at least equal to those received in the previous crop year, describes the kind of action we were hoping the Government would take. Indeed, practically all if not all farm leaders in the country were hoping the Government would take that action. Instead, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), who was present a moment ago, announced that the freight rate increase triggered by the Act would in effect and in part at least be transferred to the farmers.
I should remind the House that last year, none of the freight rate increases were transferred to the farmers but this year they will be. On top of all the other increases in costs grain producers have to face, they will now be faced with the increase in freight rates announced by the Minister today.
I would like to remind the House of the price cost squeeze about which we are speaking. The House will recall that a year ago, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) announced a 19 per cent cut in wheat prices, a 28 per cent cut in barley prices and a 28 per cent cut in oat prices.
This crop year, 1987-88, there was an announcement of further cuts. Wheat prices will be cut by 18 per cent, barley by 25 per cent and oats by 28 per cent. This will put prices for these products at levels similar to those of 1976-77, over 10 years ago. However, costs are about three times as high as they were that year.
To put it in specific dollar terms, prairie farm operating expenses and depreciation charges in 1976-77 were about $3.5 billion. The projected expenses and charges for 1987 are over $8 billion, yet prices are back to where they were in 1976-77. The Minister of Transport announced an addition to this today.
Speaking of the Minister, he comes from Newfoundland and was saying there were no grain growers there. He sort of implied that because of that, this was not a particular problem. This reminded me that one of the real problems is that the Government is not listening. This is a national problem, not just a western problem about which the Government really has not been listening. It consults but it does not pay much attention to what is being said.
One of the things for which farm leaders have been asking and waiting is a meeting with the Government to discuss possible deficiency payments for the 1987-88 year. In fact, that is the basis of the debate that has been going on for the last two days. Why will the Government not hold that meeting? Why will it not even set a date for it? The Government says it wants to consult but it does not even hold a meeting with farm leaders to discuss possible deficiency payments for the current crop year.
The lifting of the moratorium affects farmers in all parts of Canada including Newfoundland, though the Minister of Transport made no reference to that. Apparently he did not realize that that was part of the motion that is being debated. The lifting of the moratorium on farm foreclosures will obviously affect Saskatchewan most of all as well as Alberta and Ontario, but it will also affect the Atlantic Provinces and my own Province of British Columbia. Farmers will be going down the tubes after tomorrow when the FCC foreclosure moratorium is lifted.
I was astounded when I heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) say on The Journal last night that most farm organizations want the Farm Credit Corporation moratorium lifted. I consulted with my colleagues who are in touch with the leaders of farm organizations and they informed me that all three prairie Wheat Pools with over 100,000 members as well as the National Farmers Union are absolutely opposed to the lifting of the moratorium. I really do not know where the Minister of Agriculture was coming from when he made that statement last night.
If I may turn for a moment to British Columbia, the lifting of the moratorium on farm foreclosures will have an immediate serious effect on at least 60 farmers, many of whom are tree-fruit farmers. Ultimately, it may affect another 300 or more.

April 30, 1987
Let me put the statistics for British Columbia on the record. According to the Farm Credit Corporation, the number of British Columbia farmers in arrears is 488 and these farmers are in arrears to the tune of $15.7 million. Of those, the number of farmers who are two years or more in arrears is 249 with a total dollar value of $12.6 million in arrears, the bulk of the amount. Of those, the number affected by the lifting of the moratorium is 60. The reason I say the 60 will grow to more than 300 is because those farmers who are in arrears two years or longer are not likely to be able to survive as farmers in the Province of British Columbia.
I find rather incredible the implication of the Elon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King) that everything the Government had been doing was fine and good and that British Columbia farmers were doing well. In fact, a good many of them are very seriously in debt. Indeed, that has become one of their major problems.
I would remind the House that according to the President of the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, the problem with arrears is even more extreme than that shown by Farm Credit Corporation statistics. A few months ago President Geen said the accumulated debt tends to feed on itself. Those who have not been able to meet their annual commitment to the debt are getting into worse shape. -We are going to see more people leaving the land, including third generation farmers.
The other reason that the problem is more serious than the statistics suggest is that most of the debt in B.C. is owed to the banks. Only a small proportion, about 2.7 per cent, of the FCC loans is to B.C. farmers. Dropping the moratorium tomorrow will be a clear signal to the banks to think of further foreclosures themselves. I do not have the figures of all the loans owed to the banks, but it is obviously a very great deal more than those owed to the FCC. The problem for the farmers of British Columbia is indeed serious and not to be lightly touched upon as the Hon. Member for Okanagan-Similkameen seemed to do.
I was listening to the Minister of Transport, and both he and the Minister of Agriculture seem to be taking their orders from The Canadian Bankers' Association. Today I read the background paper submitted to the Standing Committee on Agriculture about a year ago by The Canadian Bankers' Association. To summarize briefly, the association concludes that people are going to be forced out of farming. The family farm will not be able to continue and there is nothing much one can do about it. It is the way the market operates. They
have no intention of seeing anything more than a few transition programs undertaken by Government. They make some very specious arguments. For example, the industry, while continuing to support agriculture, must also meet its obligations to depositors and shareholders. As such, the banks are strongly opposed to any government credit legislation that disrupts the lender/borrower relationship and retroactively changes contractual powers and obligations. The banks question the effectiveness of government subsidy or income-support programs due to their discriminatory and costly nature and often untargeted thrusts.
What a lot of gobbledegook. What they are really saying is that they want a totally free hand and they have no interest whatsoever in the survival of the Canadian farm and farm family, apart from some transitional programs.
They end their brief by saying proposals involving income support, target prices, agri-bonds, subsidized loans and interest rebate subsidies should only be adopted where long-term benefits clearly outweigh the costs. No consideration should be given to debt moratoriums or compromises.
That is The Canadian Bankers' Association, and the Minister of Agriculture seems to be taking his orders from them, both in lifting the moratorium tomorrow and in absolutely refusing to make any deficiency payment commitment to farmers for the next crop year.
I have noted the effect not only on grain farmers but, in my case, as far as the moratorium is concerned, on the tree fruit farmers, dairy farmers, and mixed farmers generally in my province. This is having and will continue to have a Canadawide impact. Therefore, we urge the Government to set a meeting date now with the farm leaders of this country to discuss the grievous debt problem, revoke the lifting of the moratorium, and discuss the deficiency payment program for the 1987-88 crop year. Farmers must know now and the Government has said it will consult. If it does not want to see further deterioration of agriculture in Canada, it must meet immediately with the people concerned to discuss these problems.
This is not a new form of Government intervention. This is part of the Canadian practice of making sure that our agricultural economy is strong and that it will not simply go down the tubes as has happened to many individual farmers already. We are asking the Government to take these actions for the sake of all Canadians. We have a highly integrated economy in so many respects and what happens to farmers affects all of us.

Thursday, April 30, 1987

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this debate is really part of a cry for action on behalf of hundreds of thousands of Canadians involved in the western grain industry, the western grain economy. I think it can be said quite accurately that there are three cornerstones to the foundation of our economy. One surely is the western grain economy and our agricultural sector generally. The others are automobiles and forest products.
The Government has gravely weakened if not sold out a major part of our forest sector through its foolish and weak-kneed deal with the U.S. on softwood lumber. In that deal it quite unnecessarily caved in and agreed with the U.S. to impose an export tax on our sales of softwood lumber to the U.S. In the free trade negotiations now under way the Government seems ready to sell out, to undermine, to weaken another cornerstone in the foundation of our economy, the Canadian automobile industry.
I say this because the Government has not denied reports that it is willing to give up, in these free trade negotiations, the tariffs which exist on imports of cars and parts into this country from the United States. If this happens there will no longer be any way to enforce on the North American automobile companies which are subject to the Auto Pact the Canadian content and product requirements, the safeguards which are so important for the preservation of the industry and the jobs in it.
If there are no tariffs which can be imposed on the North American automobile companies, if they do not meet the production, content and job requirements of the Auto Pact, we will in effect no longer have an Auto Pact and our Canadian auto industry, one of what I have called the three cornerstones of the Canadian economy, will be gravely weakened and seriously damaged.
The Government also seems ready to sell out or weaken the Canadian auto industry in another crucial way. It refuses to insist, by means of law if necessary, that the new Japanese and Korean manufacturers setting up plants in this country play by the same rules as the North American manufacturers with regard to meeting requirements for production, content and jobs. As the Government continues to allow these plants to be set up essentially to put together parts and components imported from offshore, these plants will likely-and I say this
with great regret-displace two or three Canadian jobs for every job they create.
This point was well made and confirmed in a speech made by Moe Closs, President of Chrysler Canada Limited, to the Canadian Club of Montreal yesterday as reported in the Montreal Gazette as follows:
He said Canada's industrial base could be seriously weakened by all the offshore automobile investments in Canada because the Japanese and South Koreans don't play by the same rules.
"I don't see anything fair about all these new auto companies being enticed to set up shop here without having to make the same kinds of commitments in jobs, purchases and investments the North American auto companies have always considered the price of admission".
This very important speech was also reported in La Presse of Thursday, April 30.

Mr. Speaker, I believe it is important to quote a few paragraphs of this article which summarizes the views of a major Canadian automobile industry spokesman, Mr. Moe Closs, and I quote:
The automobile industry is concerned abut the possibility of 40,000 layoffs in Canada, which represent 30 per cent of its total work force of 130,000, and the possible closing of one or two plants because of unfair competition from foreign manufacturers with the support of Ottawa, Toronto and Quebec.
Moe Closs emphasized that each assembly plant of foreign manufacturers in Canada which does not meet the requirement of the Auto Pact (60 per cent of Canadian content) replaces three old jobs with one new job.

I pointed out how the Government, through its foolish policies, is weakening, undermining, selling out two key cornerstones in the foundation of the Canadian economy, our forest products industry and our auto industry. I believe Canadian farmers and Canadians generally can now well be afraid that the Conservative Government is getting ready to do the same thing with Canadian agriculture, especially the western grain economy. This puts at risk not only the foundation of the economy of the three prairie provinces, but a way of life, thousands of family farms and the survival of thousands of rural municipalities and small towns, the tax revenues of which depend on the ability of these farms and the families living on them to exist and pay taxes and to use their income to buy goods and services from businesses in these communities.
I think it could be said in light of recent events that western farmers, farmers generally, and Canadians generally could have a well grounded fear that the Conservative Government is abandoning Canadian agriculture, and especially the western grain economy.

April 30, 1987
When someone from an urban area of southwestern Ontario rises to speak on this kind of subject there are always those who ask why such a Member would rise to take part in the debate. It should be clear that Members of Parliament are here to work for the best interests of the entire country, not only for their own riding, community, or even their own region.
By virtue of being elected to serve in the House of Commons we are all compelled, in fact duty bound, not only to vote but to understand and give consideration to the needs and problems of our entire country; the needs and problems of the fishermen of Newfoundland, the forestry workers of northern Ontario and British Columbia-

-the needs and problems of workers employed in the Montreal East plants which are closing, those workers in the CN Moncton plants which, because of a lack of policy and support from this Conservative Government, are losing their jobs, on top of the several hundreds of jobs which have already been lost because of the unfair and inefficient behaviour of this Conservative Government.

We must understand that the purpose of a national Government and, therefore, of a national Parliament is to enable us all to work to help one another and provide, with a sense of sharing and compassion, a way of making the country work for all its people and all its parts to the mutual benefit of every one of its regions. Each Member in this House of Commons should be able to say that every part of Canada is part of his or her country. I hope that if and when the need arises, Members of Parliament from our prairie provinces or our Atlantic Coast will take an interest in the needs and concerns of my city and my region, just as I am anxious to do when it comes to the needs and concerns of their regions.
However, as the Member of Parliament for Windsor West I do have a concern about the needs of all of southwestern Ontario, especially the peninsula that makes up the County of Essex. I hope Members of this House are aware that the County of Essex is a very important agricultural area, as is the entire southwestern part of the Province of Ontario. In the County of Essex we have a tremendous industry growing cash crops for canning factories. We grow tomatoes, peas, corn and all sorts of fruits and vegetables. That is why major canning companies such as Green Giant and Heinz are located in my County of Essex.
In our region there is also a substantial dairy farming industry, and the growing of corn and wheat is very important in southwestern Ontario including the County of Essex. In fact, I was once told that southwestern Ontario is a major grain producer which grows more wheat than most of the Province of Manitoba,
Although I must say that the wheat growers in my area do not benefit from the support and protection of the Canadian
Wheat Board. Agriculture therefore is of importance to the economy of Essex County, wherein the City of Windsor is located, and the entire southwestern Ontario region. It is a source of employment, not only on farms, but also in food processing plants. The people of my area are very concerned about the crushing burdens of debt and low commodity prices which face all too many farm families in Essex County and southwestern Ontario.
Together these two burdens of debt and low commodity prices, especially in recent months, have been delivering an unfair and, as I said, a crushing blow to all too many farmers in Essex County and southwestern Ontario, for whom not only their immediate livelihood but an entire way of life is as stake.
We have had a crushing blow in terms of debt and low commodity prices in my area, but there has been an especially heavy blow when it comes to the way these twin burdens have been placed upon the shoulders of farmers in western Canada and the western grain economy.
Only last week the Conservative Government announced that initial prices for wheat would be 18 per cent lower than those of last year. Now, just a few days after this bad news, the Government delivered another serious blow to western grain farmers-in fact, to farmers in my area and across Canada- by saying that as of tomorrow it will lift the moratorium, which has been in place for some 19 months, on foreclosure action by its Farm Credit Corporation on farmers in arrears on mortgages that they had obtained from that federal government agency.
One of the Ministers speaking in this debate said that the lifting of the moratorium would involve only 50 farmers per month or some 600 per year. If that is correct, it is still 600 farmers too many. The evidence is that the numbers will be much, much higher.
As has already been pointed out in the debate, some 6,000 of the 75,000 accounts with the FCC have been in arrears for more than two years. The experience with the FCC is that if a loan is in arrears for more than two years it almost invariably leads to foreclosure.
The Government has never explained satisfactorily why it was so heartless, insensitive, and uncaring as to lift this moratorium only a few days after it announced that initial prices for grain would be 18 per cent lower this year than they were last year. As I said, the lifting of the moratorium not only affects western Canada. It affects many farmers in my area.
I should like to refer to what Janice Vansickle, the agriculture reporter for The Windsor Star, wrote about this in yesterday's edition of that newspaper. She said:
A day of reckoning is about to dawn for 110 farmers in Essex and Kent
counties covered by a moratorium on foreclosures by the Farm Credit
Corporation.
The article went on to say:
Local farm leaders generally lashed out at the federal Government for
removing the moratorium.
April 30, 1987

"It's a pretty ruthless step", said Claude Giroux, who stepped down last week as president of National Farmers' Union Local 309 ... The removal of the moratorium indicates the Government is backing down on its commitment to help farmers through a period of crisis in agriculture, said Giroux-
The article went on to say:
The locals' new president, Roger Rivest, questioned the ability of the federal farm debt review board in Ontario to deal with a flow of FCC clients.
As we know, "the boards were put in place last August to act as mediators in credit disputes between farmers and their creditors". However, The Windsor Star went on to report:
Most farm leaders-believe they are not yet functioning properly and lack the authority to obtain legal binding agreements between farmers and creditors. "The farm debt review board has no power," said Rivest.
In today's edition of The Toronto Star, George McLaughlin, Chairman of the Farm Debt Review Board for Ontario, said that "about one Ontario farmer in five will leave the land during the next five years". Mr. McLaughlin went on to say that he asked for "an 18-member board, up from the current 11, to handle the load". He does not have enough people to handle the existing load, not to mention the additional load which will be created when the FCC starts its flow of foreclosures.
According to The Toronto Star, Mr. McLaughlin also said that "the review board had already received 425 applications from farmers and completed 193 reviews. He went on to say that of those completed reviews, only five had been translated into firm legal agreements". That is not a very strong endorsement of the efficiency and the usefulness of the board by the very person which the Conservative Government appointed to chair it.
Obviously, farmers have to be sceptical about the value of these farm debt review boards. Farmers across Canada are being squeezed, not only by low prices for what they grow, but by the problem of debt. There is a strong reason the Government should continue the moratorium against foreclosures of FCC mortgages. It is the absence of an effective system to deal with the farm debt crisis. Farm leaders and individual farmers across the country say that the Government has not put in place an effective system for this purpose. We in the Official Opposition call upon the Government to say today, before the debate ends, that it will continue the moratorium on foreclosures of FCC mortgages.
The Government says that if it does that, the banks will be unhappy and that farmers who have their mortgages with the banks instead of the FCC will also be unhappy. The Government is not here to serve the banks; it is here to serve the people of Canada.
In these circumstances the Government should not drag down the clients of the Farm Credit Corporation to the level of pressure which is being imposed upon clients of the chartered banks, pressure that might be increased if the Government's moratorium on foreclosures of Farm Credit Corporation mortgages is raised. Instead, it should take action right now to get the banks to commit to having an equivalent moratorium on their mortgages so long as the Government's FCC moratorium is in place.
That seems to make more sense than to pull down the clients of the FCC in the agricultural community to the level of those
farmers who may now be facing more pressure by way of foreclosure from the chartered banks.
In the face of the 18 per cent drop in initial prices of grain this year, surely the Government must commit itself today, before this debate ends, to putting in place deficiency payments to bring returns to grain farmers up to the level where they will be equal to those of last year.
Earlier in the debate the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) rose to his feet with a great deal of fanfare and said:"Oh, we are doing something. We are going to provide a subsidy of $64 million on freight rates for shipping grain". The 18 per cent drop in initial prices alone is worth $1 billion. While I am sure $64 million is welcomed, it is only a pittance or a drop in the bucket in the face of the reduction of $1 billion in income. Also, farmers will still have to pay $11 million to $12 million in increased freight rates.
All the Government has done is to go through a smoke and mirrors exercise, holding out the hope of survival to farmers, but as they get close to it, like a train moving away from them, it gets farther and farther away.
I conclude by saying that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) in his trip out west should not be looking for photo opportunities. Instead, if it cannot be done in this debate, he must reinstate the FCC moratorium on farm foreclosures, introduce a proper debt restructuring program, and announce a real deficiency program for this year's crop. Nothing less will do, if the Government is serious about preserving one of the three crucial foundations of the Canadian economy-the western grain industry-and the way of life it represents.
We owe it to the people in the western grain industry to ensure that this debate does not end unless we get this type of commitment from the Government. I call upon the Government to show some small element of heart, concern, and caring, by making this kind of commitment. This is the very least it can do for the western grain economy, for agriculture generally, and for the entire economy of the country.
