speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of State (Privatization) and Minister Responsible for the Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to speak in this debate today. I did not intend to start this way, but I do want to deal with the moratorium the Opposition House Leader has called upon us to reinstate.
Let me point out to the Hon. Member that there are about 225,000 commercial farms in Canada, 75,000 of which do business with the FCC. After the moratorium is lifted, the FCC will deal with a potential 50 foreclosure cases a month. Only 20 per cent of these are in arrears, including some 6,000 that have made no payments for at least two years. This means that one-quarter of 1 per cent of Canada's farming community will potentially be affected by this moratorium.

April 30, 1987
I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the moratorium was imposed while programs to assist troubled farmers were being developed. Those programs include the interest rate conversion program that assists over 5,000 farmers, the shared-risk mortgage program, commodity-based loans and farm debt review boards. As well, the moratorium was creating a two-tier system in agriculture: those farmers who were protected and those whose creditors were not the Farm Credit Corporation and who therefore had no protection.
The lifting of the moratorium is supported by organizations like the Canadian Cattlemen's Association which talked about distortions caused by the debt moratorium although it sympathized as did others with our reasons for bringing it in in the first place. The association said that this was not a good solution because it provided no lasting benefit to Canadian agriculture. That is what I would like to talk about throughout most of my address to the House today.
It was interesting that in the first part of his address, the Opposition House Leader did not refer to farmers at all. He talked about the automobile industry, the forest products industry, fishermen and railway workers. Then he finally got around to talking about farmers. However, I did agree with him when he talked about being an urban Member from southern Ontario. I myself am a Member from Toronto. There are compelling reasons for people like me and the Hon. Member to talk about farmers, and those reasons are how important farmers are, not just to the Canadian economy but to every consumer in Canada, and the way of life they represent.
I feel particularly strongly about this because, although I am an urban Member, like many Canadians and probably many in this Chamber, my roots are with the land. My family farmed in Ontario for 150 years. My grandfather who owned the farm in 1929 came very close to losing it then because of the kinds of conditions we are seeing today. He was able to save it through hard work and community assistance, but it took him many years to pay for what happened to him in 1929. That is why we on this side of the House recognize the importance of farming to our communities and that all issues that affect farmers affect Canadians across the land.
I would like to point out how the situation facing Canadian farms affects women and their lives on the farm. Of course, there is nothing new about women taking active and equal roles on the farm, but two things have changed over the years. Farm women are now far more involved in the decisionmaking aspects of the family farm than they were years ago. Second, the structures on the farm have changed. When my grandmother worked side by side with my grandfather, they had help in the house, on the land and in the barn.
Now there is a wider public understanding of the contribution of farm women and how it has increased so much throughout the last generation or two. Women on the farm are now involved in all aspects of the farm business, from domestic activities to work in the fields. Studies show that 49 per cent of farm field work and 97 per cent of farm domestic work is done by women. Something that has not changed is that most farm
women are responsible for keeping the books as well, just as my grandmother did.
One of the problems with the family farm today is that with increased pressure on families, more and more women are seeking employment off the farm. That creates additional pressures on farm women and their families. They are continuing to do the domestic work and the work in the barn and the fields. They are also taking jobs in town. Along with the lack of availability of help, that is leading to a greater dependence on child care, a need that must be met, a need to which the Government has been committed since its first day.
High quality child care is particularly hard to find in rural areas, particularly in the spring planting season and the fall harvest when care is sometimes required around the clock. At the same time, women working off the farm require year-round child care. The demands are diverse and our sensitivity to those issues has been expressed many times. I have been in touch throughout the past year with farm women across Canada to deal with how we can jointly find a solution to this problem. That is why when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) has talked in the House and in public about our commitment to child care, he has always talked about flexibility. He knows that women in rural Canada have different needs than women in the cities.
Farm women have played such an important role throughout the history of farming, but so has this Party. In the history of Canadian farms, the Progressive Conservative Party has always had a strong relationship with farmers. In fact, I could say it is a relationship that is unique among Canadian political Parties. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that created the Department of Agriculture. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that founded the Farm Credit Corporation. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that set up the Canadian Wheat Board. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that established crop insurance. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that brought in the Agriculture Stabilization Act. It was the Progressive Conservative Party that set up the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation administration. The list goes on. I will bet you your very last bushel, Mr. Speaker, that if it is positive for Canadian agriculture, it was put in place by a Tory Government.
Let us now turn to some more recent history that has led to the problems Canadian farmers are now facing. The problems faced by farmers in Canada today arise out of both domestic and international occurrences. Domestically, the Canadian farming community was devastated by the economic conditions of the early 1980s when a Liberal Government was in power. I can understand why the Opposition House Leader did not talk a lot about farmers in the first part of his address. Interest rates in excess of 20 per cent crippled the farming industry. The economic policies of the Liberal Government contributed significantly to the large number of farm bankruptcies which occurred from 1981 to 1983. It was this attitude of the Government led by the then Prime Minister who asked why he should sell their wheat, that devastated the Canadian farmers. That is why the policies we put in place and the temporary moratorium were so needed.
April 30, 1987

The attitude of the former Prime Minister is not the attitude of our Prime Minister, our Party or our Government. Our record in agriculture is second to none. We have implemented a 16 point agricultural program that has been widely praised. As the Prime Minister stated in this debate, when Canadian farmers are in need, this Government responds. That is why we have committed $1 billion to assist grain producers. Without this program, farm income would have declined by 17.9 per cent this year. That is the kind of action we are prepared to take.
The Liberals would not sell our wheat. We are selling Canadian wheat.
In our Party we know that Canadian farmers are efficient. They are on the leading edge of agricultural technology. Throughout the world they have a record second to none. Our farmers are adaptable. Our farmers work hard while dealing with one of the most difficult climates in the world. But, of all of us closest to this great land of ours, we recognize that our farmers know of the richness of our country more than anyone else.
We are committed to selling Canadian wheat. We are selling 25 million tonnes of grain to the U.S.S.R.; 4.5 million tonnes to Brazil; and 2.5 million tonnes to Egypt. We are proud of the products produced by our farmers. We care enough not just to sell those products internationally but to drive forward for a better deal for Canadian farmers.
Last year we provided $150 million to grain farmers hit by the drought and by grasshopper damage. We provided $705 million under the Western Grain Stabilization Act, providing much needed cash to farmers for spring seeding. We have amended the Western Grain Transportation Act to protect farmers from sharp increases in freight rates. We have established a 10-year $700 million loan program to provide commodity-based mortgages. This initiative helps those farmers with substantial debt problems.
Earlier today my colleague, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), discussed in the House his new measure to protect farmers from the statutory increase in 1987-88 western grain freight rates. So when the Opposition House Leader said that farmers will spend more on freight, I think that for the record I should point out that when farmers deliver their grain to the elevator this year they will pay $6.32 per tonne on average in the upcoming crop year. That compares to a rate of $7.70 paid by producers in 1984-85 prior to the present administration coming to power. It is an 18 per cent decrease from what was paid by producers in that year. The federal Government will pay the average $2 per tonne difference to the railways.
Our Government established farm debt review boards to provide independent third-party review, thus assisting farmers who were having difficulties with their creditors. Providing this third-party analysis is an assistance and comfort in many cases that has been able to have an influence on a farmer's ability to keep his farm and to ensure the survival of the farm business.
The pattern is clear. This is a Government that understands the Canadian farmer. This is a Government which, throughout the history of the country and the history of the Party, has understood the Canadian farmer.
Let me get back to the international work that we have been doing to improve trade in agricultural products. We have been in the forefront of nations calling for new ground rules. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had agriculture discussed at last year's economic summit for the first time ever. That was an initiative of our Prime Minister. Our Prime Minister and this Government are going to bat for farmers hurt by protection in other countries, hurt by the fact that it is a deliberate policy in European communities to protect their farmers and to subsidize them no matter what the cost to the consumer.
We, as a Government, have involved Canada in the Cairns Group, nations formed to counter the power of the European Community, the United States and Japan. We are in the forefront of negotiations in GATT to stop the international trade war in agriculture. We are involved in trade talks with the United States that will be of great benefit to Canadian farmers. We know that our farmers can compete with any of those farmers in any of those countries if they are given a fair chance to do so.
On a political level, western Canadians and farmers have never been better represented in Cabinet, in Government and in caucus. I will not list the great extent of their involvement since the Prime Minister pointed that out to the House in this debate. However, I can say that when I look at our Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and our Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), and when I listen to the voices that they represent on behalf of Canadian farmers, as a Member from Toronto I am very proud to support them in their endeavours and to sit beside them in Cabinet and in this House.
On an economic level we all know the disastrous effects of the Liberal economic policies on Canadian farmers. Our Government's economic policies have had a positive effect on farmers, a stabilizing effect under enormously difficult circumstances for farmers and for this Government. But we have never, ever, betrayed our farmers, and we never will. I would like to remind Hon. Members that just by our general economic policies a 1 per cent decline in interest rates represents a savings to Canadian farmers of $130 million a year.

April 30, 1987
1 am proud of our record in agriculture. We intend to build upon it. Traditionally, our Party has been the voice of Canadian farmers in Parliament, and this will continue. It will continue as long as this Government remains in office with its representatives, not just from western Canada but Members such as myself who come from downtown urban centres and who are totally committed to the Canadian farmer. We will keep working diligently to ensure a better life for the people on our farms, men and women, and to ensure that the children on the farms will have the right to inherit a stable and happy farm environment.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a chance to speak in this emergency debate today which concerns the current crisis facing grain producers. My Party, the Liberal Party, is concerned by the tremendous tragedy that is taking place in the western grain industry.
The Conservative Government has failed the producers, despite the good words that have just been spoken by the Minister. It is clear that the Conservative Government believes grain producers will have a great future in two or three years' time when the market turns around. But most western farmers are not very certain in their own minds whether that will be the case, because there has been absolutely no commitment of a deficiency payment for the new crop year. Farmers do not want nice words, such as those just expressed by the Minister. They do not want nice words for the future. They want money now. They need it, and they need it badly. They should get it from the Conservative Government.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That is what they are getting. They are getting $1.3 billion in the next month. That is money. That is cash. That is now!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: I realize that the Minister is very concerned and he is becoming very nervous. I certainly appreciate that he is very sensitive because it hurts. It certainly hurts-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: All I am trying to do is tell you what is going on so that you do not make a fool of yourself when you speak.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: The Conservatives have made a mess of farming. It hurts them. Certainly this debate is a clear indication of how nervous and how desperate is the Minister.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Canadian Wheat Board)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: It is a clear indication of all the things that this Government has done for farmers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Last year, when grain prices went down by 20 per cent the industry said that, in constant dollars, grain prices were at the same level as they were in 1933 under R. B. Bennett. Tory times are tough times. This has been said many times in the past. I think it has to be repeated today. Tory times are tough times. They certainly are for a great number of western farmers who must now realize that, because grain prices have gone down by a further 18 per cent this year. There is not only the 20 per cent reduction of last year to consider, but the additional 18 per cent which will take place this year.
Western wheat growers were saying to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who is the Liberal
critic for agriculture, that the crisis today is not so much with respect to price, although that is certainly a serious problem, but that the major problem is the uncertainty of government policy. They have said to my colleague that they do not know whether there will be a deficiency payment or a special grains program, and they do not know on what basis.
This is unacceptable because other governments are taking care of their farmers. They are letting them know exactly what they are going to do for them, or what they are doing for them now. This is not the situation with the Canadian Government. We know what the Government of the United States is doing for its farmers, and we see what is happening in Europe. Those Governments are providing all kinds of support and help for their farmers.
Earlier in this debate, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) indicated that he was going to take steps to reduce freight rates. In this regard, it is interesting to make some comparisons. In 1984, the freight rate was $7.70 per tonne. At this time, it would be $8.32 per tonne. Taking into account the $2 subsidy announced by the Government, the rate will be $6.32 per tonne. This subsidy on freight rates will reduce the cost to the growers some 8 per cent. Let me remind the Minister and others that the price of wheat in 1984 was $170 per tonne. The price for the 1987-88 crop year will be $110 per tonne, a difference of $60, or roughly 35 per cent.
If the Minister of Transport is serious about helping our farmers, if he really wants to do something, why does he not reduce freight rates by 35 per cent? We have had a reduction of 35 per cent in the price per tonne of wheat, and certainly the same reduction should apply to freight rates. If he were to do that, I would applaud the initiative of the Minister. But, all the Government can do after this two day debate is to come out with that kind of insignificant support.
It is incredible to me that this Government can make the claim that it supports our farmers. What it has come up with is a farce. We on this side of the House want to vigorously express our opposition to the lack of action on the part of this Government.
The U. S. Farm Bill is not going to be changed in the near future, and certainly not during the term of the Reagan administration. In addition, it is clear that the U. S. Export Enhancement Program will be strengthened, increasing yet again competition for Canadian Wheat Board sales.
As a result of the information we have received of late, and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), wrote to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), and despite all the apparent goodwill, all of the niceties between the President and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), it is clear that American policies are hurting Canadian farmers and Canadian workers, and our Prime Minister is doing nothing about it. Yet, he tries to make us believe that he has a very special relationship with the President of the United States. Indeed, he has; he is selling Canada to the Americans at a very low price.
April 30, 1987

My colleague the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry today wrote the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I will take a moment to read that letter. It is as follows:
It has come to my attention that the U.S. Department of Agriculture has today prepared a new set of agricultural trade subsidy initiatives that include measures of great damage to Canada.
Specifically they are proposing to include under the Export Enhancement Program an offer of 1.25 million metric tons of barley to Saudi Arabia, a traditional Canadian buyer.
If this measure is approved by the Trade Review Committee of the U.S. administration in the next week, it will mean a loss of 75 to 85 million dollars to Canadian farmers.
The Minister today spoke of providing $64 million for western Canadian farmers. A single sale of U.S. grain to Saudi Arabia will cost Canadian grain producers $85 million-much more than what the Government is prepared to give them today.
The letter goes on:
This initiative certainly flies in the face of assurances apparently gained from President Reagan that he would be considerate of Canadian agricultural concerns-
Well, these concerns are not being given very serious consideration.
In addition to this sale to Saudi Arabia, we have recently been told that the Americans have negotiated a sale with the U.S.S.R. Under that agreement the Americans will sell to the U.S.S.R. four million metric tonnes of wheat, and for every three bushels of wheat bought by the U.S.S.R., the Americans will provide one bushel at no charge.
This is the type of endeavour that other countries are becoming involved in so as to sustain their agricultural industries, their farmers. We would like to see what this Government is ready to do to sustain our own farmers.
Unfortunately, the attitude of the Government thus far has been rather puzzling. If our agricultural industry is to survive in the face of international competition, we are going to have to provide more in the way of deficiency payments, more special grains programs, and more aggressive marketing.
In closing, I should like to refer to another aspect of government initiative that is, to say the least, a real slap in the face for our farmers. I refer to the decision taken earlier this week by this Government to lift the foreclosure moratorium imposed upon the Farm Credit Corporation.
This action will permit foreclosure proceedings to be commenced against those farmers whose Farm Credit Corporation loans are in arrears. FCC loans represent 30 to 40 per cent of long term debt in the agricultural sector, and we are told that 6,000 of the 75,000 accounts with the Farm Credit Corporation have been in arrears for more than two years. This has just been confirmed by the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) who spoke just before me.
The history of the Farm Credit Corporation has been that if a loan is in arrears for more than two years it almost invariably leads to foreclosure. That means that 8 per cent of the Farm Credit Corporation loans are certain to face foreclosure proceedings.
The Minister of State for Privatization has just said, "Don't worry about this, we are only going to foreclose on about 50 a month". I believe that is what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said as well earlier in the week. That means that about 600 farmers a year will have to worry about foreclosures. This is incredible. I am not concerned about thousands of farmers, I am concerned about every farmer who has to face foreclosure. It is unacceptable for the Minister to say that we should not worry, that only 600 will be foreclosed upon. We should have a policy which protects every farmer and no foreclosures should take place. This is absolutely unacceptable. This kind of thing will not wash.
I believe that if the Government has lifted the moratorium on foreclosures, then it is lifted and it may apply to many thousands of farmers. The Government should take every step possible to prevent this from happening. It is certainly agony for farmers who have devoted years, their entire lives in some cases, and have planned great future projects for their farms, to see them go by the wayside because of the incredible misunderstanding or bad heart of the Government.
It has been said many times that the Conservative Government is very close to big business, the big multinationals, the big oil companies, and the big banks. Time and time again the Government has passed legislation in the interests of the prissante, the people who are rich and influential, but very seldom does the Government take up the interests of the poor, those who are in difficulty. I say to the Minister of Agriculture that this is the time to act. This bad decision could be cancelled, because it will only come into effect tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Farmers don't want it cancelled. Farmers want it lifted.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Regardless of how the Minister wants to sugar-coat it, this is not the way to do it. The moratorium has been in place for 19 months. During that time the Government should have put in place a debt restructuring program to solve the plight of farmers. Had it put in place a proper debt restructuring program the moratorium would not be needed in place at all. However, the Government did not have such a program and the moratorium bought it time. The Government had 19 months to put in place a debt restructuring program which could work well. As the Minister knows, the things which are in place do not work. The situation is getting worse and worse.

April 30, 1987
In conclusion, the Leader of the Liberal Party put the situation quite clear earlier in this debate when he made a vibrant plea to force the Conservative Government to work for the farmers. On behalf of farmers he said that unless special programs are put in place to cope with it, we will see the loss of an entire way of life in rural prairie communities across the country. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said that action is needed now. I want to repeat his words.
The Government should come clean, give a commitment to a deficiency payment, stop foreclosures which will begin tomorrow, and put in place a proper debt restructuring program. If the Government does not do so the problems faced by western Canadian agriculture and agriculture in other parts of the country will be horrendous. People in this House, the Liberal Party, and many, many Canadians across the country who are concerned about agriculture are willing to make that commitment. The Government must make that commitment now to our rural communities. It is absolutely essential. I hope this debate has opened the eyes of the Minister and has opened his heart and his pocket, because the farmers desperately need money and they need it very soon.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gladly participate in this debate. I want to refrain from rhetoric, place facts before the House, and deal with this matter in a manner which I hope will be helpful.
I am honoured to represent the constituency of Saskatoon West, which is a very important part of the great Province of Saskatchewan, a province which relies on agriculture, on a per capita basis, more than any other province in the country. I am very proud to represent a rural area in my constituency, although it has diminished over the years since I was first elected.
I am very proud of how many of our Ministers and Members have participated gladly in this debate. We have a record of which we can be justly proud in most difficult circumstances. I want to compliment in particular my colleagues, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). As a western Canadian representative in the House of Commons, I feel comfortable in Government with the representation which these two Ministers have given us in these important portfolios. I say that on behalf of my constituents.
The Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), who brought this matter forward, knows that farmers in Saskatchewan are not a bunch of dolts. They understand exactly what is going on. They follow the proceedings of the House of Commons very closely and are not taken in by the hysterical rhetoric which I have heard from opposition Members.
When the Liberal-NDP coalition brings forward a motion in an attempt to demonstrate that they represent western farmers, nothing could be further from the truth. It pains me and western Canadians to see Liberals stand up in this House and suggest that they are somehow interested in the plight of
the farmers of this nation. Nothing could be further from the truth.
We heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) participate in this debate. I want to remind people that the Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Finance in the Government of the Right Hon. Pierre Trudeau. He had great influence in that Government. Where was the Leader of the Opposition when Mr. Trudeau asked western farmers, "Why should we sell your wheat?" and turned his finger on western Canada? He was silent. Now all of a sudden he has a newfound interest in the western grain farmer. This is not being believed at all in western Canada.
Our policy was developed in the tradition of John Diefen-baker with whom I had the great honour of serving, as did many of us in this House. The leadership which was given by John Diefenbaker with regard to western Canada is being continued under the leadership of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Indeed it is a fact that the Prime Minister first came to Ottawa to work for the Minister of Agriculture in the Government of Mr. Diefenbaker, and that was the Hon. Member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). That was his exposure to politics in Canada. That has given him an abiding faith in the sanctity of the farmers of Canada.
I say to my colleagues in the House of Commons that I do not want to indulge this evening in anything except the facts relating to the very serious question facing farmers across the nation. On CBC this morning I heard the Hon. Member for Prince Albert, who precipitated this debate, complimenting the fact that the Government had taken initiatives in terms of international discussions to deal with the root problem of the difficulties facing Canadian farmers today, that is to say, the position of commodity prices in Canada.
I must compliment him for saying that. In fact, he complimented our leadership, the Prime Minister in particular, on the CBC farm program at six o'clock this morning. I give him credit for stating a fact which I think has not come out of any member of his Party during the course of the debate. He gave proper recognition to the role played by the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board.
What are the facts? We in the Government have come forward at a time of crisis and difficulty for western farmers in a way which any thinking Canadian would have to say was fair and reasonable and demonstrates our priority toward agriculture.
I should like to give some indication of comparative figures of spending, because the Opposition keeps talking about the money we should be spending. Federal support to agriculture in Canada in 1983 totalled $300 million. However, what is it now? It is anticipated that this year we will be spending something in the vicinity of $3 billion.
April 30, 1987

What was the prime interest rate in 1981? What were farmers paying when they had to go to banks and credit unions for assistance to carry on their operations? Have we forgotten what it was? It was 22.75 per cent. What is it now? It is 9.25 per cent.

What was the cost of a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in 1981? The interest rate at that time was 23.75 per cent. Today it is 10.25 per cent. That is a 12.5 per cent difference.
We must ask ourselves why the Liberal-NDP coalition is raising this debate at this time. It is clear that the only reason is that it wants to prevent the passage of other government legislation. It has nothing to do with agriculture. Opposition Members want to stall the business of the House because they do not want to deal with Bill C-22 and other legislation in the House of Commons. This is not bona fide.

Mr. Speaker, I think I have hit a responsive chord. The agricultural critic of the Fiberal Party, who stands in the House to speak about agriculture, understands precisely what it is. I think the people of Canada should understand why we are here. They have given us a telling blow, but this time it was with the point of their chin. They are giving us on this side of the House an opportunity to remind Canadians-and we do it gladly-that we in fact have a commitment or priority to
agriculture which has been unexceeded, quite frankly, by any other Government in the history of Canada.
There has been much talk about farm bankruptcies, but I think the fact is that it is a regrettable matter. We understand that. I know what it is like to go home and see farmers in difficulty, wondering what they will do this year and living in a situation brought on by international circumstances. 1 understand all that because I go home every week-end. I do not maintain, as do some Members, a residence in Ottawa or Aylmer. I go home and talk with these people, and I understand what they are saying. We are working as hard as we can, within our financial ability, to bring some relief to farmers.
Fet us look at the number of farm bankruptcies under the Liberals. In 1981, there were 261 farm bankruptcies nationally. In 1982, there were 410, which was a 57 per cent increase; in 1983, 488, which was practically a 20 per cent increase; in 1984, 551, which was a 13 per cent increase; in 1985, 508, which was a 7.8 per cent decrease; and in 1986, 440, which was a 13 per cent decrease.

Mr. Speaker, I was on a roll and he actually managed to put me off by pointing out that you are very distinguished. He interrupted my discussion.
Let us look at the Special Canadian Grains Program of which 1 am particularly proud. Members of the Opposition ask what the Government is doing for the Province of Saskatchewan as if it were doing nothing, not taking its responsibility. Let me just tell the House what the Government is doing, what kind of cash is now being placed in the hands of Saskatchewan farmers alone. As a result of that $1 billion payment under the Special Canadian Grains Program, we in Saskatchewan will realize $415.6 million. Without that payment the farm income would have been desperate. By virtue of that payment alone, there has been an increase in the income of Saskatchewan farmers of 82.5 per cent. 1 think that increase is not insignificant.
The Saskatchewan portion of the Western Grain Stabilization Act payment will be $382 million. Rounding that off, $800 million in total that will go to Saskatchewan. That is not an insignificant amount of money that will be received by farmers within five weeks.
An announcement was made today on western grain transportation. While we are having this debate, the Government is routinely facing a very serious question brought on by Liberal legislation which forced the freight rate up substantially and dramatically by something in the vicinity of 39 per cent. Over the course of the last weeks and days, the Government was addressing this problem in the anticipation of a substantial increase in the cost of transporting grain. Today the Government responded to the increase brought on by the Liberal legislation which was passed with the support of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). We felt that the increase was not acceptable so we decided to make a payment in anticipation of the increase to ensure that no increase of any consequence is borne by the western farmer.
I do not see opposition Members congratulating us on taking this position. They are silent and they should be ashamed of themselves. If we are to have fair debates, I expect the Opposition to be critical at the proper times but when an action is taken by the Government which does bring relief, I would simply ask for fair play on the part of opposition Members. I would ask them to acknowledge such action.
The Hon. Member for Papineau spoke of representatives of big business and asked who represents it. I think he forgets the
fact that his leader was on the boards of directors of many corporations including the Bank of Montreal and Canadian Pacific. I do not know who represents big business in the House, but I do not think the Minister of Agriculture does. I do not think the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday), the Hon. Member from Sarnia, the Hon. Member from Sept. Isles or the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin) represent big business. Do these look like big-time bankers to you, Mr. Speaker? These are honest-to-God common people representing their constituents in a way of which I am very proud.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they talk about out of the mouths of babes. What I just heard from the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) makes babes sound as though they are speaking sense.
What we have just heard from the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West is bafflegab. I was not even supposed to be here. I am supposed to be away on a short maternity leave enjoying my family. However, when I saw this nonsense going on on the government side, I could not take it any longer. I had to come here to start calling a spade a spade and to speak for the record.
The Hon. Member invoked in solemn tones the memory of John Diefenbaker. At the same time, his own Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has appointed at the expense of the public purse Dalton Camp, the very man who did in the former eminent Prime Minister, the man who stabbed him again and again. Dalton Camp is now being paid to be chief adviser to the Prime Minister. I cannot believe that the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West would be able to talk about Diefenbaker while Dalton Camp is sitting in his cabinet room advising his colleagues. Dalton Camp is the kind of adviser who makes speeches like the one made by the Hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mrs. McDougall). We heard her describe herself as an urban Member and she admitted that although she had some rural roots, she was not that familiar with the current situation in farming. We also heard her say that the reason the Government will end the moratorium on farm foreclosures as of midnight tonight is because it does not want a two-tier system.
April 30, 1987

I believe a number of government Members were present when the Eton. Member for St. Paul's said that she did not want to have a two-tier system. Fine, the Conservative Government will be implementing a one-tier system and driving more farmers into bankruptcy. It is driving more family farms to end a great history. Is that the kind of tier this Party promised the people of Canada when it went to the voters on September 4, 1984?
With the departure of Bill Fox, perhaps we will get some new script writers. I certainly hope so. We heard the litany of former Liberal sins and we heard about interest rates back in 1981. I would like to ask Members on the government side what those same farmers are now paying in the spread. As any Hon. Member knows, the real cost of borrowing to farmers is the cost of the spread, not necessarily the interest rate. The cost of the spread has not been reduced substantially.
We heard what the former Liberal Government did and did not do. Presumably, on September 4, 1984, the people of Canada made a judgment and they gave a mandate to the Conservative Government, the largest mandate in the history of Canada. Now, almost three years later, we are seeing the Government's inaction on agriculture.
The Minister in charge of privatization read off a check list of monies that had been given to farmers in the form of subsidies or other goodies. It took the Government only 48 hours to come up with $1 billion to bail out Canadian banks. Yet the same Government dragged its heels for months on end until it was on the edge of an election in Saskatchewan. It took a call from the Premier of Saskatchewan to force the Prime Minister to change his mind and come across with some much needed cash for western farmers.
We know that the Prime Minister himself has flown over the western provinces more times than he would care to admit. Even though he has promised to go to western Canada next week, I suspect that he may decide to fly over again when he receives the most recent piece of news which is that today, the United States signed a 4-million-ton deal to sell wheat to the U.S.S.R. That 4-million-ton deal represents one-half of the annual Canadian wheat sales to the Soviet Union.
Where is the benefit accruing to Canadians as a result of our great relationship with the United States? The United States is undercutting our markets with the European Economic Community and with the U.S.S.R. At the same time we host the President of the United States to come here to tell us how we should be moving toward a free trade system, a free trade system which will destroy whatever semblance is left of our agricultural community.
There are promises and more promises that have been broken. You have heard, Mr. Speaker, from some of my colleagues today who have outlined the hypocrisy of a Government that came into power with 338 promises and then leaves
all the work to the Opposition. It has left all the work to people such as the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) who time and time again in this House has stood in his place and asked the Government to come across. He has asked the Government to come across with a deficiency payment which will be equal at least to what the farmers received in the last fiscal year. He has asked the Government, because no firm restructuring program has been introduced for debt refinancing, to waive the decision to end the moratorium on FCC farm foreclosures.
The Hon. Member for Algoma, along with the Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), the Leader of the Official Opposition, have travelled the country on a Liberal task force asking farmers what they think. So too we in the Liberal Party can be justly proud of another one of our members who has carried a one-man, one-woman fight across the Prairies in the person of our Senator Hazen Argue and his wife, Jean. Many of us know that he has taken to his trailer to go out to the small communities in Saskatchewan and Alberta to find out from the farmers and the farm wives themselves just what the Government can do to assist them. He has taken his fight even to the point of demonstrating before the American Embassy to ensure that the American Government starts instituting some fair trading practices so that we Canadians can compete on an equal basis.
I heard the Hon. Member for St. Paul's talk about the efficiency of Canadian farms and the efficiency of Canadian farmers. Nobody doubts that we have some of the most efficient farmers and most efficient farm production in the world. But when we are competing with subsidies in the United States and in other countries which are so great that our farmers cannot even recoup the cost of planting, then we know that this Government has to get in there and fight toe-to-toe to establish the principle of fair trading practices among nations. We talk about Canada being at the leading edge of the GATT negotiations. Yet we have seen what that has yielded for the Canadian farmer-a big fat zero.
Today, we know that the Prime Minister is meeting with his provincial colleagues. If I were a western Premier I would say to the Prime Minister: "Don't bother visiting us. Send cash. Don't bother, Mr. Prime Minister, showering us with more flowery promises, we have seen the 338 promises that went along with your election brochure and we simply do not believe you".
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture in a brochure which was given to all members at the end of January, 1985, cite chapter and verse the promises made by the Prime Minister when he was Leader of the Official Opposition. Times have changed and his tune has changed. We have heard the Government talk about the woes of past Liberal administrations. We have heard it again and again and again. It sounds like a broken record.

What the farmers want to know, and what the people of Canada want to know, is once given the largest mandate in the history of Canada when is this Government going to start to deliver for the little people? When is this Government going to start to deliver or is it simply going to chop off those farms that are now teetering on the brink? We heard the figures-it is only 50 a month, said the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for Privatization. Some 50 farms a month will be going down the tubes as a result of an action which will be consummated at midnight tonight, and this Government has a chance to stop it now. It has a chance to follow through on its promise to develop a restructured debt capacity through the Farm Credit Corporation, until that restructuring has been carried out to place a moratorium on all FCC farm foreclosures.
I know that I could go on at length, but there are many other members of my Party who would like to call on the Government-

speechtext:
What we probably could do as much as anything else is begin to look for solutions to a massive problem. Without becoming overly hostile, I must say that I listened to the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) make some comments about what a fine job the Conservatives have done throughout history. I am sure she mentioned that in order to give the House some direction in terms of coming to a resolution to this problem. As I recall, she talked about the Conservative Government putting in place, because of its great concern for agriculture, institutions such as the Wheat Board. She talked about attempts to obtain price stabilization, prairie farm rehabilitation programs and a number of things that rose out of the Great Depression.
Up to 1929-30, the Liberal Government had been in power. It brought us up to and beyond the bank of the abyss, and tore Canada apart from one end to the other. It created enormous circumstances complicating and making the Depression worse.
Unfortunately-and this is something the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall) forgot to mention- between 1930 and 1935 we had a Conservative Government in power. In the first four years of the R.B. Bennett Government, the problems that had been inherited from the previous Liberal Government worsened. Under R.B. Bennett, we saw one of the greatest wreckages of the Canadian economy and Canadian agriculture in the history of this country.
In the last year of the term of that Government, the Prime Minister, R.B. Bennett, a Conservative's Conservative, suddenly said: "We have done all things wrong. Things have to be changed 180 degrees". And they came up with some of the most far-sighted solutions that this country has ever seen.
I believe R.B. Bennett suffered a heart attack early in that year and was unable to give his energy and direction to seeing those programs through to completion or to debate them during the following election campaign, and when the Liberals were returned to power, they cut many of them, with the result that it was many years before many of them saw their potential realized.
The point of the exercise, Mr. Speaker, is that the Progressive Conservatives, after four years of damaging activity, did come to recognize that their course of action was completely wrong. In 1935, the final year of their term, they made some of the most dramatic and important changes-changes that
were designed to help agriculture, help alleviate unemployment, and generally improve the economy.
That is what was forgotten in the speech of the Minister of State for Privatization. Hopefully this Government will see the error of its ways and change its course, in much the same way as the R. B. Bennett Government changed its course in the final year of its term, and try to get something in place that will help this country and help agriculture.
The Comox Valley has some of the small amount of Class 1 agricultural land in the entire Province of British Columbia. There are some very hardworking and committed farmers in that valley, people who work their guts out in order to keep the family farm going, in order to keep agriculture an important part of the economy of that valley.
The Province of British Columbia, in a move to protect farmland, passed a land reserve program under which farmland would be protected. That measure was supported by the majority of the British Columbia population. But what it did for farmers was to remove other economic options for them. They had to farm.
Under the previous Government, as has been mentioned many times during this debate, we had great fluctuations in farm product prices, with always rising costs, the result being that farmers went into debt. We also had a period of extremely high interest rates.
I was quite interested in the remarks of the Member for Hamilton East (Mrs. Copps) when she said: "It doesn't really matter what the rate is; they are concerned about the spread".
Well, if a farmer is paying between 22 and 25 cents interest on every dollar that he owes and not 10 cents, or 10 per cent, certainly there is a great difference. While the interest rates are better now, for a period of time earlier in the 1980s they were so bad that the existing debt accumulated at an enormous rate, and the largest percentage of debt, in many cases, was the accumulated interest payments.
The Canadian Bankers' Association, an organization known as the true friend of the farmer and as the absolute supporter of the principle of maintaining the family farm in Canada, had some interesting insights when they appeared before the Standing Committee on Agriculture in 1986. They in fact advocated throwing farmers off the farm, throwing families out. They recommended a transition program for the purpose of relocating farmers, retraining them, and getting them off the farm-I assume to turn the farms over to corporate agriculture, something we have seen in the United States and in eastern Canada.
They also recommended that farm financial review boards be established. This is something about which the Government made a serious error. Had the Government, in legislation, provided a solid basis for those financial review boards, they would be an effective agency today. They could bring together the farmer and his creditors for the purpose of making a financial arrangement that was realistic, that was viable, that would preserve the family farm-everything that has been talked about during the course of this debate.

April 30, 1987
Had the Government given those review boards the teeth to make binding arrangements between the farmer and his creditors, it would have a better platform now on which to induce further financial assistance for farmers. It is absolutely critical to bring about a stabilizing agreement between the farmer and his creditors. That is absolutely crucial to any farm reconstruction effort that we embark upon.
What does the Canadian Bankers' Association say about that? "Absolutely not". It wants the financial review boards to have the power to give advice only. Well, I do not know of any banker in this country who takes anything by way of advice. He simply looks at his accounts and collects his money.
Review boards with the power to compel reasonable arrangements for repayment, payments that would permit the farmer to survive and allow him an income, are what is needed. Such boards would allow this Government the opportunity to make meaningful additions in terms of assistance programs.
There are the old promises that this Government made prior to coming to power. It talked about agri-bonds as a source of funding for farm loans. Those election promises have never materialized.
Another recommendation of the Canadian Bankers' Association: No debt moratorium. The Canadian Bankers' Association, a true friend of the farmer, has put together a prescription to destroy family farming, to put farmers off the land and replace them with large corporations, thus breaking one of the strongest foundations of Canadian society. We in this Party are not prepared to stand by and see that happen. That is why this debate is under way. Hopefully the Government, when this debate ends, will declare that this moratorium will continue until an effective policy is put in place.
Mr. Speaker, as it happens, before coming into the House, I was speaking to a farmer from my constituency. It would perhaps be interesting to review what happened in his particular circumstance. He will be one of the statistics when the Farm Credit Corporation lowers the boom. He meets a lot of the criteria.
Those on the other side of the House have said that only 50 farms a month will be affected by the lifting of this moratorium. When the Minister was asked how that could be, he said: "Well, the Farm Credit Corporation has sufficient staff to handle that number only".
Well, it strikes me that, just taking the criterion of the Farm Credit Corporation that anyone who is two years or more in arrears will be foreclosed, we are talking about thousands upon thousands of Canadian farms that will go down the drain. And one would assume that, the minute this moratorium is lifted, the other creditors, in order to protect their position, will push the button-

speechtext:
That is truly unfortunate, Mr. Speaker. I, for one, would be more than prepared to hear what the Minister has to offer to assist farmers.
If it is not true that the Farm Credit Corporation can handle only 50 cases a month, then I would ask the Minister to put on the record what in fact the number is. I should like to know how many will be pushed over the edge each month.
It strikes me that once other creditors see the Farm Credit Corporation moving on a farm, and there are assets on that farm, other creditors, such as the bank-and the banks still have an enormous amount of outstanding debt on farms in this country-will push them over the edge in order to claim assets that they have nailed down. Other creditors would push them over the edge. Removing this moratorium tonight would put farmers in real jeopardy from their other creditors. The Farm Credit Corporation may not have sufficient staff at this time, but other creditors may start the entire process rolling and push them into bankruptcy before the Farm Credit Corporation gets around to exercising its options.
I believe this is one of the most ill-conceived and regrettable situations that we have seen in the House of Commons for a long time. Thousands of people will be affected by this. Other agencies will wish to begin the process of recovering assets from insolvent operations.
There was discussion earlier about policy which the Government should follow. First, it must not allow the moratorium to be lifted. Second, there must be some work with free trade. Farmers and the Canadian agricultural industry cannot be exposed to the direction in which the Government is travelling. Marketing boards and other such agencies have protected farmers for years. They have allowed them to manage supply, market demand, and keep prices at least somewhat ahead of production costs. If that is destroyed by free trade there will be no more Canadian farmers.
April 30, 1987

If Americans are allowed to ship milk into Canada below the price of Canadian produce, we can kiss Canadian dairy farmers goodbye. The same proposition applies to vegetable producers and orchardists. I think we are in for some very serious trouble across the board if a free trade agreement allows Americans to push their products into Canada and ties the hands of our marketing boards. There will be serious consequences. If financial institutions thought the Canadian Government was going to do that they would begin to grab the assets of farms before all was lost with the advent of free trade. This is a very serious matter indeed.
The first step must be the cancellation of the lifting of this moratorium. A debt review board must be created which would have the power to make binding agreements with creditors so that the farmers can continue to exist and earn sufficient income to feed their families while debt repayment is ongoing. That would ensure the existence of the farmer and is absolutely imperative. The Canadian Government must guarantee that free trade will not kill Canadian marketing boards and thereby the Canadian farmer. I do not think any reasoning Member of Parliament would want that situation to occur. Yet the Government has not said that it will protect the marketing board system and supply control system in the Canadian economy.
We all recognize that the Government, to its credit, has placed $1 billion at the disposal of Canadian farmers. It has made efforts to reduce freight rates. There is a certain amount of cynicism about the coinciding of the $1 billion program with the Saskatchewan election, but nevertheless, it was SI billion which moved in the right direction. There is a multimillion dollar program on freight rates which is another move in the right direction. Unfortunately it is not enough. If we are to save the family farm and agriculture there must be a continuing injection of cash to relieve the debt burden of Canadian farmers. That is an absolute must.
Another item of importance is encouraging a rational approach to marketing areas which are not now covered so that farmers can have a price support system which will allow them to produce food for Canadians at prices above the cost of production. As an example, the potato industry in eastern Canada has an extremely important market in the United States. At the same time, potatoes are shipped from the United States to British Columbia and Alberta in almost unregulated amounts at unregulated prices which forces the price of Canadian products below the cost of production.
The anti-dumping tribunal in British Columbia imposed a tariff to stop that importation. The imports have now shifted to Alberta and the Alberta surpluses are now being pushed into British Columbia. Farmers are continually handicapped by the lack of control of potato marketing in Canada. There are many other such areas of concern. A national marketing board which is encouraged to develop the rational marketing of products in Canada would certainly be very useful.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, this moratorium must not be removed. The results would be absolutely chaotic. We must give teeth to the debt management review boards and allow them to make binding agreements between the creditor and the farmer which will keep the farmer on the land. More cash must be put into debt relief by both provincial and federal Governments. We must guarantee Canadians that free trade will not kill Canadian agriculture. Marketing boards must be left intact and given a free hand to manage the Canadian market. Where marketing boards do not exist to provide price and supply stability in the Canadian market they must be encouraged and developed.
Federal and provincial Governments must participate together in this and we must succeed if we want to keep in place something which we all support, namely, the family farm in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this very important debate. However I am somewhat disappointed by some of the reactions of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) who fled like a mouse a moment ago after stating in this House that times are hard when Conservatives are in office. Well, I must say I have an impassioned recollection of the time when the Constitution was brought home, when he was there, and when he proved to be one of the participants responsible for the exclusion of Quebec from the agreement. Today, at Meech Lake, they have been trying to redress these past mistakes.
That being so, I think the important thing now is to concern ourselves with western farmers. Earlier this week the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said in the House: I rather doubt that the major newspapers of this country will give front-page treatment to this question. Sad to say, he was right.
Again today, after so many hours of debate by Members here in the House and given the fact that the three Party leaders want to help western farmers, I was disappointed and surprised that the vital question of western Canada farm community problems was covered in a few short seconds on English TV and not even mentioned on the French network. I must say this really does something to me. 1 cannot understand that our major newspapers and the media would choose to ignore the urgent problems of the residents of a large part of this country. Still, today's La Presse did carry a very interesting article by Pierre Gingras. Mr. Gingras acknowledges, as we do, that there are problems in the agricultural industry. The important thing is, however, that he also acknowledges in his article the work done by the Conservatives, by my Party, by my Prime Minister, by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and by my colleagues during the 30 months we have been in power, to help farm producers.

I remember that when I first came here, and I come from a rural riding, I was not an expert on agriculture. However, just about everything is produced in my riding. Some of my best friends are farmers, and I am in touch with them regularly. I have learned a lot about agriculture. Since this Government came to power, and my colleagues will agree, we have tried to correct the mistakes made by the previous Government with the support of the New Democrats. For two and a half days we have heard the Opposition criticize here in the House every procedure and measure introduced by the Government. They have criticized but they have failed to propose any new approaches to solve the problems of western farmers.
This afternoon, when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) announced that the Government would spend $64 million on the transportation of western grain, I saw opposition Members smile.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: That's not true.

Mr. Speaker, when the Liberals had the floor and were talking their heads off, we suffered in silence. So I would ask opposition Members to return the favour, even if my comments fall somewhat harshly on their ears. How could they be expected to address the problems of the west when they only have a single Member from that area? And let's not forget that the Liberal Leader went out west 32 times in 18 days during the past three weeks. It is unbelievable. Maybe the Party bought him an airplane, but he sure is doing a lot of travelling out west. Thirty-two times in 18 days. That is really something. But maybe that is only media talk. I read that today in the papers.
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that I find unacceptable that those people there in Opposition are bent on destroying and will not recognize all the help this Government has been providing to farm producers. Just the day before yesterday, we were working with the Minister of Transport to try and find a way to reduce costs. It was unacceptable, of course, for the rates to go up 39 per cent while the price of wheat declined 18 per cent. It was unacceptable, and a solution had to be found. We found one: we are proposing to inject $2 per tonne in assistance, so that the increase will only be 5 per cent rather than 39 per cent. And they are scoffing at that. They suggest we do not want to help farm producers.
April 30, 1987
Mr. Speaker, since we were elected, in 30 months, we have taken more than 400 initiatives in agriculture alone. This is one area where we did not cut. Quite the opposite, we have been constantly adding funds for the farm industry. We invested nearly $7 000 million in agriculture, mostly in western Canada of course. There was the dairy policy that benefitted of course Quebec dairy producers. But those are tools that had to be provided to our farm producers, and we did so with very great pleasure.
There is also another aspect the Opposition does not seem to understand. As a Government, we have been working in constant consultation with producers, whether from eastern, central or western Canada. We always consulted them, and the proof is the farmers are pleased with the work we as a Government have been doing in this House. As far as I am concerned, I can state that I am very proud of the work done by my Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, and so on. All my colleagues did a tremendous job on agriculture, this is something that has to be told.
The New Democratic Member earlier referred to concerns over free trade, I must again remind him that a commitment was made here on March 16 that marketing boards are not on the table. And I personally remember seeing Liberals and New Democrats oppose that motion. This is really something. People may have a short memory, but I can tell you we will remind you of that. You voted against that motion. But we have stated on a number of occasions that marketing boards were not on the table. Do you think otherwise we would have introduced the kind of long-term dairy policy that had been requested for years by farm producers? Since 1981 we were calling for a long-term dairy policy, and we came up with it.

Let me finish, you will speak when your turn comes. You will all have an opportunity to speak. The debate has not yet ended my friend. Take your time.
I have taken the liberty, Mr. Speaker, of reading over some speeches made by my colleagues opposite. We now have some 150 pages; or rather, yesterday afternoon at four o'clock, we already had reached 150 pages. Needless to say, I did not find the best speeches among the Liberals or the New-Democrats. I did not find in them any food for thought or any new idea. The Hon. Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) said at the beginning of his speech:
April 30, 1987

-I should like to take this opportunity to state the policies of the NDP-
I could perhaps say that "N" stands for narrow-minded, "D" stands for demagogues and "P" for professional, and this is the New Democratic Party. I did not find anything in that speech. He spoke 20 minutes but said nothing.
If I turn to another agricultural expert, the NDP member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), she said that in order to help western producers, we had to provide them with daycare centres. I do not think that western people need daycare centres this evening. What they needed to know was the announcement made this afternoon by the Minister of Transport, that is they will be given financial assistance of $64 million to help them move their wheat. That is the kind of assistance needed by farmers and it will be provided to them.
We have been carrying out negotiations throughout the world for the first time. There is a detail that is often ignored, Mr. Speaker, because the Opposition does not mention it. There was never a Canadian Prime Minister before the present Prime Minister who demanded that priority be given to agriculture in the GATT negotiations. And that was done at the Tokyo Round. But who asked for it and who did it? A Liberal Government would never have had the nerve to consider such a step. And they are the same people who went out west and laughed at western producers. We told the people in western Canada: We are going to work hard to sell your grain. We told eastern producers: We are going to try and help you sell your products throughout the world. We are going to try and end the world trade war. There is not a single farm producer in this country, Mr. Speaker, who would claim that Canada can sustain a trade war against the United States or against the EEC on grain shipments. I think everybody in Canada realizes, and farm producers certainly do, that if we really want to deal with the problems in the agricultural industry, we will first have to negotiate at the GATT level.
Meanwhile, we have to take action on a day-to-day basis. And as I said earlier, we have taken hundreds of measures in the past 30 months to help the agricultural industry, and I am thinking of apple growers in Quebec and British Columbia, of the new marketing boards that will be set up for potato producers, and so on. Hatchery egg programs have been set up at the request of farm producers. These are some of the things we have done and will go on doing, but listening to the empty speeches of opposition Members here in the House is not going to help the cause of agriculture in this country.
Quite the opposite, Mr. Speaker, it is by trying, and I would very much like, by the end of this debate, to hear the concrete proposals you will be coming up with and to hear also, when you tell us your concrete proposals, how much money is involved and where that money will be coming from. Because there are facts opposition Members seem to forget. You say: "Spend, spend, spend!" but you do not ask where the money will be coming from. This we found out when we came here in
1984, that little surprise of the $240 billion deficit. Except that now the debts have to be repaid. I appreciate that to a New Democrat paying one's debts is not important. Even if we were to mortgage the forty-second generation in this country, that is of no matter to them, because they will be dead. No problem. They will have had their way and let the others pay. But something else is required to manage the country soundly, to show that we are a responsible nation. And the proof we are a responsible nation is that interest rates came down. Why? Because we kept sinking the country lower into debt, or because we had realistic policies?
