speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why has this country become so aroused? Why is it that the House of Commons has now been involved in an emergency debate for three days? It seems that the Government struck a nerve in a way it has so far failed to do in any other thing it has done. The action it has taken has touched hearts and minds and has affected us deeply.
Tonight, the Government is to lift the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures. The lifting of the moratorium has touched the hearts and minds of Members of Parliament and it has certainly aroused the media. The media has reported this debate very fully, despite the comments made by some of my colleagues. The country is aroused because the issue comes down to a simple image which comes to mind, an image which all too many older Canadians hold in their minds from the Great Depression. It is the thought of farms being foreclosed on.
We recall the stereotype of a person dressed in a black suit with a long moustache and a black hat who went from farm to farm with writs of foreclosure in his hands. That image is still in the memories of people who lived during the last Depression and remember the stereotype of the heartless person who would come to the farm to throw the people out after all their lives, hearts and savings had been put into that farm.
We are not simply dealing with vast figures, we are dealing with the thought of a farmer waiting for someone to come and close down his farm at a time when other parts of the country are enjoying great prosperity. It so happens that I represent such a part of the country, the area called the Golden Horseshoe, though we certainly do have problems. It has touched the minds and hearts of people in every part of Canada to realize that, at what is supposed to be the end of the recession, we are seeing situations that remind us grossly of the terrible and bleak days of the worst part of the Great Depression of the 1930s.
The image we have in our minds is that there are people who are down and now we are kicking them. We heard that the Wheat Board announced that prices for 1987 would be 18 per cent lower than they were in 1986, but we knew that in 1986 the prices for wheat were 20 per cent lower than they were in 1985.
As if these blows to people who are trying to stay on the land and have committed themselves to improvements were not hard enough, within a day after the announcement of the reduction in prices the Government made the incredibly insensitive and unfeeling announcement that the moratorium on foreclosures would be lifted. That announcement means an open season on Canadian farmers, some of whom fought in wars, the heart of our country, the pioneers. That they will now suffer this kind of treatment is something that has touched the heartstrings of all Canadians.
What has brought on this debate? It was not another discussion about interest rates, it was this image in our minds. This image is what is hurting our consciences. We cannot go to
bed at night without thinking that things like this could happen to us, and knowing that western Canadians will experience this kind of suffering.
Today the Government announced a reduction in the impact of the blow to farmers caused by new freight rates. Nonetheless, this announcement is still more bad news for farmers, because it amounts to an increase of about 6 per cent in grain freight rates. That is the net result of the so-called good news. The announcement still means that the cost of shipping grain is going up, not down. While the price of wheat goes down, freight rates are still going up and that is another bad piece of news. How could the Government, knowing that this bad news about freight rates was on the docket, then have proceeded to announce the lifting of the moratorium on foreclosures?
Canadians have been aroused by this heartless approach to human situations. It brings back to our minds the worst images of the Great Depression. It brings back to our minds the thought that the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall), who spoke to us a while ago, was able on an emergency basis to rush to the banks with $1 billion-worth of aid. She has not found in her heart a strong enough motive to rush to the Cabinet and call for an end to this attempt to lift the moratorium. Why has she not fought for those people who will suffer now? She was so anxious to save western banks that she found $1 billion. How about throwing $1 billion at western farmers?
We know that the Government did throw $1 billion at farmers in general. We also know that that was linked to an election in Saskatchewan-a very cynical kind of gift. Indeed, members of the Opposition, people from the west and western farmers have been begging and pleading for months, in fact, for years, for that type of assistance. It only came in time to help the Conservatives win a provincial election. That is hardly what people regard as being a responsive, compassionate reaction.
We find that what we are asking for at this moment, what we are calling upon the Government to do, is to stop the cancellation tonight of the moratorium on farm foreclosures. We are asking the Government to have some kind of compassion today and to go to the aid of those who are the weakest among us. That is what we are asking.
I do not think that my colleagues pretend that they have all the answers. Nor do I expect the Government to have all the answers. But the answers that the Government is giving are absolutely unacceptable. What the Opposition can say is that this step is heartless. When the Minister of State for Privatization talked about the fact that her family had been on the farm during the Great Depression and that they almost went under, but the thing that saved them was hard work, was she perhaps implying that it was hard work that was needed on the part of western farmers and maybe if they worked a little harder they too could save their farms? That is not acceptable. We know that many of the people who are facing foreclosure have certainly worked hard enough on their farms.
April 30, 1987

The problem is not that they are not willing to work. It is that the price of wheat has gone down, that the Government has taken away their protection which would give them a further chance to continue their businesses. This is what we are concerned about. This is the type of advice we can give the Government. A five-year old could give that advice to the Government, but it is lacking in compassion and concern for the people who are on the farms and who are facing the possible loss of their way of life, the possible loss of all the work that they have put in and that their parents have put into their family farms.
This is a very cruel moment in the life of the country, which is why this debate has been going on for so many hours. It has struck a nerve. It touches us personally to our hearts that we are living in a country of reasonable affluence and yet we are watching our fellow Canadians face such an unacceptable fate. For what? They do not deserve it.
This is a Government that apparently cannot get its act together. It is unpopular because it apparently cannot show that it has compassion for the people. I ask Elon. Members to consider the various steps that it has taken, whether it be with respect to patent drugs, which shows a lack of concern for senior citizens, or whether it is about the provinces which will have to provide more money for the cost of drugs. The Government has shown no compassion when it talks about cutting rural post office deliveries and eliminating rural post offices. Nor has it shown compassion when we consider the tax system which has, in effect, provided the most terrible blows to people who earn in the area of $15,000 per year.
When we look at the tax increases that have been thrown at these people since this Government has come to power we see that they have increased by 75 per cent while on the other side of the coin those who earn $100,000 find that their taxes have risen by only 4 per cent. That is not compassionate.
Peter Cook, who writes as financial critic for The Globe and Mail, when speaking about the action of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) stated that he has gotten away with raising personal income taxes by 19 per cent, sales taxes by 33 per cent, excise taxes by 18 per cent, and gasoline taxes by 120 per cent. These are enormous increases in taxes. Yet we have a quotation from the same Minister of Finance who has done this to the people of Canada made on August 28, 1984. He said:
We have no intention of raising income taxes to Canadians. What we have to
do is get down government-
He has got down Government. He has got it down on the people. He has certainly raised the taxes and completely broken his promise.
On March 1, 1985, the Minister of Finance said this:
I don't want to increase taxes ... A tax increase, certainly a general tax
increase, puts a dampening effect on the economy and I don't want to see us do
that.
When we look at the way he has structured the taxes he certainly has put a dampening effect on the poor. They are the ones who are paying the taxes while the Government has provided a capital gains relief of $500,000 in a lifetime for those who make much more money.
Yes, this is a Government which lacks compassion in some amazing ways. It seems to be able to come up at the most amazing times with destructive types of decisions that hurt the poor, that make the poor poorer and the rich richer. The small businessman sees higher postal rates. Independent oil companies see their businesses threatened and, in some cases, they have been driven out of business. We saw that sales taxes were imposed when the Government came into power at a rate of 9 per cent. They are now at 12 per cent. In addition, the Government has slapped some brand new taxes on items which relate to hygiene, drugs used by senior citizens and some children's foods. This tax of 12 per cent which the Government has slapped on is a sales tax which is put on to the backs of the poor.
The Minister of Finance has said that such sales taxes are regressive, yet he has resorted to imposing more taxes which hurt the poor because they cannot afford the same taxes that the rich can afford. In other words, if a tax of 10 per cent is placed on a product then a poor person has to pay the same amount of increase as does a rich person. That is why such a tax is regressive. In other words, the impression the Government continues to give, whether in the tax field, the business field or in the area of the Post Office-whatever it seems to touch-seems to hit the chord of hurting the poor, the beaten, the down-trodden. The Government seems to pick on them.
In the case before us the Government has taken the most obscene type of action we have ever seen. We see a situation in which it will foreclose or allow foreclosures on the family farms of hundreds and hundreds of Canadians. I have risen to speak on this matter because I know what is at stake. It is whether or not we have compassion. It is whether or not we will see from the Government a realization that, unless it changes its ways, it will not be at the rate of 24 per cent or 25 per cent support in the polls, but will drop even further, if that is possible, because people everywhere in the country, not just in the centre but even those in the west, will now come to the conclusion that the Government has no ability to show compassion. It seems absolutely unable to get its act together, especially in terms of the west. Even westerners are now losing confidence in the Government. That is too bad.
This situation is threatening our unity. We have always felt a sense that Canada was a whole country, a totality, and that when one part of the country was in need we came forward with equalization payments to try to balance out the situation. We followed the motto "bear ye one another's burdens". That is a compassionate concept. It seems in this particular situation that we are not willing as Canadians to bear one another's burdens at all. We see the Government letting everyone loose, and whatever happens to them the weak ones will fall behind and be eaten up. That is a policy of laissez faire, a policy which they literally are carrying out. In so doing, they conjure up in our minds an image from the Great Depression, the image of a Government that allows its farmers to be put to the wall.

April 30, 1987
A Government that permits foreclosures to take place conjures up the worst images we could possibly have. It is a Government that shows a lack of concern and compassion.
This Government, by its activity and its actions, is threatening Canadian unity. It causes people in the west to think that we in the east do not care. Well, we do. We in the east and in the centre of this country care about what is happening in the west. In this particular case, let it be understood that we do care. We do not want the west to think that there is no future with us; that we don't care, that we have no sensitivity. That is why this Government is indeed in a sense threatening our sense of unity. We must bear one another's burdens; we must care about one another.
Hon. Members opposite can smirk and laugh as much as they wish. They are going down further in the polls. The Hon. Members opposite are laughing at what I am saying. They are free to do that. The people in the west are not laughing, Mr. Speaker; we are not laughing. This is a matter of Canadian unity, Mr. Speaker; it is not a laughing matter.
We have to show concern for our western provinces, because the people in the west really do wonder about us. They wonder whether we easterners do care-and we do.
I conclude my comments with one last plea to the Government, to continue the moratorium on farm foreclosures. The lifting of that moratorium will take effect tonight at midnight, and I plead with the Government to respond to the Opposition, to respond to its own Members, to respond to the people of Canada and in fact continue the moratorium until it has found a better way to find some reasonable protection for our farmers.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this landmark debate on the crisis facing Canadian farmers today.
I should like to start by paying tribute to my colleague, the Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), who initiated this emergency debate a couple of days ago. He is himself a farmer, and he has done a great deal to sensitize those of us in the NDP caucus who haven't been as aware in the past as we should have been of some of the problems and concerns facing Canadian farmers. I am pleased that he has shown this kind of leadership in the House, along with my colleague from, the Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), our spokesperson on agriculture. These two individuals have played a real leadership role, not just within our caucus, but in this House, in bringing to the attention of the Government the concerns facing the farmers across this land.
The crisis facing us relates to the decision announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to lift the moratorium declared on September 17, 1985, on Farm Credit Corporation
foreclosures. It is of some significance that the Government has announced that this moratorium will in fact be lifted on May 1, tomorrow. And what is the significance of May 1? May 1 is May Day.
Mr. Speaker, the farmers of Canada are being hit with the lifting of the moratorium on May Day! May Day is the traditional symbol of distress. I think it is of considerable symbolic significance that this Government, on May Day, should be once again attacking the farmers of Canada by lifting the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures.
We heard earlier from the Minister of State for Privatization (Mrs. McDougall), "Well, you know, it is only a small number of farmers who will be affected; it is only one quarter of 1 per cent of the farmers who will be affected." We heard that from the Minister of State for Privatization, the same Minister who was heard some time ago to say that the motivating factor in our economy is greed. Well, it is not surprising that that Minister should exhibit such a heartless attitude toward those farmers who will be driven off the land as a result of this Government's decision.
I wish to put some figures to the statistic that the Minister so blithely dismissed. My colleagues have already spoken to the breakdown in the various provinces. I wish to speak for a moment about the national implications of the lifting of this moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures.
As of April 1 this year there was a total of 14,597 FCC loans outstanding, 6,000 of which were two years or more in arrears. Of the 6,000 that were two years or more in arrears, some 1,300 are affected by this moratorium. That means that 1,300 families may be driven off the land with the lifting of this moratorium. In some cases, their farms have been handed down from generation to generation, and as a result of this Government's heartless decision these people will now be driven off the land.
The Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) laughs. He laughs at the farmers who are being driven off the land. Well, he will have to answer to the farmers in his constituency for his laughter, and his contempt for their plight.
Even though this Government says that it is only one quarter of 1 per cent who will be affected, the reality is that it amounts to some 1,300 families.
Mr. Speaker, the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine continues to laugh at the farmers of western Canada from behind the curtain. He hasn't even had the courage to speak out in this debate on behalf of the farmers in his constituency. He has been silent, Mr. Speaker. He has been totally silent on the plight of the farmers in Winnipeg-Assiniboine and he will pay the price for that at the next election.
April 30, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I want to talk a bit more about these figures. We have heard from government Members that it will be "only 50 farmers every month who will lose their farms". My colleague from Prince Albert has actually made some inquiries of the Farm Credit Corporation, as a result of which he has learned that the FCC does not have the staff to send out the foreclosure teams to shut down the farms at a rate faster than that. What a disgraceful commentary on this Government's farm policies!
The reality, Mr. Speaker, is that the lifting of this moratorium is going to have devastating consequences on the farmers of western Canada.
It is not just the lifting of moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures that is going to have devastating consequences; it is also the fact that other financial institutions will take this action as a signal that it is open season on those who have defaulted on their loans.
Canadian farmers have accumulated debt in the order of $24 billion. Once the Farm Credit Corporation foreclosure moratorium is lifted, the banks and the other financial institutions will take it as a signal to move in, and yes, Mr. Speaker, it will be open season on farmers.
Last summer I travelled to my constituency by train, and 1 will never forget a family that boarded the train in Moose Jaw. They had lived on a farm that had been in their family for three generations, and they could no longer stay on that farm. They had been driven off their land and were travelling by train to British Columbia to try to make a new life for themselves. That destructive erosion of the family farm in Canada will be repeated in increasing numbers as a result of the Government's heartless decision to lift the moratorium on foreclosures by the Farm Credit Corporation.
Women on the farm have traditionally been among the hardest hit in times of adversity. Not only have women been forced to work off the farm to supplement inadequate incomes, they are increasingly being called upon to do work on the farm without pay. The work which was formerly done by hired hands is now done by women because farmers cannot afford to pay for hired hands. In addition, they continue to perform their traditional roles on the farm, which includes raising children. They are obviously working in partnership with their husbands in many cases, but the reality is that in too many cases it is women who are bearing the brunt of the burden.
As I said, women are being particularly hard hit. They lack retirement security, child care facilities, crisis shelters and women's centres. They are often faced with discrimination from lending institutions.
It is also important to note the harsh personal impact of the financial crisis facing the farming community. In terms of stress, for example, in Saskatchewan farm accidents account for 40 per cent of the fatalities despite the fact that farmers make up only approximately 20 per cent of the labour force. The suicide rate of farmers in Alberta in 1984 was 40 per
100,000 compared to a rate of 15.5 per cent per 100,000 in 1981 and compared to a rate of 18.1 per 100,000 for the rest of the population in 1984. The suicide rate was almost three times greater for farmers than it was for the rest of the population.
The Canadian Mental Health Association learned through a study in Saskatchewan that 88 per cent of the farmers surveyed had experienced stress-related symptoms including health problems such as headaches, mental fatigue, insomnia, depression, anger and frustration which sometimes led to communications problems and alcohol abuse. In Ontario suicide is the number two cause of death on farms following only machinery accidents. We can see that the personal toll of the crisis in the Canadian farming community is very great indeed.
I do not often make reference in the House to a publication called Western Report. Recently in its cover story Western Report dealt with what it called the death of the grain men. Inside it speaks of a requiem for the family farm, of why the small producer is being threatened with extinction. They talk about the attack on one of the country's most revered institutions, the family farm.
I would like to say a word about the family farm. I had the honour of serving as a member of the special joint committee which drafted the Constitution of Canada. I remember that during the course of that debate there was considerable controversy, which has continued to this day, on the question of the inclusion of property rights in the Constitution of Canada. The Conservative Members of Parliament who suggested that we should entrench property rights in the Constitution of Canada are now members of the Government which is driving farmers off their property.
I suggest that the Conservatives should show a little more respect for the property of farmers and for the families who are struggling to maintain their farms after generations. After all, 95 per cent of the farms in Canada are still family farms. I suggest that we show a little more respect for those farmers and their attempts to protect and preserve what is important to them, their property.
I suggest as well that we heed the cry of the Conservative Member of Parliament for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour) who said that the west is being ignored by his Government. That Tory MP from Alberta has thrown up his hands in despair. He said recently that unless the Government gets serious about the problems of western Canada, he will leave that Party.
It is a rather sad commentary that in response to the Conservative Member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) fired him as a Parliamentary Secretary and his colleagues from Alberta slammed the door and excluded him from the Tory caucus. We have not heard from that Member during this debate. He said as well that the Tory Government is creating jobs all right but is only creating them in downtown Toronto.

April 30, 1987
The plea of the Conservative Member of Parliament for Edmonton-Strathcona is being echoed across this land by farmers who are saying to the Government, "For God's sake don't hit us when we're already down". After grain prices dropped 18 per cent last year and 20 per cent the year before, and costs are going up, the Government kicks farmers in the gut on May Day. That is a tragic commentary on the Government's lack of concern for the farmers of our country.
I want to take a moment to speak about what New Democrats believe to be the two key priorities for protecting and strengthening the farm in Canada. First, it is essential that we continue the moratorium on foreclosures which was imposed on the Farm Credit Corporation in September, 1985, until a comprehensive debt reduction program has been put in place. It is important to recognize that many other farmers are not protected by this moratorium. They are at the mercy of private financial institutions, the banks. It seems as though the Canadian Bankers Association is writing the Government's agricultural policy. That association put forward five key points, each and every one of which was accepted by the Government.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) has suggested that farm organizations wanted this moratorium lifted. That is an astonishing suggestion. The National Farmers' Union, the three prairie Wheat Pools, and many other farm organizations have said no such thing. Indeed, they have said the opposite. For example, Keystone Agricultural Producers based in Manitoba has said that the termination of this moratorium will make it much more difficult for farmers to get loans from banks and other lenders.
This is a particularly critical time for farmers because they are now planting their crops and at planting time they must borrow money to purchase fuel, seed, fertilizer and chemicals for the coming crop season. At this particular time of year farmers need even more cash. Keystone Agricultural Producers have said that the Government should not lift this moratorium.
The President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Garfield Stevenson, said that the termination of the moratorium "is completely irresponsible and just not acceptable". Mr. Stevenson went on to say:
I thought the Minister had more on the ball than this.
Those were the comments of the President of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. The President of the National Farmers' Union, Wayne Easter, said the following:
1 just can't understand why he would announce it now ... Normally farmers
feel a sense of optimism at this time of year.. . But this tears the heart out of
thousands of farmers.
When the Minister of Agriculture states, as he did on The Journal last night, that farmers want the moratorium lifted, I must ask: Who is he talking about? He is not talking about Keystone in Manitoba. He is not talking about the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool. He is not talking about the National Farmers' Union. He is not speaking for the thousands and
thousands of farmers who are desperate and want to survive, not be driven off the land.
This brings me to my Final comment in respect of the importance of a guarantee that the income of farmers will be at least at the same level next year as it was this past year. It is essential that farmers who are planting now have confidence that they will get a recovery from what is planted this spring and harvested next fall which is enough to cover their costs and enough, I would add, to ensure a decent standard of living.
This Government which has bailed out banks should surely recognize its responsibility to the farmers of Canada. I point out as well that other countries, including the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, and the EEC, have recognized the importance of ensuring an adequate income for farmers.
In conclusion, I remind the House and those who are watching the debate that my Party was founded at the depths of the Depression in the 1930s. My Party formed the first Government in 1944 in the Province of Saskatchewan. One of the first acts which that Government under Tommy Douglas brought forward was a moratorium on debt for farmers. I am proud of that record of my party in defending farmers in Canada.
I am also proud that myself and my colleagues, led by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and the Hon. Member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse), are continuing in that tradition to defend farmers by calling upon the Government not to lift the moratorium and to ensure adequate income for Canadian farmers.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the temptation is too great for me to let pass the suggestion that I can think of no more appropriate Member than the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) to be speaking in the House about May Day.
Let me also note an irony, if I might, as I begin this debate. We have just heard the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence (Mr. de Corneille) and the Hon. Member for Burnaby giving their views on farm matters. Let me perhaps introduce some balance to the debate by quoting the President of the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, a western organization with a western based president, when he said: "The Canadian Cattlemen's Association supports the decision of Agriculture Minister John Wise to end the temporary debt moratorium on debts to the Farm Credit Corporation". CCA President Stan Wilson also emphasized: "Our concern is that the distortions caused by debt moratoria do more damage to the farm credit system than any possible benefit to individual farmers".
That is the voice of agriculture. They do not want damage to the farm credit system. They want the farm credit system strengthened, and they want the farm situation across the country strengthened, as do we. One characteristic about the farm situation in Canada, which is known to any of us familiar with agriculture, is that it is in a state of crisis now. That is known. That is recognized by every honest Member in the House.
April 30, 1987

Elowever, another characteristic of the Canadian farm community is that it is made up, to a singular degree, of individuals who are honest, who are realistic, and who know that there are no magic solutions. They will have noted, as we did, that in this week alone in the Canadian House of Commons the New Democratic Party has proposed spending new billions of dollars on Dome Petroleum, has proposed spending new billions of dollars on the Post Office, and has proposed spending new billions of dollars on agriculture. Those are the three items proposed by that Party in one week.
Ladies and gentlemen-excuse me, Mr. Speaker, I have been away from the House of Commons too long-there may be disagreements here about how some of these problems can be resolved. However, there is no illusion among the agricultural community in Canada about the fact that the long-term solutions to the problems with which we are dealing will not come easily.
I had the good fortune-and I will not pretend to be a farmer-to grow up in an agricultural community in western Canada. One thing which is evident to all of us who had that experience is that when the farm community is in crisis, it is not a local or isolated crisis. It speaks of a region in crisis; indeed, to some degree, a whole economy in crisis. When there are problems in agriculture, they extend to every other part of the large rural community.
That is not something we read about. That is something that if one grew up in Viking in Vegreville, as did the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), or in Provencher, Manitoba; or in wartime Saskatchewan; in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan; or in Drumheller, Alberta, or in High River, Alberta, as did Members of the Cabinet, one grew up knowing the realities. Because the Cabinet of Canada is composed today of men and women who grew up directly with the cyclical and deep problems agriculture faces, we understand that the problems will not be resolved suddenly. We understand that there must be a very serious effort on the part of the Government of Canada, domestically and internationally, to solve some of the problems.
It is not a matter of getting up and saying, as a former Prime Minister unhappily did, that he is not going to sell your wheat. We have an obligation to try to sell the wheat of the farmers of Canada. We have an obligation to try to achieve a better international trading system. We have an obligation, when there is a crisis in farm income, to inject money into the western Canadian economy and the whole Canadian economy.
The Government has accepted that obligation. We will continue to do that. Indeed, the record of the Government in terms of action on agriculture is unsurpassed in the last two decades or three decades in Canada. Most farmers understand that and respect that.

speechtext:
1 take part in this debate as both a western Canadian and as the foreign Minister of the country. I
have been back in my constituency speaking, among others, to people operating centres for women in small towns like Whitecourt. There is a crisis there. There is the implication for farm families, as has been indicated by the Minister of State responsible for the Status of Women and others in the House. That is part of the reality.
The sense of crisis in Canadian agriculture is deep and is growing. In Barrhead and in Fort Assiniboine in my constituency, the price of barley today is in real terms about what it was in the 1930s. Some 50 farmers in Manitoba declared bankruptcy in the last year. In Saskatchewan there were 45. In Alberta there were 93. In Ontario there were 102.
Costs of production continue to climb as prices drop. A growing number of farmers have to work out to keep their operations going. Many individual farm families face the prospect of having to get out of agriculture. The problems are complex. Nobody, least of all farmers, pretends that there are easy solutions either at home or internationally.
The Government has acted on a wide range of agricultural issues. We have delivered relief from capital gains tax. We have frozen freight rate and elevator handling charges on grain handling and on grain transportation. We twice amended the Western Grain Stabilization Act so that it is now a true instrument for stabilization. We have established a farm debt review board. We have removed federal sales and excise taxes from farm fuels.
Last year, in the face of grave crisis, we committed $1 billion to grain producers under the Special Canadian Grains Program. Not counting that $1 billion expenditure, the budget for the federal Department of Agriculture last year was 60 per cent higher than it was the year before the Government took office. With all of that spending on agriculture, our over-all fiscal management has been so successful that the interest rates farmers pay are from 4 per cent to 5 per cent lower than they were three years ago.
Our calculations are that every 1 per cent drop in interest rates results in approximately $240 million for Canadian farmers. These actions are important. They are only part of the program for agriculture of the Government. The priority of agriculture in the Government is high and is growing.
There was a comment made by one of the Hon. Members opposite who talked about the need for Canadian farmers to have confidence about money which will be coming in next year. The projections for federal Government spending next year for support for western Canadian agriculture suggests that there will be more than $3 billion going from the Government, that is, in 1987 and to western Canadian agriculture. That means that western Canadian farmers can have confidence that in calendar 1987, there will be more money coming to them from this Government than there was in calendar 1986. That is simply a projection of reality and one that should be understood across Canada.

April 30, 1987

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I will speak tonight particularly about farm policy and foreign policy because if they were once separate, they now come together. There is a constant and a clear interlinking between what happens in foreign capitals and what happens in every farm across Canada. Every day, political decisions in Paris, in Washington, in Moscow and in other capitals affect the markets and prices for Canadian farmers. Mikhail Gorbachev is a very important man to the farmers in Fort Assiniboine and Barrhead in my constituency.
The common agricultural program of the European Community has done as much damage to the farmers of Alberta as the National Energy Program did to our oil workers. Let me talk for a moment about the European Community and the problems that have been built into the whole system of agriculture as a result of the policies of that Community.
The European Community has changed from a net importer to a major exporter of farm commodities. For example, in the crop year ending 1966, the European Community imported nearly 11 million tonnes of cereal crops. Sixteen years later in the crop year ending in 1982, the European Community exported well over 6 million tonnes. That trend has continued and it has continued because of a growing program of subsidy that has become a pattern in Europe and has been responded to by subsidies in the United States. It is catching the farmers of Canada, the farmers of Thailand and the farmers of other countries that are efficient in production but do not have giant treasuries to subsidize agriculture in a very serious domestic and international problem.
In 1958, the European Community exported only 23 per cent as much food as it imported. By 1985, the Community exported 60 per cent as much food as it imported. Even considering the fact that the Community had expanded its membership significantly over that period, increasing population by 60 per cent, that is a dramatic turnaround in food production and it has to do with subsidy.
European farmers receive prices for commodities which are as much as four or five times the world market price. For example, European farmers get the equivalent of $450 Canadian per tonne for Durum wheat when world markets indicate that is worth something just over $100 Canadian. Canadian farmers receive $130 Canadian for that. Another example is barley for which prices in my constituency are down to Depression year levels. European farmers get the equivalent of $400 per tonne of barley while the European Community sells that same barley for $80 per tonne or less on world markets. That means that the export subsidy alone on barley is five times the current world market price. That is the problem facing agriculture in this country and in others. The question is, what do we do about it.
That is a serious question. It is too serious a question for mere partisan division and debate. It is a very basic and serious problem. Let me tell the House about some of the things we are doing about it. We are acting on a number of fronts internationally.

Mr. Speaker, we are seeking new markets for Canadian products. This of course includes traditional activities such as negotiating an agreement with the Soviet Union for the purchase of 25 million tonnes of Canadian grain over the next five years. Actually, despite a massively subsidized and fiercely competitive world grain market, we managed to increase our market share by nearly 2 per cent last year. It is true that prices were low, but we are better off increasing our market share even if prices are low, than losing on both counts.
This trade initiative also includes new sales to Egypt and Brazil and more possibilities in the Pacific Rim. We have food aid programs in Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Ethiopia, Jamaica, Sri Lanka, Sudan, Tunisia, Peru, Senegal, Mozambique and Ghana. These programs have resulted in the purchase of $163 million worth of Canadian wheat, $47 million worth of Canadian flour, $61 million worth of canola and $51.8 million worth of other products.
Some of these development programs have modified the consumer and production habits of other countries, thus creating new markets for Canadian products.
We also promote agriculture related trade as often as possible, and we do so in two ways. One example is a recent visit to the Soviet Union by the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board and Canadian business people. That country is our biggest wheat buyer. If the Soviet Union would rather deal with Canada it is partly due to our reputation as a reliable supplier. The interest of the Soviets can also be attributed to the fact that we actively seek Canadian markets for their products so as to achieve a better trade balance. Progress comes slowly, but this initiative on the part of Canada is essential if we expect to continue to have access to the major market which the Soviet Union represents.
In another vein, we encourage Canadian agricultural service industries to expand their activities at the international level. Last September in Venezuela and Argentina I headed a delegation including representatives of Canadian agricultural companies. This enabled companies like Regina's Prairie Microtech and Calgary's Agriteam to explore new possibilities of trade and business markets in joint ventures in South America. This way, Canada's contacts in the agricultural sector are increasing in countries where new markets might open up for commodity harvests, technology or Canadian know-how.

And in the Middle East.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext:
There are possibilities in the Pacific, and this is a part of what we have to do as a country and a part of what we are now doing.

Most important, we are tackling head-on the fundamental international agricultural problem and that is the problem of international subsidy. It is as threatening to agriculture in the 1980s and 1990s as the drought was in the Depression. The agricultural trading system is in deep trouble with artificially depressed international prices, subsidized export competition and a growing proliferation of non-tariff import barriers.
We have two complementary goals. The first is to break the cycle of subsidy which has led to the trade war between Europe and the United States, a war whose casualties grow in Canada, in Australia, in Thailand and in a dozen other countries whose treasuries are too small to compete with the European Community or the United States. The second is to establish fair, firm international rules of trade in agriculture, rules that will increase the role of efficient producers and reduce the role of direct and indirect subsidies and protection.
Let me recount to the House briefly some of our experiences in the last year. Almost a year ago exactly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and I were at the meeting of the OECD in Paris and we heard to our great surprise Ministers speaking for European Governments beginning to criticize the common agricultural program. That had not happened before. I must tell the House that the Ministers who uttered those criticisms were Ministers of Finance, not of Agriculture, the people who have to pay for the subsidy programs. However, that was an indication that there might be a possibility of change in European attitudes toward subsidy in the Community. We did not simply note that as a phenomenon. We came back to Canada, we sat down with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and we developed together the opportunity that existed for a country like ours to take advantage of these changes that were developing in the Community, to take advantage of the possibility of some self-questioning, to begin to break this terrible, crippling cycle of subsidy.
The Prime Minister of Canada took to the economic summit in Tokyo as Canada's principal emphasis in that summit the need to give priority to breaking the cycle of international subsidy in agriculture.
I have been to three economic summits. I know that not before-at least not before my experience-has there been a situation in which the President of the United States, the President of France, the Chancellor of West Germany and other leaders have been forced to defend practices which they themselves found difficult to defend in the summit context about agricultural subsidy. One of the European leaders who was there, and I will not identify the country, made a very significant comment. During a discussion that would not have occurred without the initiative of the Prime Minister of
Canada he said that everyone recognized that this was a problem that everyone shared but that no one could solve on their own. Recognizing that, Canada proposed at the summit that we should try to solve it together.
We came away from the summit and tried to put in place a very special experiment in international relations. We tried to put together a special group of leading international experts who might in preparation for the Venice Summit coming up in June be able to identify subsidy practices in each of the summit countries on which action could be taken at Venice. We were making progress on that proposal. We had funding from foundations in Canada and the United States. We had agreement from several countries, including the United States. We had the enthusiastic interest of countries such as Thailand, Argentina and others. For a while we had the agreement of some European countries. Then one European country said that, no, they would not agree. The proposal then came apart. We were not able to proceed with what may have been-what had the promise of being-a Canadian breakthrough in this cycle of subsidy. That did not work. But it was very much worth trying, as it is very much worth trying for this country to find other means by which we can break the cycle of agricultural subsidy that is at the root of the problem being discussed in this House and the problem being felt on farms across the country.
We have acted on other fronts. I led the Canadian delegation to the GATT talks in Punta del Este, Uruguay, last year. In the past, agriculture has been a casualty of the GATT. It has been something that has been shunted aside when nations gathered together to deal with international trading rules. Well, this year that was changed. While there were many countries which took part in the change, one of the leaders in achieving that change was this country and this Government. We do not believe that the world can long afford to put agriculture to the sidelines. We do not believe that when new trading rules are put together they can treat agriculture as though it were unimportant.
Agriculture is essential. Fair trade in agriculture is essential. If we are going to achieve that then we have to have trading rules that are acceptable to and guide the practices of countries around the world. We have made a start on that. We have made a start on that in the GATT. But, again, there is much more that needs to be done. Again, this Government is exerting our leadership to try to ensure that we are able to make that type of progress.
There was a group established, as a result of an Australian initiative, with our active help. It is the so-called Cairns Group, a group of a number of countries such as Canada, in conditions such as ours, victims of the subsidy practices of the Community and of the United States, which gathered together in Australia to prepare for the GATT negotiations in Uruguay. Within three weeks that group will meet again in Ottawa at the invitation and under the chairmanship of the Government of Canada. We think that that type of pressure has to be maintained.

April 30, 1987
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling that my time is up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not abuse the generosity of the House. I appreciate the fact that there is real interest in what we are trying to do internationally. I very much hope that we will be able to make progress in the meeting that the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), along with my colleagues, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), will be convening in Ottawa.
There are two other important meetings coming up in the immediate future. One is the next meeting of the OECD in Paris in two weeks' time. The other is the summit in Venice. It is the intention of the Government to continue at Venice the initiative which the Prime Minister of Canada began in Tokyo, and to continue in the context of the economic summit to try to reach agreement on some progress against the practice of subsidy. We are not sure we will succeed. We know we are asking fundamental changes in practices and traditions that have grown up, particularly in Europe, but the size of the challenge should not turn us away. The size of the damage has to drive us to try to achieve some change. As we did in Tokyo, and as we did in Cairns and Uruguay, and as we will do in Paris, we intend at the economic summit meeting in Venice to try to get some progress.
The Prime Minister raised the matter at the meeting earlier this month when the President of the United States was here. He has raised it in a number of other direct conversations with other summit countries. We hope to make progress.
Finally, and not to abuse the time of the House, we have in the context of the OECD the grouping together of modern economies. We have suggested that there might be agreement on some basic principles regarding international trade in agriculture. We have been in touch with all of the Governments of the OECD and we have set forth some principles that we hope might be the basis of the approach we all can follow together as an alternative to the subsidy cycle that has been so devastating to our economy.
Those principles are, first, that agricultural policies must become more price-responsive. Second, support for agriculture should avoid production incentives. In other words, support should be for farmers and not for farming. Third, countries should freeze and seek to reduce governmental assistance measures that artificially depress world prices. Four, countries should not introduce new import barriers that are not already mandated by existing legislation. Finally, and this is essential to it all, these basic principles must be implemented by us all, together. As was set out at the Tokyo Summit, this is a problem we all face. None of us can solve it alone. But if we cannot solve it alone then a country such as Canada can at least exercise leadership in trying to get it solved. That is what we are doing and that is what we intend to do.
In the last year alone the Prime Minister has held three formal meetings with leaders of Canadian agriculture organizations. I do not believe that that has ever happened before in Canada. It will happen again prior to his departure for the economic summit in Venice because we have found before that in terms of the effectiveness of our case internationally and in terms of consensus at home it is very valuable to draw in the leaders of agriculture in this country.
So what the Government is doing in agriculture is continuing action at home that is unprecedented in recent decades. We are carrying out extensive and continuing consultation with farm leaders. We are maintaining a very vigorous pressure internationally to change the cycle of subsidy that is at the basis of our international agricultural problems.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this very important debate on a crucial matter to the economy of Canada and, in particular, to the western economy. I want to begin by congratulating all of those Members who have participated in the debate because the subject matter is of great national importance and it ought to be debated in that way.
It was my hope, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) would have availed himself of the opportunity-and perhaps he would have had the time available to him-to talk about the recently announced sale by the United States of 4 million tonnes of wheat to the Soviet Union and what that sale will do to the price of grain in Canada and what it will do to the economy Canada.
It was my hope, too, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have responded, in some measure, to the letter forwarded to him today by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).
April 30, 1987

As that letter is now a public document, I should like to take a moment to read it into the record. It is as follows:
It has come to my attention that the U.S. Department of Agriculture has today prepared a new set of agricultural trade subsidy initiatives that include measures of great damage to Canada.
Specifically they are proposing to include under the Export Enhancement Program an offer of 1.25 million metric tons of barley to Saudi Arabia, a traditional Canadian buyer.
If this measure is approved by the Trade Review Committee of the U.S. administration in the next week, it will mean a loss of 75 to 85 million dollars to Canadian farmers.
This initiative certainly flies in the face of assurances apparently gained from President Reagan that he would be considerate of Canadian agricultural concerns, and I would ask you to immediately demand that this damaging measure by the U.S. administration be withdrawn.
Mr. Speaker, those are just two initiatives with regard to the foreign policy aspect of this subject that I would have hoped the Secretary of State for External Affairs would have touched upon during the course of his remarks, and perhaps at another time, or indeed later in this debate, he may want to expound upon them.
Government Members have stood in this place and talked about some programs and some initiatives that have taken place over the last two and a half years. I have listened to their speeches quite attentively, both from my place here in the Chamber and through the Oasis system that is available in our offices.
Mr. Speaker, it is their job to talk about government programs and initiatives. The issue before the House in this debate is the present crisis and what the Government is prepared to do about it. I do not believe that on any side of this House any Member is questioning what the problem is.
No Member-and I may have missed the speeches of a few of the speakers in this debate; a great many have spoken-no Member has disagreed with the fact that there is a crisis situation in the western economy as it relates to grain producers. The question is: Does this Government have the political will to address the situation? But to cite the benefits, chapter and verse, is not going to help the farmers who are in a crisis situation today. And no doubt there are some benefits arising from such programs as the Rural Transition Program. The establishment of the farm debt review boards is another initiative that they hauled out.
The problem is that the Government, up until now, has been refusing to address the very serious crisis situation existing in the western Canadian economy.
Mr. Speaker, I know something about crises. I know something about setbacks. I know about property foreclosures. I have seen entire families and subdivisions of families move out of communities. We in Atlantic Canada know something about that.
What is required, Mr. Speaker, is not only goodwill, good intentions, or even a meaningful and dynamic record, but the political will on the part of the Government of the day to exercise its authority, both legally and monetarily, in order to address the situation.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has some 225,000 farms, of which 175,000 are commercial farms. The Farm Credit Corporation estimates that 8 per cent, or 13,000 farms are insolvent. Of those 13,000, 6,000 have not made any payments on their loans for at least two years. Some 52,000, or approximately 30 per cent of Canadian commercial farms are facing moderate to serious financial stress. Real interest rates paid to farmers are as high or higher than they were at their peak in the early 1980s. An example: The current real farm interest rate is about 6.57 per cent, while it was 8 per cent to 8.5 per cent in 1981.
Members opposite have said that only 600 farmers a year are going to be affected, or 50 a month. Mr. Speaker, do you realize the consequential effects of that? And I am thinking not only of the symbolism of the Government of Canada foreclosing on 600 farmers a year, but the consequential effects on the Canadian banking community, on unsecured creditors, on secured creditors. The trustees in bankruptcy will be the real winners when it comes to the moratorium on foreclosures.
Surely the people of western Canada and those individuals who have their loans with the Farm Credit Corporation are entitled to some sense of fairness. Mr. Speaker, I was part of a Government that was stupid enough to implement an audit program for fishermen of Atlantic Canada. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the lifting of this moratorium is just as stupid if not more stupid than what we did some years back.
It is really not appropriate to be partisan in this debate, but I can tell you that we paid dearly for that mistake, and I suggest that this Government will pay just as dearly as a result of this action against the farmers of western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, much has been said and much has been omitted in the debate which has taken place in the Chamber over the last two days. April 30, 1987
high interest rates. It wasn't the international situation. It wasn't the economies of the superpowers or of the European Community that had to do with interest rates; it was you, the terrible Government". Now that the tables have turned and the western grain producer is in this situation they look to the heavens, they look behind them, they look to the media, to the Opposition and, when they are really desperate, they look to the NDP. You cannot have it both ways. Parliament is a place to which men and women of good faith come to tell it like it is. We are here for one reason. Some may interpret it differently, but there is one unequivocal reason why all Members of Parliament are in this Chamber and serving in public life, and that is to serve.
The question is not one of what the problem is and not one of what the solutions are, but simply of where the political will is to exercise the authority which the national Government has on this issue. 1 can say proudly that yes, I have travelled to western Canada and no, I am not a farmer, but I have listened to their plea, I have heard their argument, and I sympathize with them greatly. They do not want any handouts from Government. They do not want to be on their knees. They only want an equal chance which the Constitution has guaranteed them. Instead we have heard rebuttals, deferment, and that they are considering it.
The latest gimic is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). He is going to take two planes, four cameras, a couple of bearers in Gucci shoes and go to western Canada to make a whistle-stop tour. Does anyone want to make any wagers that the Prime Minister will be announcing a few cheques along the way? He is a political opportunist. Members may laugh, but if I am wrong they can come back into the Chamber and raise it. This is shameful.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) has said clearly time and time again in the House, outside the House, in western Canada, in Atlantic Canada, in Toronto and in Montreal that the Government must announce deficiency programs so that farmers can make their plans for this and subsequent crop years. He has said that the Government must reinstate the FCC moratorium on farm foreclosures and that it must put a proper debt restructuring program in place. Those are three things that we do not have to ask the United States or the European Economic Community for. Canada can do those things today.
In concluding my brief remarks on this most important subject matter I say sincerely that I have listened to what Members from western Canada have been saying and I will continue to listen. I believe the way in which to solve this particular crisis is to show some real leadership domestically. You cannot go on the international stage and say one thing then do the opposite domestically. Canada must be consistent. That is why I raised in my initial remarks the conduct of our neighbours to the south who have continuously, since entering
preliminary negotiations with regard to a free trade agreement, been giving it to us in the neck.
Let it be clear, Mr. Speaker, that I am not anti-American. I may be anti-United States administration, but I find the people of the United States to be a great people. I do not like it when a sovereign nation such as Canada is continuously and repeatedly confronted by the administration to the south which, for its own reasons, selfish as they may or may not be, singles out Canada and the sectors of our economy which are suffering as a result of the lack of leadership of the present administration. Much can be said and much more ought to be said. The Government will pay the price.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to participate in this debate. I had visions of not being able to participate in it because I was up in northern Saskatchewan when I heard about it and was afraid it would be all over by the time I got back. When I arrived yesterday afternoon the debate appeared to be over and I was afraid I had missed out. I am pleased to be here and participating now.
I was in Lac La Ronge in northern Saskatchewan participating in an agricultural meeting of the native population of northern Saskatchewan. It was a meeting of SIAP, the Saskatchewan Indian Agricultural Program, which is intending to expand the agricultural base.
My background is as a seedgrower and farmer from the northeast corner of Saskatchewan about 20 miles from where the trees start, north of which there is no farming. We grow a tremendous variety of crops and while we are certainly affected by the fight between the European community and the United States we have a bigger variety of markets. The crops of wheat, oats, barley, canola and flax seed have been affected very seriously as have other crops which may not be considered very important in the larger scheme of things in the prairie provinces.
April 30, 1987

However, dehydrated alfalfa, dried pea, lentils, fava beans, canary seed, some mustard and such, have been very seriously affected and did not qualify for subsidy under the special Canadian grains program, much to the disappointment of some of those growers. They grew many of these crops to relieve the over-production problem and were hoping to find a market for these lesser grown crops which cannot be grown in areas farther south.
Last year we had some good crops of grass seed and alfalfa. The prices were very good. There was a bright spot in that particular area. However, the biggest bulk of our acreage is in common crops. Certainly our farmers are hurting simply because input costs are very much higher than they are farther south.
Fortunately the Conservative Government has been able to help my constituents ever since it came into power in September, 1984. The very first time it helped was in an area in my constituency which suffered from a lot of rain and severe flooding. The Conservative Government subsidized these people to the tune of $7.5 million. Perhaps that does not sound like a great deal of money, but that particular area had been without crops for a good many years and the provincial Government also put up $7.5 million. This helped to save some of those farmers. They certainly appreciated it. I am sure some of them would not be there today had it not been for that particular help. Of course, they have participated in all the rest of the programs which most of the previous speakers have covered. I am sure you are quite familiar with them, Mr. Speaker.
There has been much rhetoric on the part of the Opposition about the lifting of the moratorium on FCC mortgages. I checked what some opposition Members have been saying about this particular matter. So far in my study of the "blues" I have found nothing that made much sense in terms of a solution on the part of the Opposition. As a matter of fact, one of the reasons I am here is because I became kind of angry sitting on a tractor one day and said: "I guess I'll have to do something about it". I got involved in politics simply because of some of the policies which were in place.
I know that members of the NDP have supported the Liberals. I heard much rhetoric from them about money going out of the country for various reasons. In 1982 when they changed the Farm Credit Act from being an assistance to farmers to a banking institution, the situation was made much tougher on farmers, simply because they were borrowing money on long-term agreements and at long-term interest rates which are very difficult for farmers to get out of. The New Democrats supported the Liberals on that particular one.
Since 1982 I believe $1.3 billion has been borrowed in the way of long-term money by FCC and over 50 per cent of the interest on that money goes to countries other than Canada. I
wonder how the NDP can say that it supports farmers when all this money is going out of the country and not recirculating back to farmers. It is very interesting that they come to these conclusions when it suits them to be critical, forgetting some of the mistakes they have made themselves.
We must have a little optimism in the farm area. I know there are some sections in agriculture, particularly in western Canada, and in livestock in eastern Canada, which have improved the outlook of farmers. In western Canada the livestock industry is doing well. The cattle and hog industries are doing well. Grass seeds and other products such as lentils are doing well. It is not a complete bust in the over-all farm economy picture. Those who are prudent are able to survive. They are not able to make money but they are able to survive.
The hope of the recovery of farm prices is always there. There is only a slight difference between surplus and shortage. Not long ago in the House we worried about hog producers. There was much talk about supply-management and various short-term solutions. However, the United States came out with a 7 per cent decrease in the farrowing of hogs some three months to six months ago, and the prices have certainly increased considerably. The same could happen to the price of some grains, perhaps all of them. Who knows?
It is a pretty good thing that some of the previous speakers in the Opposition are not the farmers out there. It is probably a good thing that farmers are all busy in the fields these days and not watching this particular performance.

As the convict said to the judge, "No, noose is good news". I do have some good news. I have the pleasure of announcing today, for the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), that the cheques for the initial payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Act were mailed today. I have some figures here that will help put a little smile on some western farmers' faces. To Saskatchewan, my home province, 57,713 cheques were mailed out, to the tune of $382 million. That will be a big help to the economy of that particular province. To Alberta, 34,950 cheques were sent, to the tune of $184 million. To Manitoba, 20,589 cheques were sent, to the tune of $134,100,000. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to take part in this emergency debate, although I must confess that, contrary to the Minister, 1 am not a first-class expert in the area of agriculture. But there is no need to be an expert in that area to realize that the actions taken by this Government are typical of a Government which unfortunately does not care about the future of hundreds and even thousands of farm producers who are affected by them. And even if my friend who has just concluded his remarks could mention a few measures taken by the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, I do not believe they are adequate and will really solve the problem which has made this emergency debate necessary.
This emergency debate was initiated following the insensitive announcement by the Government Monday morning that it was ending the moratorium in effect since February 17, 1985, on the loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation. It is a tragedy, Mr. Speaker, and it is not without reason that it was described as a historic event. With this decision, the Government is destroying the way of life of the family farm. It is attacking farmers at a time when they are already in a position of weakness, losing their self-reliance and have realizing that the Government is not going to help them at all. That is why they are calling on their elected representatives to emphasize their very severe economic plight and that of their families. They are asking for programs to be implemented right away. They are asking the Prime Minister to set up without delay federal-provincial programs which might allow them to remain on their farms, and more specifically to provide them right away with significant deficiency payments for the 1987-88 crop year.
In spite of all that, Mr. Speaker, the Government dares tell farmers and Members of this House that its last gesture will only have a slight effect on farmers generally. It dares say so when it knows quite well that in fact, its action could be
disastrous for all farmers affected. However, there will not be any disaster, because as a result of pressures made by farmers in the three Prairie provinces, the Government will have no option but to make specific commitments on the matter. It will have no option, if it wants to continue to boast about everything it does for farmers.
In the first place, with respect to declining prices for various grains, farmers want to know what will happen during the 1987-88 crop year and whether the Government will maintain the level of agricultural assistance, and they want to be informed right now. The Government should tell them under what circumstances a deficiency payment will be made under a special grain program and what the amount of such payment will be.
As I said, the Government should clearly and unequivocally announce what assistance it will grant farmers during the current crop year. As a result of the measure hastily taken by the Minister when he removed the moratorium on foreclosures made by the Farm Credit Corporation, that decision has raised to an intolerable level the stress experienced by thousands of farmers.
The initiative taken by the Minister will allow foreclosures against farmers who are in arrears in the reimbursement of loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation, loans which represent 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the long-term debt in the agricultural sector. There are arrears of over two years on some 6,000 of the 75,000 loans granted by the Farm Credit Corporation and in such a case the organization almost always decide to proceed with the foreclosure.
It is not 25 per cent, as suggested by the Minister responsible, but approximately 8 per cent of farmers who obtained a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation who are threatened with foreclosure. The Minister said that we should not worry, that there will be only some 50 foreclosures a month, that the staff of the Farm Credit Corporationm cannot do more and consequently, the number of farmers who have some reasons to fear foreclosure is restricted to 600. What a joke, Mr. Speaker. How can we know, as the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) asked, what are, among the 6,000 loans which could lead to a foreclosure, the 600 cases which will actually be foreclosed? That is what the bank manager will ask the farmer who is seeking a loan to continue his operation. If the manager tells him that the Farm Credit Corporation is carrying out foreclosures, the farmer will be able to reply that he should not be concerned about that, the Minister having indicated that there will not be more than 600 foreclosures a year out of 6,000. He may add that if he is the last one, his property will not be foreclosed before 10 years from now.
This moratorium has been in effect for the past 19 months. The Government should have used this time to devise a debt restructuring mechanism to help farmers. If it had acted then, there would have been no need for a moratorium, but the Government has failed to act and the moratorium was useful in gaining time.
April 30, 1987

In the meantime, however, no debt restructuring mechanism was set into place. In my opinion, we should continue the moratorium and take this opportunity to devise better programs.
Mr. Speaker, so much for the actions taken by the Government which are causing farm families to go bankrupt, filling them with anxiety and spreading distress as well as financial, economic and social destruction in the agricultural community.
Only a Minister of Agriculture perfectly insensitive to the reality of the situation could make such decisions. The Government did not consult the interested parties to try and find a solution. It has even failed to meet with the farm producers, as well as the representatives of both the federal and provincial governments, the farm organizations and the banking institutions.
When we asked in the House whether it would be useful to meet with the banking institutions which are holding 69 per cent of the loans to discuss this issue, the Minister in turn asked: Why should we do so? Why should we discuss the situation with the banks? We know why the Government should talk to banks. It is because all bankers today are telling themselves, when reading the statement made last Monday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise): If the Government can foreclose, why can't we? They will start looking at their overdue loans.
When farmers start canvassing, looking for loans in order to produce, looking for credit for the coming crop year, how do you suppose those banks will react, Mr. Speaker, after the Government of Canada made that shameful and despicable announcement that it is lifting the moratorium and will let the FCC's mechanism shatter farm communities? This is an open invitation to banks and other financial institutions to follow suit. What is now preventing them from doing so? How could they feel obligated when the federal Government, which normally has a duty to look after farmers, when a public institution or at least what used to be one behaves in such a way?
We are faced with a crisis that requires immediate action to save family farms in western and eastern Canada. It is not good enough for Conservatives to refer to what they have done-they must solve the present crisis. They cannot rest on their laurels. This is not good enough, it will not help people through the current crisis.
Our Party urges the Government to do something. It must recognize that farmers are now in a very tight situation. It must recognize the emergency situation. Now is the time to act, not six months down the road. Farmers must be given a chance, they must be allowed to adequately plan their crops. Our Party urges an extension of the moratorium, to avoid unnecessary stress to farmers. Our Party also urges the announcement now of a price support program for this year's crop, in order that western and other Canadian farmers know where they stand. It is my hope that the Government will act before midnight, so that the odd hundred farm producers in
Quebec who are facing foreclosure will not be penalized and hit by those foreclosures.
