speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to take part in this emergency debate on the crisis our Canadian farmers are going through. Since I represent a city riding, one might wonder what kind of an impact my opinion can have, but as a Canadian woman I am concerned about the well-being of all our farmers.
The crisis our farmers are in right now will affect all of us at a certain point in time. We are all consumers and we all need a strong and healthy agricultural sector. I am glad that the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) mentioned figures in his remarks. Otherwise, the Government might have eluded the problem once again. The Hon. Member for Algoma suggested Tuesday night that the Government had to take a clear position and make a commitment to assist our farmers before it is too late.
On Canada AM this morning, the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board clearly demonstrated that the Government, by dropping the moratorium, really does not want to help farmers. Yesterday afternoon, the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) blamed the Opposition for its refusal to congratulate the Government on its initiatives on behalf of this sector of our economy. There really is not much reason to congratulate the Government. Canadian voters will keep in mind the horrible nightmare our farmers are going through because of this Government.
It is hard to imagine that a technologically advanced country like Canada can show such indifference to our farmers. Our farmers have always been proud to contribute to our economy, but now we penalize them by forcing them to abandon their way of life, their farm, and their means of subsistance.
That economic sector affects our daily life the most. Dairy products, vegetables and grain products are always present on our tables. It is high time we give back some dignity to our farmers.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made the electoral commitment to assist this sector of our economy.
They try to sweeten the pill in each Speech from the Throne through tax initiatives that are beneficial to farmers. Yet today, they blatantly turn around in order to better stab them in the back. Our farmers are discouraged.
Let us face the problem. Many farmers throughout the country and especially those in the west have financial problems for various reasons. According to the figures reported by Ralph Ashmead, Research and Development manager of the Canada Farm Credit Corporation, 68.8 per cent of our farmers have a stable financial situation; 23.2 per cent have cash flow problems whereas 8 per cent are insolvent. In Saskatchewan, 11.4 per cent of farmers are insolvent and in Alberta 9.9 per cent of them are. Those are, I believe, the two most deeply affected provinces. According to an article published in The Ottawa Citizen dated April 28, 1987, and I quote:

April 30, 1987

The average FCC loan is about $120,000. An average of 22 per cent of loans to western producers are in arrears, compared to 17 per cent in Ontario and 9.6 per cent in Quebec. In the Atlantic provinces, the percentage of loans in arrears ranges from 17 per cent in Nova Scotia to 33 per cent in Newfoundland.

Mr. Jules Modderman, of the FCC, said:

Only 2 to 3 per cent are in danger of losing their farms.

Only 2 per cent to 3 per cent is not serious for our friends in the Government. For the Liberal Party, Mr. Speaker, it is far too much. It is easy for us, Members of Parliament, sitting comfortably in Ottawa with our generous salary, to say as that public servant did that only 2 per cent to 3 per cent of our farmers may lose their farms. It is easy to speak heartlessly about a bankruptcy when we are not personally affected. For our farmers, things are different. It is often a family farm handed down from generation to generation. Our farmers have developed that land with their hands like a sculptor has a work of art.
The Liberal Party is asking today that the moratorium that has existed for over a year and a half be maintained. This is the basis of all our social programs. In the past, we thought it right to assist the unemployed until they could find work. Today, when the price of grain is at the same level as in the thirties, the Government decides to end the moratorium. Why did the Government decide to do it now? Why did they say no to farmers? They did not say no to the two western banks that went bankrupt last year. Mr. Speaker, they have double standards.
When ordinary farmers are concerned, the Government has nothing to offer. This is the difference between the Conservatives and the Liberals. Only the polls and the rich are important to the Conservative Government, it does not care about ordinary people. Canadian farmers are facing the lowest wheat prices since 1933 and this is the time the Government chooses to end the moratorium.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced his decision one week only after wheat prices went down by 18 per cent. Wayne Easter, Chairman of the National Farmers Union had this to say to The Globe and Mail last Tuesday:

"I just can't understand why he (the Minister) would announce it now".

And he added:

"To lose your farm is the same as capital punishment. When they lose their land, farmers feel that the life has gone out of them."

I heard a Conservative Member say this morning that the Liberals were at the root of the problem. They keep repeating that same story since 1984. However, in this case as in most other cases, the responsibility rests with the Government which decided to end the moratorium one week after the fall in the price of wheat. This decision has all the trappings of a conspiracy, given that it comes from a Government with a majority large enough to do as it sees fit.
Since 1984, the Conservatives have afforded again an unwarranted level of protection to drug firms which are already billionaires. They managed to shore up two banks which had gone under while at the same time attempting to deindex Old Age Security pensions. And today, they are putting a large number of farmers out of business. All of this teaches us that the Government cares a lot about the haves but considerably less about the have-nots.
Mr. Speaker, it is a well known fact that the Liberal Party has always attempted to narrow the gap between the rich and the not-so-rich in order that all Canadian men and women might benefit from the collective wealth of Canada. We in the Liberal Party are of the opinion that it is only natural that those who are well off should help those who are less well off. Our unemployment insurance program is a case in point. It has often been said that the Liberal Party has an acute sense of political timing. The same cannot be said of the Conservatives. We would never have dared to do what the Minister of Agriculture has done. When things are looking bad is not the time to make them worse. When the price of grain is so low is not the time to lift the moratorium. The Government has a moral obligation to postpone the termination of this moratorium. The Government should show leadership and come up with a debt restructuring program to help our farmers.
History is bound to repeat itself, it would seem. Indeed, in 1930, a Conservative Government was brought to power with a comfortable majority by a disgruntled electorate. Five years later, that same Government fell. The Conservative Government ignored repeated requests by the unemployed for an employment policy, preferring to cause that famous Winnipeg riot. That was a Tory Government listening to the people in the 30's. This modern version of a Tory Government listening to the needs of the people decided to end the moratorium on farm foreclosures at a time when grain prices are at their lowest.
The signal the Government is sending, Mr. Speaker, is this: If your industry has a problem, do not expect the Conservatives to help you.
April 30, 1987

That is why 1 am now turning to the maple syrup industry. Mr. Speaker, the maple products industry also is on the verge of facing major financial difficulty. What is the Government doing? It is reviewing the situation with its friends down South.
Sugar-bush owners have been trying to get the message across for a long time. When will we decide to listen to them? When are we going to take their concerns seriously? Are we going to wait till an emergency arises? The emergency already is here, Mr. Speaker.
The Government is not interested in farm problems. This is what I tell maple producers: Do not wait, act now. Show your concerns. Make a lot of noise, because this Government is hard of hearing.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to leave Elon. Members and Canadians with a thought that was expressed by Mr. Gerard Fillion, that famous journalist who came from the Lower St. Lawrence, and I quote: "What is urgently needed is to ensure that farmers, who are both highly skilled workers and entrepreneurs, enjoy a standard of living similar to that of city dwellers with equivalent skills."
That Mr. Fillion wrote on May 12, 1943. And like the Union des producteurs agricoles, I say: Forty-four years after that statement was made, the challenge is still relevant.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate. Having been involved in the dairy business all of my life, I can fairly well say that I have some knowledge of agricultural issues.
I have followed closely the Government's program of agriculture initiatives. I spent the first 25 years of my life on the family farm, and during the latter part of that period, was directly involved in its operation. I have also held office in local and area agricultural organizations in the County of Welland and in the region of Niagara. While Ontario does make a sizeable contribution to Canada's wheat and grain production, the Niagara Peninsula, where my riding of Welland is located, is best known in the agricultural industry because of its productive fruit and vegetable growing areas.
For instance, 90 per cent of all the grapes grown in Canada is produced in the Niagara Peninsula. The farming areas of Thorold and West St. Catharines in my riding of Welland have some of the finest and most productive vineyards in the country.
The Welland riding is also very dependent upon the agriculture industry and the western grain producers in particular, because of the presence of the Welland Canal which runs through the entire centre of the riding and, of course, is an integral part of Canada's grain shipping route to the East.
The canal is central to the western grain industry and the western grain industry is central to the economy of the Niagara Peninsula. The growth of the Cities of Welland, Thorold, and St. Catharines are due to the Welland Canal which was built primarily to provide efficient transportation for the western grain being exported to Russia and other parts of Europe.
In 1829 when the canal was first built it was called the grain lane to Europe. It provided the means to bring grain cheaply and quickly from the interior of the country to the St. Lawrence River and on to Europe. The canal made it possible for grain carrying ships to conquer Niagara Falls, making it possible to link the Canadian West with 2,200 miles of continued inland waterways to the Atlantic Ocean.
Since 1829, the canal had been rebuilt four times. It has gone from a 20-lock system to an 80-lock system, making it progressively easier to ship western grain in ever greater amounts in even larger ships across the Niagara Peninsula and up the St. Lawrence Seaway to their destination.
The Seaway's corporate plan indicates that the Welland Canal, without improvement, would not be able to handle increased demand that will be placed on it in the future, a demand placed on it primarily because of the increased need for shipments of Canadian agricultural products.
As part of the Government's commitment to the growth and prosperity of Canadian agriculture, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) announced last November the allocation of $175 million for the rehabilitation of the Welland Canal.
Again and again, in so many areas of government policy, agriculture appears as a primary consideration. Agriculture means jobs. It means a considerable number of jobs in my riding of Welland because agriculture has a domino effect on so many other industries.
When a strike recently left grain shipments sitting for weeks in silos in Thunder Bay, every available ship, including ships that had been out of service for over a year, was called into service to meet the requirements of the Canadian Wheat Board. One hundred and fifty to 200 ships were needed to move the grain and even with such a volume no bottlenecks appeared along the Seaway. The wheat was delivered on time. The co-operation of the shipping industry and the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority was crucial to meeting the needs of the western grain farmers.
The $175 million improvement to the locks on the Welland Canal is proceeding at the present time. Between the closing of the shipping season last November and the opening of the season this spring, major reconstruction has taken place on Lock 7 in the City of Thorold, where a $7.5 million contract has been let. These locks are more than 50 years old. Over the next five to seven years, all the eight locks will be rebuilt and refurbished. The producers of this country, therefore, will be able to look with confidence to the canal and the Seaway as a continuing dependable and capable shipping route.

April 30, 1987
I am proud of this Government's record in agriculture issues. I am proud of the direction we are going in ensuring that agriculture is front and centre in the GATT negotiations and in our trade talks with the United States.
Canadian farmers can be sure that these trade talks with the United States will bring a good deal for Canadian agriculture or no deal will be made. With the importance that has been placed on agriculture by this Government, I am confident that the current economic slump in world grain prices will be weathered and our agricultural industry will emerge stronger with the persistent efforts of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise).
When our Government took office, many thousands of Canadian farmers were suffering from the devastation of high interest rates that characterized the last years of the former administration.
In an effort to assist many of these farmers, the present Minister of Agriculture introduced a moratorium so that no Farm Credit Corporation clients would be forced to leave farms while programs to assist them were being developed, and programs were developed. For instance, an $80 million interest rates conversion program administered by the Farm Credit Corporation assisted over 5,000 farmers. Rates have been locked in at 16 per cent and this program reduced these rates by some 4 per cent. The federal Government, therefore, subsidized the corporation loss resulting from the conversion program.
Our Government has given agriculture a priority that is unprecedented. Our record is second to none. Agriculture means jobs. About 1.6 million jobs. We promised in the recent Throne Speech to spare no effort in seeking to protect the interest of Canada's farming community in the face of unfair pricing and subsidy practice conducted beyond our borders. We are providing the largest farm assistance package ever. The billion dollar special Canada Grains Program is putting a billion dollars of new money into the pockets of our farmers.
This Government, led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) successfully pushed for agriculture to be included in negotiations under GATT. For the first time, agriculture will be on the table. Bilaterally, we are continuing to push for a better mechanism for settling agricultural trade disputes with the United States. We are seeking secure, reliable access for our farm products.
A motion passed in the House of Commons on March 16, 1987, supports the negotiation of a trading arrangement with the United States while protecting our agricultural marketing systems. Since we took office in 1984 we have introduced over 400 agricultural initiatives at a cost of nearly $6 billion. That is over one new initiative every other working day. I will enumerate some of those initiatives.
First, we provided $200 million in drought assistance for the western provinces. Second, we abolished capital gains tax on the sale of farm land up to $500,000. Third, we effectively eliminated all excise and sales taxes on farm fuels, saving
farmers $185 million per year. Fourth, we established farm debt review boards now operating in every province and assisting financially troubled farmers to come to agreements with their creditors. Nationally, arrangements to save the farm have been made in over 50 per cent of the cases. Fifth, a new long-term dairy policy has been established. Sixth, we have new Farm Credit Corporation lending programs with the lowest agricultural credit interest rates since 1979. Seventh, lower interest rates are helping our farmers. Every 1 per cent decline represents a saving to Canadian farmers of $130 million a year.
Our Government has delivered, Mr. Speaker. The promises made during the 1984 election have materialized and more. They have been outlined over and over again by my colleagues on the government benches. They include, as I said before, 400 separate initiatives which will benefit Canadian agriculture by over $5.76 billion. Despite this, more help is needed. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) are continuing to consult with farm leaders to devise new ways to assist farmers in need, not only to assist them at home, but the Government is providing assistance in opening up new markets for Canadian wheat and other agricultural commodities.
The announcement today by the President of the Wheat Board of a $64 million assistance program to protect farmers from a statutory increase in the 1987-88 western grain freights and the allotment last fall of $175 million by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) to rehabilitate the Welland Canal will assure grain producers of the continuing dependability of this historic shipping route are further and continuing indicators of the Government's commitment to Canadian agriculture.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak in a debate on the crisis situation facing our grain producers. In my riding, agriculture plays a very important role, but the industry certainly has its problems. If we are to understand the situation of our grain producers and the context in which they operate, I think we have to try and put ourselves in their shoes. Farmers have to get up in the morning, prepare their equipment, work all day, seed their fields and spend the whole summer working on their land, and at the end of the year, after the harvest, they are not even sure of recovering their production costs. And why not? There are a number of reasons.
First of all, we heard not long ago that this year, the price of grain will drop 18 per cent, and this comes right after last year's drop of 20 per cent. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, the feelings of a farmer who has to cope with this kind of situation. Or perhaps, try to imagine, in the very same situation, the professional or even Member of Parliament. We have to ask
April 30, 1987

ourselves how many of us, how many workers would be willing to function in that kind of situation? EIow many workers would be able to work for a whole season and finally earn the kind of pay that has no relation to all the work and effort expended throughout the season? Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the kind of situation facing our farmers. They can look forward to a season of seeding, working the land, harvesting and then, no money in the till because they will not be getting any return on the work they have done.
Mr. Speaker, all this work will be done in a climate of uncertainty. Why the uncertainty? Whose fault is it? Certainly not the fault of the Canadian farmer.
The farmer in this situation is an innocent victim of circumstances, because there is a crisis ... In fact, during the few days we have been discussing this problem, everyone has agreed that farmers are in a crisis situation. It is a crisis created by foreign governments' intervention in grain production. There is a subsidy war going on between the Common Market countries and the United States. Both parties subsidize grain production without any consideration for the world situation and without any consideration for the harm they are doing to Canadian producers. These governments want to grab the whole market, and they are pouring more and more money into their subsidy programs. And what is our Government doing? Well, nothing for the time being. The Government does not even want to ensure some kind of return. It does not want to provide payments to farmers who are about to seed their fields, payments that would at least cover production costs.
In Canada we already had a situation where some farm operations were experiencing serious difficulties. A number of them were on the brink of bankruptcy. This is why, in a move designed to relieve the stress felt by farmers, a moratorium was imposed on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures of farming operations. But now that we have just learned that wheat prices are going down, the Minister is telling agricultural producers that the moratorium will be lifted. From now on the Farm Credit Corporation of Canada will foreclose farming operations, those which are in financial trouble, of course. In an attempt to allay our fears, they say the FCC will be allowed to foreclose at the rate of only 50 a month, or almost 600 a year. Really, Mr. Speaker, it is a shame to let these farmers go bankrupt. A whole way of life is threatened.
Efforts have been made over the past two days to find a villain, to find somebody who might be blamed, to find somebody at whom we might point a finger. And I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what is the use of all this. Would the agricultural producer feel any better if he knew they have found someone to blame, that he can point his finger at somebody? This would not change anything at all in the present situation. These past few days, Mr. Speaker, they have tried to boast about what certain people did, including the Prime Minister, they bragged about the merits of certain programs, of course. If everything that has been said is any indication, it would seem that we should not even be going through this crisis. But the crisis is
there, it is a fact. Every month we will see 50-odd farmers go under. We will see a way of life disappear gradually. And in all this tragedy, Mr. Speaker, there is the human tragedy.
Much has been said about statistics, about subsidies, about interest rates. Much has been said about a lot of things. There were only a few references to the human tragedy, men and women and children who will have to witness in sadness the seizure and sale of everything they own, their home, their house. Mr. Speaker, what are we going to do with all these farmers who will find themselves on a labour market where the unemployment rate is already rather high, too high for them to expect to find work and be able to earn a decent living? And all those families will experience conflicts because, in such situations, people's nerves are all on edge. People no longer have time to listen to one another. They no longer understand one another. They function in a serious state that leads to conflict. Of course, Mr. Speaker, in such an atmosphere, the Canadian family, the farm family will suffer and pay dearly for the crisis it is going through.
What about the communities that will be affected, Mr. Speaker? I can tell you about that because right now, in New Brunswick we are experiencing massive layoffs that could be called disastrous. You know all about it. We have lost, in the southeast area of New Brunswick, particularly in Moncton, some 800 jobs. Young families are without jobs. They must find another place to live, sell their possessions, because the area cannot absorb all those jobless.
It is as if a storm or a cloud brought over the community a sense of failure, of despair that is very difficult to shake off.
The same thing will happen in farming, Mr. Speaker. What will become of those who will stay, who will try to scratch a living? Needless to say, Mr. Speaker, the lifting of the moratorium will weaken the confidence of those people in the Government.
The timing is bad. It is very bad. The moratorium should have been maintained a little longer to allow the farming sector to get back on its feet. For some of them, even many of them, when things are back to normal it will be too late, they will no longer be there. They will be gone.
In my riding, Mr. Speaker, I have tobacco farmers and you know the situation they are in. The Government is asking them to diversify. They are being asked to go into new crops. I know they are watching what is going on here. Imagine their feeling, now that they realize that the Government is abandoning them at a time when they are most in need of help and assistance. They feel alone and they will not have the heart to go into new crops or even diversify their operations.
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, it is not easy. There is no magical solution, because if there were it would already be in place. The fact remains that we have a crisis situation. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is to restore farmers' confidence. We need to help them. They have to be supported for a little longer.

April 30, 1987
In closing, I plead with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) to reinstate the moratorium on farm foreclosures for a while to try to regain the confidence of the Canadian farmer. I also plead with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture to announce a deficiency program for this year's crop at least equal to what was given last year.

Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, for farmers it will be a summer of uncertainty and even despair. Mr. Speaker, I beg the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture to act in order to restore the confidence of our farm community in the Government, by taking some action which will reassure this industry.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to participate in this debate which is now in its thirty-second hour. I believe I am the forty-third Member to speak from this side of the House.
This has been a historic debate and it is appropriate that this day, April 30, will, I believe, also go down in history because of news we have just heard that tonight the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the 10 provincial Premiers have come to an agreement on the basis of which Quebec can enter into the Canadian Constitution. They will meet again in five weeks to ratify those arrangements. I think that is an issue we all care very deeply about in this country. I think it shows, with good will and willingness to accommodate different interests, how we can make some very significant progress. We are deeply heartened by what we have heard tonight of that progress.
I think in a sense the same thing applies to agriculture. The problems we are facing in Canada, particularly those affecting our grain farmers, will not be remedied by any one single solution, any one initiative, but only by a wide range of responses which people across this country and around the world must deal with.
Having had the honour just over two and a half years ago to be elected to this House by the residents of Capilano I must admit that I had very little background in agriculture. 1 have never been a farmer and my riding does not include farmers. I thought when I came to this august House that probably agriculture was one issue that I would not have to be too concerned about. There were many other issues of particular interest to my constituents on which I thought I would probably spend my time. How wrong I was. I became aware, perhaps for the first time in my life, just how fundamental agriculture is to the way in which the Canadian economy works and the way in which Canadian society works.
I think what I have found moving over the last 32 hours is the fact that Members from right across the country, on all sides of the House, from both urban and rural ridings, have taken part in this most important debate. It is an issue that we
all feel very deeply about: the future of the farmers and farming communities of this country.
Perhaps those of us who are city dwellers take for granted the contribution of farmers. It is easy for us to go into a store and buy a loaf of bread, buy a cake, and not really think about the blood, sweat and tears that have gone into growing the grain used to create the product that we so quickly take off the shelf. We also perhaps grumble if it has gone up a cent or two in price. However, if we are to work as a society we know we have to understand the problems facing the farm community.
Over these last 32 hours I have heard some very moving speeches about the farm families and their situation today. Most important, I think it is very evident that this Government does not take for granted the contribution and importance of the Canadian farmer. We have heard time and time again over the last few days about the efforts this Government has made to provide assistance to the farmer and deal with the fundamental problems facing Canadian agriculture. I thought I would just try to summarize some of the points and the issues I have heard about over these last several days.
The problem facing the Canadian grain farmer is a two-part problem. One part has to do with the cost of production. We responded in a number of ways to that over the last few years. However, the major problem is obviously the price that the farmer receives for his commodity, a price which, as a result of international agricultural subsidies, has been dropping lower and lower. We all know that. Whatever kind of work we do, whether we are shipbuilders, small businessmen or anything else, if our costs are greater than the price we receive for our goods, we have a problem. So our efforts as a Government to deal with both sides of that equation have been multi-faceted.
We have also looked at the problem from the point of view of time, recognizing there are some short-term initiatives that we can take, have taken and will continue to take to address that facet of the problem. There are other facets of the problem which can only be addressed by middle to long-term approaches which will take some time to accomplish. It is well known that the agricultural industry contributes to the economy of this country, over $20 billion at the farm gate. As well, the agri-food industry in this country employs about one in every four workers and contributes about 18 per cent of our GNP.
Let us consider what approaches the Government has taken to deal with the problem facing farmers, particularly western grain farmers, with respect to short-term responses to meet immediate concerns. First, the House has heard repeatedly in the past few days that we have dealt with the issue of the removal of capital gains tax on the family farm. It introduced the special Canadian grains payment.
We have dealt with the fuel tax rebate to reduce the fuel input costs to the farmer.
April 30, 1987

The Government's over-all economic initiatives in dealing with government expenditures and sound fiscal management have meant a decrease in interest rates by over 4 per cent. We know that for each 1 per cent reduction in interest rates there is a saving to the Canadian farmers of some $140 million. This means there is $600 million less that Canadian farmers must pay to banks or financial institutions to support their operations than was the case a few years before the Government took office.
Other measures include the $64 million assistance program announced this morning by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) jointly with the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) to protect farms from the statutory rate increase in the 1987-88 western grain freight rates. Increased subsidies have been provided in this area because farmers would not be able to cope with those increases.
In 1983 the federal Government provided some $350 million in subsidies to Canadian farmers. That has increased in 1987 to $3 billion; made up of $1 billion in the special Canadian grains payment, approximately $1 billion in Western Grain Stabilization payments, and another billion dollars between the Western Grain transportation assistance crop insurance and other agricultural Stabilization programs.
The Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Scowen) stated a few minutes ago that the cheques worth some $705 million for the Western Grain Stabilization Program are going in the mail today to farmers in Saskatchewan, Alberta, Manitoba and British Columbia. That money will mean a great deal to the farmers as they begin their season's work.
The Government has consulted farm groups on a continuing basis. We have come forward with measures that have helped farmers considerably and certainly helped to create a much better environment than previously existed. In fact, it is expected that net revenues for western farmers will actually be up from $2.2 billion last year to $2.5 billion this year. That general improvement for western farmers is a result of the Government's assistance.
Let me deal with the middle and long-term solutions we must consider for other problems. This week, the Minister announced that there would be a change with respect to the Farm Credit Corporation, with the controlled phase-out of the moratorium, effective from May 1. Hon. Members will know that there are approximately 225,000 commercial farms in Canada, 75,000 of which do business with the FCC. About 20 per cent of the FCC clients are in arrears, including some 6,000 who have made no payments for the last two years.
The plan is that the FCC can deal with about 50 cases per month on a national basis. Therefore, about 600 to 800 farmers will be affected annually by the lifting of the moratorium, which represents about one-quarter of 1 per cent of Canada's farming community.
Let me emphasize that the lifting of the moratorium was only done after a range of other measures were put into place to assist troubled farmers. These include the $80 million
interest rate conversion program, the shared risk mortgage program, the commodity based mortgage, and 10 year $700 million program of which about $100 million has already been taken up.
Farm debt review boards have been put in place to give farmers in financial difficulty access to an impartial review of their situation. Of course, there is the Canadian Rural Transition Program.
Earlier this evening the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) mentioned the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, a highly respected organization involved in the farming community which issued a press release this week supporting this decision by the Agriculture Ministers. In fact, Mr. Stan Wilson, the President, indicated:
The decision by the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board to reduce the initial prices for prairie grain, and this week's end to debt moratorium, were tough, responsible, but realistic. We cannot pretend that world grain prices are higher than they really are and certainly no one benefits from the extension of debt moratoria while farmers sink deeper into debt.
He went on to say:
As responsible farm leaders, we must do more than continually criticize the actions and decisions of our Ministers. We need to take more responsibility for contributing to farm policy formation in Canada.
It took great courage for both Mr. Wise and Mr. Mayer to make these decisions. As producers, we recognize that courage, and support the measures taken.
I also support and applaud my colleagues for taking a difficult but realistic and correct decision.
Another important area with respect to the costs facing farmers is that of soil conservation. Recently, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced a special research facility of $6 million in a special program in Vegreville. We are familiar with the work of the Canadian Soil Conservation Council, the SWEEP program, and the $62.3 million in the PFRA. All of these initiatives and perhaps more will be needed in the future to ensure that Canadian soils remain productive and of high quality so that our farmers can be as efficient and productive as possible while reducing their costs and becoming more financially viable.
1 want to conclude by briefly dealing with the issue of price. We have heard very often over these last 32 hours that the real problem with price is in the international sphere. We know that we must work to break the cycle of international agricultural subsidies. This cycle which is creating international havoc in the agricultural community must be stopped.
I am proud of the leadership that our Government, the Prime Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and our Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney) are showing in leading this issue at the international scene.
Last year at the Tokyo Summit, the Prime Minister took a leadership role in bringing this issue to the fore and working in an attempt to get a response from his colleagues.
I had the opportunity to attend with the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the ASEAN Foreign Ministers' meeting in Manila. Again, we brought this issue to the fore.

April 30, 1987
Thailand, Indonesia and Australia have the same concerns. Out of that meeting the response that came was the development of the Cairns Group. Canada, through our Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, attended that first meeting last summer in Australia to work together with these 14 countries to try to come forward with effective ways to influence the international community to get rid of international agricultural subsidies. That work is going on at an increased pace.
We know that at the next meeting of GATT for the first time agriculture will be on the table and will be recognized as one of the most important items to be discussed at GATT.
Our trade Minister was recently in New Zealand for trade talks with colleagues from other countries. Again the issue of agriculture was at the top on the agenda, and from that meeting Canada will now be hosting a meeting of the Cairns Group at the end of May, bringing together representatives of those countries to continue our discussions and initiatives.
Just this past week our Minister for International Trade in Tokyo was lauded for her work, again at the quad round, of raising agriculture to a level of importance and getting international recognition for that. Our Prime Minister at the Venice Summit will be going back again to work with his colleagues. It will not be an easy process. It will not happen overnight, but by increasing international pressure, particularly, as we know, in the EEC and the common agricultural market which has created a lot of these problems for us, we hope and we will be working hard to continue to ask for fundamental changes in the international community because it is only in that way that we will ultimately be able to solve the problem that our Canadian grain farmers are facing.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned in his speech, there are certain principles that must be followed in dealing with the international issues. Policies must be price-responsive and we must reduce activities which reduce world prices. First, the basic principles that can be agreed upon must be implemented by all because it will not work if only a few countries do it. This is an effort where all countries will have to work together if it is going to work for all of us.
When I think tonight of what has happened here in Canada where we have 10 provincial Premiers with widely differing points of view under the leadership of our Prime Minister who, after 15 years, have now come to an agreement about a vital national issue, the inclusion of Quebec in our Constitution, I guess I am heartened and optimistic that that same leadership of our Prime Minister and my cabinet colleagues will be lent and that we will see the kinds of changes occur in the international scene that will assist our Canadian farmers as well.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been listening patiently to the Members opposite during this debate telling us in the House just what great guys and gals the farmers are, telling us how they have worked hard and how they deserve such excellent treatment
from their Government, also knowing what poor treatment they are getting from the Government. Not only are they getting poor treatment but it seems the Government is kicking them while they are down. The Government has brought an end to a 19 month moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures only one week after giving farmers the news that grain prices will drop by 18 per cent.
As one farmer has said, why give us the news that you are going to stop the moratorium on foreclosures now? Spring is the hopeful time of year. It is the time of year when we are planting and when we feel that things can change around. To tell farmers that they are going to have their prices reduced by 18 per cent after their prices were reduced by a tremendous amount last year, only to tell them that they are open to foreclosures again, is absolutely callous.
What we are going to have is many, many farmers losing their farms. This year alone there will be 6,000 farms eligible for foreclosure. Of these, 10 per cent will actually be foreclosed. There will be 600 farms closed this year. We have heard about the concern of this Government and how it wants to help the farmers. Yet, during this 19 month period of the moratorium on foreclosures, the Government did not arrive at a decision that would come to grips with this very serious problem. If the Government is so serious about helping the farmers, why during this period could the Government not arrive at a long-term solution? The Government went through a 19 month period sitting on the problem doing nothing about it, hoping it would go away, only to realize that the problem will not go away by itself. Instead of doing something, the Government just abandoned the farmers. That is treachery.
What is the situation in Canada? In western Canada of those with loans, 22 per cent are in arrears, in Ontario, of those with loans, 17 per cent are in arrears, in Quebec, of those with loans, 9.6 per cent are in arrears, in Nova Scotia, of those with loans, 17 per cent are in arrears, and in Newfoundland, of those with loans, 33 per cent are in arrears. The average loan of the Farm Credit Corporation is $120,000. It is absolutely mind-boggling how the Government feels that this problem is going to correct itself. This is a crushing debt. These are people who have actually followed the Government's programs, who have had faith in the Government, in what it has said, only to be led down the garden path.
Where is this friendship which the Government has with the United States and the European Economic Community? These two jurisdictions are stabbing Canadian farmers in the back, yet we are ploughing along merrily as if nothing happened. The Government is tra-la-laaing down the road as if there were no cares in the world. Does our Government feel it can jettison the farming community? What is it that the Government has planned for the farming community? It just cannot let a situation like this go on and on without winding up in a catastrophic state, but that is exactly what is happening. We need a debt restructuring program. We need some kind of solution.
April 30, 1987

We need a dialogue with the banking community. The banking community is owed almost $9 billion from farm loans and the FCC is owed almost $5 billion. This is not going to go away. What are we doing? We are driving people off the farms. Farms are being closed down. Now there will be more closings because of the Farm Credit Corporation's foreclosures. There are suicides and marriage breakups in the farming community. There is a tremendous concern among people in all walks of life for the farming community.
It is ludicrous to think that this will go away by itself. Do we want to keep people on the farms? If the Government does not, why does it not have the courage and the decency to say that this is not a concern of the Government, that it does not want to keep families on the farm?
If we are going to keep families on the farm, we cannot deceive them. We cannot turn on them. We cannot tell them one thing and build up their hopes only to bring their hopes crashing down at a time when they are most vulnerable. Farmers want the same prices as last year and they are entitled to that. What they are going to get for their crops is going to be less than their cost of production. How can the Government expect farmers to carry on like that?
Farmers want to know when they plant and harvest their crops that they will be able to survive. Can the Government actually tell them that? It has not told them that yet. Oh, sure, there are cheques going out from the arrangement which was made for the farmers last year. What about the situation in which farmers find themselves in this year? What is the Government going to do?
What is wrong with giving the farmers an undertaking? It is not fair to leave them dangling by their fingertips over a cliff the way the Government is doing. It is not enough to say that these problems are caused by the trade war, and the subsidies which are given by the European Economic Community and the United States to their farmers. It is of no use to say that this is too bad and we are working to fix it. This has been going on for months and what has happened? Certainly it is not going to have any long-term value.
It is of short term political value for the European Economic Community and the United States, but why can the Government not convince them of that? Where is the respect the Government likes to think it has in foreign circles? It is not being listened to. Can the Government not make the case that Canadian farmers are being decimated by the policies of the United States, the Government's very good friend which it is trusting implicitly in trade negotiations, that it is playing up to with the future of the wheat farmers and the future of our oil and gas reserves in western Canada?
The Government remains silent when people like Bruce Smart, the Under-secretary of Commerce of the United States, makes ridiculous statements about meeting to negotiate away Investment Canada because it may not agree with the position of the United States? He more or less said, "If we get
rid of Canadian wheat farmers, that is less world competition for us". It is callous.
The farmers are referring to May 1 as black Friday. Why not? They have nothing to look forward to as far as the future of their loans which are in arrears are concerned. Those who have had their loans in arrears for two years are really fair game tomorrow for the Government's agency. Black Friday is less than an hour away. Do you not think that they realize that on the farm, Mr. Speaker? Do you not think that is something that is very well known to farmers?
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) said that the controlled phase-out of the moratorium and removal of the ban will not precipitate an immediate flood of foreclosures. That is like saying that when one lets loose a plague we know it will be a while before we get it, but it is going to be just as devastating whenever we get it. How can anyone predict who is going to get it and when? Someone is going to get it immediately and that is the case with the farmers who are in arrears who will be subject to review and possible foreclosure.
I really fear for the east and the west of this country. I fear the Government is quite set in thinking that the prosperity of southern Ontario and certain pockets in Quebec is all that it wants to achieve. I do not really think it has any feeling for western Canada or even for Atlantic Canada. They certainly were great places to get seats in the last federal election but, of course, things are going to be different next time.
More important is the Government's attitude towards the people. If we abandon the people in rural communities and in our farming communities, this country is going to suffer greatly. We are going to lose a very valuable supplier of food, particularly grain, who will not be replaced. When farmers leave the farm they will not go back. It is just too expensive for them to begin again.
This is a Canadian tragedy. I really feel badly. I have a sense of hopelessness and helplessness that the Government is not heeding the warnings the farming community is giving. I can only hope that the Government will listen before it is too late.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to participate in this debate which may well become historic. I must say it has been an interesting debate for the last number of hours. We have heard concern expressed by both sides of the House. I think people realize that agricultural hardship is not a partisan issue, it hits everyone. I do not believe opposition Members can claim they have the market on hardship and knowledge of the people who are facing these problems.
I was rather taken aback by the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) who has absolutely no idea of how the Western Grain Stabilization Program works in western Canada. The Government did not lower the price of grain. It set the initial price at 80 per

April 30, 1987
cent of what it thought the market was going to be by fall. The price for grain could very well go up by fall. Therefore, the Government did not lower the price of grain. It set the initial price lower. It can only do that by law. The Government cannot go higher than 80 per cent of what it was told. I think the Hon. Member should take a lesson from his colleague from the New Democratic Party who is sitting with him now. Perhaps he could straighten him out on the Western Grain Stabilization Program and how it works.
I believe I am about the forty-eighth speaker for this side of the House. We have pretty well heard the whole gamut of problems in agriculture. I think both sides agree that there are no easy answers to these problems. There are those who feel we could throw another $1 billion and the problems will all go away. It is not that simple.
We heard the Secretary of State outlining our problems on the international market. We are being beaten into the ground by subsidy wars between the United States and the EEC which is having an affect on our prices here in Canada. I think it is grossly unfair for Members of the Opposition Parties to say this Government has not done anything, and is not going to do anything.
A number of Members who have spoken tonight have indicated the type of action the Government has taken and will be taking in the future. The Government has spared no effort, and will spare no effort on behalf of the agriculture community of Canada. The farm debt review boards are working. We have heard a great deal of discussion that they are not working and not going to work on behalf of the farmers. Each farmer in Canada has the right to appear before the farm debt review board. As has been pointed out, the review boards will be able to hear the cases of about 60 farmers each month. Therefore, approximately 600 to 700 farmers will have their cases reviewed this year. The rest will have to wait until the next year.
I think it is very unfair to say that the Government, because of the moratorium coming off, is going to drive tens of thousands of farmers off their land. That simply is not true. Those people who criticize the farm debt review boards are also criticizing the people who are serving on those farm debt review boards. There are outstanding ladies and gentlemen who are taking the time to serve on those boards and they deserve all the praise we can give them. Many of them are probably out right now, at eleven o'clock on a Thursday night, working with farmers, trying to solve their problems. I think we do a great disservice to those people who are working diligently in trying to solve the farm problems for the farmers.
We have had solutions from the farm debt review boards. Some have been accepted by the farmers and the farming community. They are going the last mile to try and keep farmers on the land. It is not a matter of them going in with the attitude that they are going to get this guy and kick him off the land and Government is going to take the property.
That simply is not true. If you are going to be a member of the farm debt review board you have to show compassion towards agriculture and the farm community. That is the type of people we have on those boards. I do not think we are doing a service to those people when opposition Members get up and criticize the boards and the people who serve there when they are taking their time on behalf of Canadian agriculture.
I am sure that you realize, having listened to these hours of debate, that this is a very emotional issue. Agriculture today has serious problems. No one is denying that. One of the most disappointing things I think as far as farmers are concerned is that when they get on their tractors to plant their crops they think that things will be better by fall. They have done that in the past. Now they know that the market-place is not going to improve a great deal by the fall. When there is a U.S. corn crop in storage that is as big as a normal year's production, you cannot be optimistic. Market forces simply will not let prices rise. We have to give all the support we possibly can to the farmers this year and you can be assured that this Government will do that, as much as it possibly can. Federal Government spending on agriculture over the past two years has increased by 68 per cent.
We have heard a great deal about the western farmer and the problems they are having. Yes, the problems are very serious. Those of us from eastern Canada recognize that. However, we have farmers in Ontario who are having very serious problems. Our corn, soybean and wheat producers are facing the same kind of problems facing western grain farmers. It is not often recognized that these farmers have also received assistance from the Canadian grains program. Some $100 million came to Ontario last year through that program. Eastern grain corn, soybeans and barley were also covered under a stabilization program. Last year payments under that program totalled $55.8 million. Last year corn farmers in Ontario received 105 per cent of stabilization. That was unheard of. It has never been done before. We have gone the extra mile with people like corn farmers to make sure they have enough money to maintain viable operations.
I am sure that you, along with many other Members of this House, have had many visits from your constituents regarding farm problems. It is a gut-wrenching business. It is not a pleasant situation. Yet I have asked them how they got themselves into this problem. They said, because a few years ago things looked good. I am not going to stand in this House and blame the other Government. Everyone can make mistakes at one time or another. However, that is where the problem began. Many farmers became over-extended. They were told to expand, remodel, buy farms, because agriculture is going to be a good business. Even during the days of the PIK program in the U.S., payment in kind, when Americans were taking land out of production, what did our Government of the day do? It told farmers to plant more. Does that make any sense? That is where our problems began and we are still living with those problems today.
April 30, 1987

Some farmers today still have to live with interest rates set by the previous Government when it kept those rates at a very high level. They simply cannot maintain a viable operation on those interest rates. That is where the problem is. That is where most farmers got themselves into difficulty.
I am not going to prolong this debate! I know other Members want to give their views on the agricultural situation. This Government has been concerned. We have a Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has shown leadership. He has gone the extra mile for farmers. He will go another extra mile. We have a Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and a Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) who work hard day after day on this problem. They are still here tonight discussing the situation and listening to views from both sides.
This problem is not going to be solved by partisan rhetoric. It will have to be solved by everyone working together. This Government is prepared to work with anyone, at any time, in any place. The Minister of Agriculture meets daily with members of the agricultural community. We are trying to solve the problems but it is not going to be easy and the last thing we need is people in this House giving us partisan rhetoric without any solutions.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate on the crisis in the Canadian grain industry from the point of view of one representing an urban constituency in central Ontario. Very often the interests of producers and those of consumers have more in common than is generally considered to be the case. Furthermore, as a Member of the Canadian Parliament, each one of us has a constituency much broader than the electoral district in which we are elected. When a Canadian citizen anywhere is hurting, that is a concern to me. Our lives are linked economically and socially. As Members of Parliament we have a duty to legislate in the best interests of all Canadians, as far as we can.
As Chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts I have been involved in hearings for the last few days on the Auditor General's report concerning Agriculture Canada. The last report certainly stressed the importance of the agri-food sector. That sector as defined by Agriculture Canada includes not only agricultural equipment and supplies, farming, processing, wholesaling, retailing, restaurants and institutional food service activities, but also important associated industries such as transportation, finance, packaging and construction. It employs about 1.5 million people, 15 per cent of total employment in Canada. It contributes about one-sixth of our Gross National Product.
Consumers in Canada spend $40 billion annually on food. That expenditure represents some 16 per cent of their disposable income. Agricultural exports exceed $10 billion annually compared with imports of about $5 billion. Agriculture makes a major contribution to Canada's balance of payments and relies heavily for as much as half of total farm cash receipts on export markets.
Food processing is the largest processing sector in Canada with sales exceeding $40 billion and a workforce of 250,000. The food service sector employs around 360,000 people, while food retailers employ about 220,000. Decisions taken about agriculture impact on the lives of many, many Canadians over and above those living on the farms.
While the motion which brought on this emergency debate was called with respect to Canadian grain farmers, there are Ontario farmers, Newfoundland farmers, indeed farmers all across the country, who are also facing foreclosure. There have been changes in the farm sector in recent years which have presented serious challenges to farmers. On the whole, farms have become more capital intensive, more reliant on borrowed capital and therefore more exposed to the risk of adverse market forces.
Farmers have also become more reliant on the non-farm sector for fuel, fertilizers, chemicals and other production inputs. Fluctuations in international prices, as well as in interest and foreign exchange rates, subject farmers to further financial stress.
A recent survey indicates that 23 per cent of Canadian farms with $20,000 in farm sales faced severe financial stress in 1984, while a further 11 per cent faced moderate stress.
As the Auditor General pointed out in his report last October:
Current market prospects suggest little or no growth in net farm income-in some commodity sectors there could well be a decline. As a result, a continued decline is expected in farmers' net worth in the immediate future requiring that very difficult adjustments be made.
That prophesy was certainly borne out. Last week we saw the price of grain drop a further 18 per cent, which followed a drop in price last year.
The Auditor General went on to say:
Another important challenge facing the sector is the degradation of Canada's agricultural land which, as announced in a speech by the Minister of Agriculture, will cost about $1 billion annually. Most of this cost directly affects farmers in the form of increased chemical costs, lower yields and reduced international competitiveness.
He goes on:
Domestically, the agri-food sector's two most critical and widespread problems are the farming community's financial difficulties and the sustainability of the land resource base. This stress is compounded by changing world markets. Internationally, the markets on which Canada is becoming increasingly dependent are at risk, with competition increasing and prices falling.
Those are some of the issues that were pointed out in the Auditor General's report last October.
Since then we have seen further deterioration in the international situation. The trade war between the United States and the European Common Market produced an artificial surplus and lower prices of agricultural products. There are the U.S. Farm Bill and the U.S. Export Enhancement Program which give export subsidies to American wheat and create more competition for Canadian Wheat Board sales.

April 30, 1987
As the United States attempts to protect itself from perceived European Common Market competition, there are times when Canada becomes caught in the crossfire. There are other times when our American friends shoot directly at our house. We do not see any great effort on the part of the Government to protect Canadian industries. The Government seems to be paralyzed as it waits for its trade agreement and fails to stand up for the interests of Canadian citizens.
There are serious problems facing our farming community and it is difficult to be clear about what the Government proposes. The Conservatives made a number of election promises in 1984. They have promised agri-bonds but we have not seen them. They promised to expand the agricultural sector research and development but the 1985 Estimates show $263 million allotted to agricultural research while the 1987 Estimates show a drop to $221 million.
At the GATT meeting in Uruguay last fall there was an agreement as a result of which, last February, the GATT organizers asked participating countries to develop some proposals concerning agriculture. Canada has not responded. Did the Government take any action at all?
A moratorium was imposed on foreclosures by the Farm Credit Corporation 19 months ago. There have been 19 months of inaction, with no attempt in that time to assist farmers to restructure their debts. It seems as though the Government sat for 19 months and hoped that the problem would disappear. Now, the moratorium will be lifted on May 1, in just one-half hour in most of Canada and in a few minutes in Newfoundland.
An article in The Ottawa Citizen on April 28 carries the headline: "Black Friday Looms For Farming Families". The article states that as many as 2,200 farmers are facing eviction. We are told that the Farm Credit Corporation can only process 500 to 600 actions in a year. What kind of cruel lottery will this be? Who decides which families will be foreclosed first?
We are told that if the corporation decides to go ahead with a foreclosure, the farm debt review board in that province will be notified and there can be a hearing. The farm debt review boards which were established last August have not exactly had rave reviews. In fact, most farmers consider them useless.
Comments being made by farmers now emphasize how cruelly betrayed they feel by a Government that has done nothing for 19 months and does not seem to have any intention of doing anything. One farmer said, "Normally farmers feel a sense of optimism at this time of year, spring. But this tears the heart out of thousands of farmers". The President of the Manitoba-based Keystone Agricultural Producers pointed out:
At this time of year, many farmers are trying to borrow money to purchase
fuel, seed, fertilizer and chemicals for the coming crop season.
A farmer needs a lot more cash at this time of year than at any other time of
year.
He pointed out that the termination of the Farm Credit moratorium will make it more difficult for farmers to get loans from banks and other lenders.
Grain farmers are generally considered to be suffering more than other farmers, but let us make no mistake that farmers generally in our country are in very difficult times. Lifting the moratorium with no plan, and just one week after the announcement that grain prices were dropping again by 18 per cent, seems both cruel and lamentably incompetent. The recommendations on what needs to be done are very clear. Surely the moratorium needs to be continued while, on an urgent basis, some method is found of restructuring debt and allowing farmers to continue. Surely even to this Government it must be obvious that it is in nobody's interest to have farmers forced off the land.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak at this late hour, although the subject is not a happy one. It is almost midnight, and parliamentarians continue to show their concern for the unhappy lot of our Canadian farmers. Mr. Speaker, this debate should not only make us reflect on the situation of our grain producers. I believe that anyone who is at ail concerned about the future of our country should start asking some basic questions about the kind of country we want to build, the kind of life we want Canadians to have, and look back to the history of this country and consider the important role agriculture has always played in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, let us look at the situation facing farmers in this country and consider that thousands of Canadian families will go to bed tonight, wondering whether tomorrow will bring them a notice of foreclosure in the mail. Will the bailiff be at the door to take away their land? Will they still be able to send their children to the same school or will they have to move? If they do not want anyone to know what they went through, they will have to move way out, perhaps as far as the city.
Mr. Speaker, that is more or less what the situation is like, on top of all the technical considerations. It is a matter of survival, of pride and dignity for many families in Canada, and during the last 30 or 35 hours, the House of Commons has considered the situation of these people who, granted, are now a minority in Canada but a minority on whom all Canadians depend. I am therefore very disappointed to see the Government has failed to provide an appropriate response to the legitimate concerns of farmers across this country and their elected representatives.
Mr. Speaker, in a society as rich as ours, one starts to wonder about the priorities of this Government. During the past two years, we have seen a Government hoping that the problem would simply go away. There are people who owe money to the Farm Credit Corporation and who had gained some relief as a result of the moratorium on foreclosures. They thought that since the situation was not going to improve, they could at least try to refurbish their operations and try to survive, without the nagging fear that the Government would come and take their land away at the very last minute.
April 30, 1987

The decision made this week will have an impact on people who owe money to the Farm Credit Corporation, but in making this decision the Government is also sounding an alarm signal for all Canada's lending institutions. If the Government no longer has confidence in Canadian agriculture, bank managers across this country are going to be in a panic. Imagine all the calls from credit union managers wanting to withdraw lines of credit.
Mr. Speaker, this decision is like a symbol. It points to a complete lack of confidence in Canada's agriculture industry. And I know my colleagues will get calls from their constituents about the credit manager calling in the middle of the night or coming to their farms in a terrible panic, because it looks like Ottawa does not have much faith in the industry anymore. Mr. Speaker, we know this is going to happen and that it will have a domino effect.
I fail to understand why the Government, which had already announced a few days before that grain producers could expect an 18 per cent cut in prices, then chose to add insult to injury by announcing it would no longer guarantee loans that were in arrears. This is creating a terrible climate in the whole agricultural sector. Anyone who thinks only one region in this country will be affected is in for a big surprise, because the truth of the matter is that farmers across this country will be affected by this decision, and farms will be up for sale all over. There will be plenty of auction sale notices in La terre de chez nous. It will also have an impact, obviously, on the value of farm property. When you get a series of sales by the Farm Credit Corporation, automatically the adjoining land, and so forth . .. this is going to have a devastating effect on the value of farm land as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, I feel embarrassed for Government Members who, after making their commitments as legitimate, elected representatives, especially those with western ridings, did not have the mental fortitude to object to the Cabinet's decisions. When Cabinet decided to lift the moratorium on foreclosures, there was not a single Conservative Member who had the courage to say it did not make sense that the timing was very poor.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Portneuf (Mr. Ferland) who was talking about the Constitution must be a little confused. We are talking about agriculture here tonight. It is a fact that in his riding as well as everywhere else, his Government's decision will have a disastrous impact on our farm economy as a whole. Instead of cracking corny jokes, I think he should show a little concern for what is happening to the farmers in his riding.
Well, Mr. Speaker, there is some kind of woodpecker on the other side, if only you could keep him quiet-

If I were in their shoes I would feel guilty about dropping a major sector of our economy like a hot potato. They are guilty of letting the Minister responsible for the Farm Credit Corporation behave like a heartless man. He does not lift a finger to prevent the seizure of farm lands where people have been living in dignity, yet in a few short months they will end up by the roadside. They know that, I trust they feel guilty, and I hope they will rise in a few minutes to apologize to their electors. The one thing I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, is that if we consider the measures which should be taken, the economic signals which ought to be sent to the whole farming community, it is definitely not by taking this kind of action that farmers will regain confidence, that we will ensure agricultural stability and proper land development-
Mr. Speaker, I heard my colleague talk about agricultural stability, yet they are about to foreclose. Some stability! Not bad, Mr. Speaker, they want to foreclose. This will prove to be a bonanza for Conservative lawyers, but what a sickening performance for the poor stiff who is only trying to earn an honest living.
Mr. Speaker, I would feel quite ashamed listening to these comments because this is hardly the time to make jokes in the course of a debate which is so important to people who will have no idea which way to turn in the coming weeks and months. Besides, everything is left in limbo, including the very nature of Canada's development because this is just another way of conveying the signal that the Government has lost faith in the agricultural community. That is the message you are sending out.

April 30, 1987
What you are doing now is making sure that farmers will realize the Government has dropped them, so we will end up in a situation where it will be ever more difficult to find people willing to put all their energy and give the best of themselves to develop Canada's agriculture. We are all aware of the exodus towards urban areas in recent years, Mr. Speaker, but we cannot afford the luxury of endangering our independence and self-sufficiency with respect to food production.
This is just one more very alarming aspect of the kind of signal being sent out, the lack of respect for the agricultural profession. The signal means that we are prepared to compromise the very future of the Canadian agricultural sector.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand, and neither could any reasonable Canadian, how the Government can announce an 18 per cent decrease in prices when we know that the price of wheat has gone down by over 50 per cent in the last four or five years.
Mr. Speaker, how many Canadian would calmly accept a 50 per cent decrease in their income? Yet, this is what has happened to farmers in Western Canada. I have visited western Canada many times myself, more often than the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), following the example of my leader. We, Liberals, want to be sensitive to the needs of western Canada. We want to make sure that we understand their problems. We want to make sure that their needs are expressed in the House of Commons, and this is why we have taken such an active part in this debate.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the guided tour which the Prime Minister will take during the next few days will incite him to reconsider the decision made by his government. I trust that his welcome throughout western Canada will make him understand the concerns and especially the feeling of frustration of western farmers. 1 find it unfortunate that we can not continue this debate for another three or four days until next week, at which time the Prime Minister could come back and report on his visit, if he's not too battered by then, because I believe that the situation is dramatic, as evidenced by the fact that this Parliament has spent 30 or 40 hours on this matter. The motion of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, is very much to the point-

cent or 7 per cent. Mr. Speaker, the farmers will have to figure it out this evening and ask themselves how they will be able to begin seeding in coming weeks. They are faced with an impossible situation.
The other aspect on which we should reflect is that the ones in difficulty today are the grain growers. However, what is going to happen tomorrow? As we have international prices for many products, as competition is fierce and as many countries subsidize their farming industry heavily, tomorrow it could be the Quebec pork producers who find themselves in difficulty, or else it could be our dairy producers, because with higher wheat prices, and so on, no one knows what will happen to Quebec farmers. Our colleagues who are now smiling at the problems of western producers should realize that Quebec producers might be the ones who will need the support of this House and this Government tomorrow. This is the essence of this country and this is why we sit in this Parliament. We have to ensure that the interests of the various regions are expressed in this House and we Liberals believe that there is now a serious inequity in Canada. We are convinced that the Government adds to this inequity by taking unreasonable action and we hope that it will finally come to its senses, because otherwise the situation will worsen and an increasing number farmers will leave the farm, which might threaten our independence and self-sufficiency. I therefore trust, Mr. Speaker, that my small contribution to this debate will raise the awareness of some of our colleagues and that, instead of laughing, they will rise in their caucus and say that such a situation is unacceptable and that our farmers deserve better. They should be able to rise and tell the minister responsible for the Farm Credit Corporation that he has lost his senses. They should be able to tell the Prime Minister: Go to western Canada and listen to the farmers; then propose new solutions because, if this goes on, it is obvious that an entire and very important sector of our economy will slowly disappear.
I therefore hope, Mr. Speaker, that all of us who have spoken on this matter have been able to make Government Members more aware of the daily tragedy we are witnessing in western Canada. We are asking one thing, that they at least go back on the decision these last few days as it will only make matters worse, not better.

Jean Chretien said against farmers during the election campaign, and 1 would suggest Jean Chretien at that point was speaking on behalf of the Liberal Party. That sentence hit the farming community very hard in Quebec and Canada as a whole, and I quote: "Farmers, farm producers are damned cry-babies. The more they get, the more they want." So that has been the philosophy of the Liberal Party over these last 20 years, before 1984. That is what the Liberal Party thought of our farm people, the most important in my view of small and medium businessmen in Canada. This is how those people were treated.
Today, the Hon. Member for Shefford rises and says he does not feel guilty of the errors made by his Government. We have been in office for two and a half years, Mr. Speaker. We have been trying for those two and a half years to correct the errors made over 20 years. I suggest that for two and a half years, or during the election campaign as my colleague stated earlier, we made 16, not election promises but 16 commitments to our farming industry, and those 16 commitments we have honoured.
He said earlier he was travelling across Alberta, in western Canada. 1 understand that for the Hon. Member for Shefford. We have not seen him in this House for a year, Mr. Speaker, he is travelling to prepare the next election campaign. You see the point?
