In turn, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the Hon. Member for Shefford that when dealing with an issue, he should tell the whole truth, and not only part of it. I heard him say a while ago that there had been an increase in the grain transportation cost. He was not quite sure whether it was 5 per cent or 7 per cent, but he should have read his document to know that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) has announced today a $64 million subsidy, which amounts to $2 a tonne. And that, my friend from Shefford should know, is less than the transportation costs which western wheat producers had to pay before 1984.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I should like just the same to mention that-I am ready for the Hon. Member for Shefford come election time-that in my Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup riding, there are 52 municipalities, including 49 rural ones with 898 farm producers altogether. I visit my riding regularly and I know these people. During that election campaign, we met a number of UPA organizations. You know that UPA stands for I'Union des producteurs agricoles. I know two such organizations in my own riding, namely the Union des producteurs agricoles de la Cote-Sud and the Union des producteurs agricoles du Bas-Saint-Laurent. You know what happens during an election campaign. These people invite political candidates to answer the following question: Suppose your political Party gets elected, what would be your commitments as a Government? Well, our Progressive Conservative Party had made 16 promises which we have fulfilled, and later on 1 will provide the House with concrete examples.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, we went to the general assemblies of these UPA producers and what did they tell us? In my Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup riding, there are for instance hog, dairy, cattle, grain and potato producers. All these people who had had open and honest discussions with the then candidate of the Progressive Conservative Party who are now their elected representatives are satisfied with the farm policies which this Progressive Conservative Government has implemented to help them earn a decent living, which is quite different from being treated as second-class citizens by former Liberal administrations before 1984.

April 30, 1987
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the House of some of the commitments of our Party. For instance, let us take the case of the special Canada grain program. Under this program, our Government will share equitably among the 10 provinces, not only western Canada, a billion dollars to increase the cash flow of grain producers. Without this program, the net farm income which would have decreased by 17.9 per cent in 1987 will increase by 1.8 per cent. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) will continue their discussions with the various farm organization leaders to get their input as to the best way the Government could meet the future needs of Canadian farmers.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Page, the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, and the provincial UPA have congratulated our Ministers not only in personal letters, but also in newspaper articles and radio and television reports. What was the response first of the Liberal Opposition, then of the NDP? What did they do? They criticized this decision which had been universally accepted. I understand that it is the Opposition's role to criticize. However, what we have on the other side is a systematic attempt to destroy everything good we do. Yet, in their 20 years in power, the agricultural community was totally ignored throughout the country.
Let me quote another passage, Mr. Speaker. "Advance payments for crops. Amendments to the Advance Payments for Crops Act have made it possible to double the maximum level of advanced payments". In Quebec, in 1984, when the Liberals were still in power, what did they do when Canada was faced with the problems of drought, a condition which also affected Quebec? The Liberal Party did not solve anything. It was the Conservative Party, when we were elected, which provided former Minister Garon with some $20 million. You remember, he was the Minister who kept the cheque in his pocket for a week and a half. That is what the Conservative Party did.
Mr. Speaker, mortgages based on the prices of primary agricultural products are to bear interest at a prime rate of 6 per cent. Changes in the capital of the mortgage will be determined under a formula which takes into account the prices of primary agricultural products. Who set up the farm debt review boards? The Conservative Party. Legislation has been passed to set up farm debt review boards composed of people with knowledge and experience in farming and financial matters. They provide the agricultural community with an independent consultative third party review mechanism, and they assist in setting up voluntary arrangements between farmers and their creditors, in order to help ensure the survival of the farm business.
These boards have been welcomed in the agricultural community and constructive arrangements have been made in most cases, thus enabling farmers to remain in the business.
Mr. Speaker, there is also the Canadian Rural Transition Program. It was set up to help families who have to leave farming because of financial difficulties. As you know, those people did not receive any unemployment insurance benefits. If they went bankrupt, they only had welfare to turn to. The Conservative Government has now set up this Canadian Rural Transition Program to help farmers make the transition to a new career.
What about interest rates? Since we came in power, Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has taken active steps to reduce interest rates, and not only in the agricultural sector. The drop in interest rates means that farmers have been able to save millions of dollars in interest payments through an interest rate which has dropped to a 13-year record low. The rate on guaranteed loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which is the prime rate plus one percentage point, has been reduced from 16.75 per cent on election day to 11.25 per cent. Mr. Speaker, I think this is no small effort on the part of the Government, an effort that we can mention with pride especially if we bear in mind that the rate of the Farm Credit Corporation has also reached a record low since 1979. As far as I know, in 1979, the Liberals were in power. The FCC's interest rate has been lowered five times since we were elected, Mr. Speaker. Short-and long-term rates have dropped substantially, which translates into millions of dollars of savings for farmers; five-year mortgage rates have dropped from 3.75 to 10 per cent, which means that we now enjoy the lowest rates since 1979.
I could talk, Mr. Speaker, about the shared-risk mortgage plan or about the capital gains exemption. Yes, 1 will talk about the latter. We used to meet in our ridings farmers who had problems, and they would tell us: "What am I going to do with my farm? I cannot possibly sell it, I would pay too much taxes?" The Conservative Government solved that problem by granting farmers, in the 1985 Budget, a $500,000 capital gains exemption, effective immediately. It was a very efficient way of eliminating taxes on the sale of agricultural properties, most of which are sold with some capital gain.
Mr. Speaker, I will not go into international trade in farm commodities as this was brilliantly dealt with, this evening, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). However, I will talk about the fuel tax rebate. This is another initiative from the Conservatives. It is rumored that farmers will continue to benefit from that fuel tax rebate as it applies to all fuels for off-highway use.
Mr. Speaker, I know my time is fast running out, but I would like to come back to something which is very dear to me and was mentioned briefly by the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) a moment ago; it is the long-term dairy policy. I recall very well that during the 1984 electoral campaign, we were challenged by UPA members and dairy farmers who were asking us whether, if the Conservatives were elected, we would sign a long-term agreement regarding the dairy policy? It had expired in 1981 and the Liberals had been promising
April 30, 1987

from year to year to renew it, but they never did. The Conservative Party, with the agreement of the Agriculture Minister, helped us. We signed that dairy policy and it had been said that the Government's $1.5 billion commitment to the five-year program will garantee the dairy industry a stability that had been lacking since 1981. Mr. Speaker, you know that means $750 million over five years for the dairy producers of Quebec who are said to control about 49 per cent of the milk production, let us say 50 per cent. We have also heard that the policy is based on the extension of the supply management system and on changes aimed at profitting the producers and the consumers. The list of controlled import products will be revised to include bulk powder mixes. Milk producers meeting the national needs will remain eligible for the federal subsidy of $6.03 an hectolitre.
Mr. Speaker, I could also tell you about the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. 1 think my time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, finally, I just want to tell people in my riding of Kamouraska-Riviere-du-Loup and to all farmers of the country that the Conservative Party is listening to them. You can rest assured we will be there to support them.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stand to participate in this debate that was commenced by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo). I want to thank him for giving us the opportunity to participate in a debate on what I think is one of the saddest and possibly most serious situations we have had in a long time.
Members will know that we are now into Friday, May 1, which many have called Black Friday for some farmers. It is black because, as of today, the moratorium that has existed for 18 months will be lifted. According to the statement by the Minister in the House the other day, there could possibly be some 6,000 farmers who will feel the economic consequences of this decision. Up to 50 a month, or 600 a year, are sure to be affected by the lifting of the moratorium on the foreclosures of FCC mortgages. I find that very difficult to accept.
I want to thank our critic for the Liberal Party, the Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), who helped to organize our side for the debate and assist our Members in participating in what I believe has been a very interesting debate. I have learned much from this debate, most of which I have attended.
Some may ask what an urban Member of Parliament from downtown Ottawa would know about farming.
[ Translation]
I am sure that the Hon. Member for Montreal-Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) has learned something, as I did, because he too has been here almost all the time and even though we are both from the city, we have been able to follow the debate. We feel we have taken part in a general education process but also
in a very urgent debate on the difficult situation facing farmers in Canada.
All Members are aware of the serious problems of farmers, particularly grain growers. We know that for the past two weeks, given the announcement of the 18 per cent decrease in prices and the lifting of the moratorium on farm foreclosures, western farmers particularly, since grain growing is very important in the west, are worried and upset and rightly so; they are certainly very upset because of that decision and they fear the impact it might have on their families, on their farms which in many cases, as we all know, have been inherited through generations and have been part of the family heritage for many years. It is a sad situation because we know that when we see a "For sale" sign, Mr. Speaker, it sometimes means more than that. It means perhaps that a sad story is unfolding because the farmer has not met his operational costs, his cash receipts are too small and he is forced to sell his farm and sometimes to go bankrupt.
For almost 33 hours, Mr. Speaker, my colleagues in this House and myself have been discussing two major topics; the 18 per cent decrease in grain prices and the Government decision to lift the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation loans, which will lead to the foreclosure of some farms.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I am no expert in agriculture, but I worked on farms probably as much, if not more, as many Members in this House when I was a boy. The tradition was to send us to work on a farm, and like a number of youths during the 1940s and 1950s I went haying, stooking the grain-

The only decision we had to make was whether we wanted our eggs boiled, fried or scrambled. That was the way of life of poor people in those days and we accepted it-

So I think I am one of those who can say: "I worked at it." I may not be an expert, but I worked at it and I know, Mr. Speaker, that is is hard work. I know the work can take a lot of time and can also be exhausting and that is why I am most saddened today, on this Friday, May 1, to take part in a debate which will cause dismay for some farmers, some farm families who, in 1987-88, will most likely be among the 600 who will be forced out of business through foreclosure by the Farm Credit Corporation.

April 30, 1987
Mr. Speaker, I would like to review what I have heard during this debate. I assure you it will not take too long. I will simply summarize if possible some points that have been made, because I have heard some good ones. I heard positive comments and other things which I think are instructive for us.
For instance, I heard the Prime Minister say yesterday morning: "We will answer every call from the west."
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was saying yesterday morning that he would answer every call from the west. The Prime Minister is going out West next week. I understand that he will be travelling to Red Deer, Lethbridge, North Batt-leford, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Winnipeg between Wednesday and Friday. Since he has invited Members and farmers to call him, perhaps his phone number would be helpful. It is area code 613-992-4211. If you live in Red Deer, North Battleford, Moose Jaw, Saskatoon and Winnipeg, please go out and tell him about your problem or call him, and I repeat the phone number, which is 613-992-4211.

He asked for it.
So, any problem should be looked after.
I have also heard the Agriculture Minister tell us in this House not to get excited, not to worry, that the matter is under consideration, that the Government will show sensitivity about possible foreclosures of farms of which there would be no more than 50 a month.

I want to repeat some of the main points made during the debate. The prices announced by the Canadian Wheat Board reflect the fifth straight decline, dropping 18 per cent from the 1986-87 prices. No. 1 wheat in 1984-85 was $170 a tonne; in 1986-87 it was $137 a tonne; and in 1987-88 it is $110 a tonne. No. 1 barley in 1984-85 was $125 a tonne; in 1986-87 it was $80 a tonne; and in 1987-88 it is $60 a tonne. These are the same figures given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) this afternoon. He was giving us his views. I appreciated the sincerity of them and I appreciate why international negotiations at this time were rather difficult because of the unfair competition given Canada by the United States and the European Economic Community in the trade war. These countries, we were told, protect their farmers with subsidies. We do not. Canada has kept its market share, but has done so on the backs of farmers who get much lower returns. U.S. farmers receive about $6 per bushel for wheat as opposed to $3 per bushel in Canada. Farm expenses continue to rise. For example, fertilizer costs, chemicals, machinery and fuel. Even the Tory House Leader, I see him rise, will want to contribute to this debate. Yes, he is in good spirits. Prices are lowest in real terms since the Depression, Mr. Speaker. I am just repeating some of the things that I have heard. The Secretary of State for External Affairs outlined them this
afternoon and I thought he made a very interesting and good speech.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
I appreciated some of the things he said. I learned certain things that he brought to our attention.
In my view, there is no provision in the Budget right now for funds for a deficiency payment. The $1 billion allowed last year was only announced in desperation during the Saskatchewan election campaign. We heard repeatedly over the last 33 hours that farmers need to know now what their returns will be so that they will know what to seed, how much to seed, and so on. Many farmers are having trouble getting operating loans from the banks and cannot afford to seed. I could go on and read editorials, articles and press clippings in which it is quite evident that this situation is critical for many farmers. It is indeed a very serious situation.
The only guaranteed assistance the farmers have is the Western Grain Stabilization Fund, brought in by the Liberals, I remind the House, and fought-I repeat, fought-all the way by those Tories who are responsible for some of the difficulties these farmers are in. They opposed it systematically but now brag about it to all who will listen.
I want to read some of the correspondence which was received by the Government as of April 28, 1987. I have a letter signed by Mr. Garf Stevenson, President of the Saskatchewan Pool. Mr. Stevenson states in part:
The Pool asks that all Members of Parliament recognize the very critical economic situation confronting western Canadian families and communities. This crisis has far reaching social and economic implications for the national economy as well as for the west.
We specifically recommend:
1.	That programs be immediately developed through federal and provincial co-operation to keep families on their farms in productive capacities.
2.	That early consideration be given to the acute need for a substantial deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year.
3.	That government continue its efforts to restore sanity in the international grain market.
These three points are indeed essentially what we have been addressing in this debate of some 33 hours. I want to address the question of the $64 million announcement made today by the Government. We have not received the press release as yet. I understand it is in the mail. However, from what we have been told in the House and what I have heard on television, there will be a payment of $64 million given to the transporters, the railroads, under the Western Grain Transportation Act. The Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), in a speech on March 18, 1987, at page 4309, said:
-it would be most helpful if the Government would make a commitment to freeze the grain freight rates, the part the farmer pays himself. Last year the Minister of Transport ordered the Grain Transportation Agency to roll back its estimate of some 31.5 million tonnes to something in the 27 million to 29 million tonnes range. In fact, it did roll it back to 28.5 million tonnes which resulted in an effective freezing of the freight rates.
April 30, 1987

We know that the freight rates rise under the Western Grain Transportation Act as railway costs rise, depending upon volume shipped. The Tories last year kept the rate from rising by forcing the Grain Transportation Agency to bring forward an artificial and unrealistic low estimate of grain to be shipped. Therefore, there would have been a huge 39 per cent to 40 per cent increase in shipping costs this crop year. The Government brought forward a $2 per tonne subsidy today on grain shipped which will hold the increase to 5 per cent. However, that 5 per cent will still have to be paid by the producer, the farmer, to the transporter, the railroad.
Freight rates as a percentage of grain prices continue to increase dramatically. Holding cost increase to 5 per cent, while decreasing price by 18 per cent is no great gift. I submit that this Government has not done anything today but play a game of smoke and mirrors, and the $64 million subsidy will not in any way affect, and I say that sincerely, this year's production and help the farmers.
I want to end my remarks on what I hope is a note of some optimism. I see three Ministers here tonight. In fact, I see a lot of Members who should be Ministers but they cannot all be Ministers. I ask the Deputy Prime Minister who is in the House to look again at this question of the moratorium on the Farm Credit Corporation. I ask him to be serious and do something. All of us have acknowledged there should be a prolongation of the moratorium. For God's sake, let us be reasonable. Have some heart and understanding and give the farmers what they want, and that is a prolongation of the moratorium.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege this morning to follow the Hon. Whip of the Liberal Party. I am delighted to understand from what he has told us that he has learned so much from this debate. His Party tonight has done an extremely fine job of catching up. It is trying to catch up with the other Party, that is, the New Democratic Party, and I notice from the record that each Party has had 27 speakers, so he did catch up. I would also like to mention, while I am at it, that we are now on our forty-sixth speaker, 11 of whom were Ministers.
The Hon. Whip for the Liberal Party also mentioned throughout his speech his ability to shovel manure and the importance of fertilizer to the farm industry. I would say that he may be one of the best people in this House in that area. I would like to commend him on his experience and the benefit it has been to him now that he is here in the House of Commons. I too shared that experience in my youth and in most of my life. I still live on a farm. However, I do not think I will catch up with the Hon. Whip of the Liberal Party.
I listened with interest to this debate over the last few days. It was reminiscent of the time when, sitting in this House, I went to the then critic for transportation who was carrying on a very strong and important debate on the Crowsnest rate. I said to the now Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski):
"What is this all about?". He took me by the arm and said, "We are just about to have a meeting". The week-end before I had told my wife that I did not know what this Crowsnest rate was all about. By the time the Hon. Member for Vegreville had finished with me, I knew much more about the Crowsnest rate than I had ever intended to know, and it was a great experience for me. It gave me a real feeling of the importance of that debate in Canada's history.
It was the present Deputy Prime Minister and his colleagues from western Canada who led this debate. I heard that because of the Western Grain Transportation Act which was brought in, we have been able to keep this rate down to $6. I recall saying how bad this increase was going to be for the farmers of western Canada.

I knew then how important it was. I had an opportunity to explain to this House the importance to my constituency which borders on Oshawa. It was a very important discussion because we were afraid that if this rate got out of hand it could have a serious effect on industry in Ontario which supplied goods and services to the West.
1 also remember other debates on the National Energy Program. I remember how one factory in Scarborough had to close down. It made nothing but half-ton trucks and it closed down for a year because of the NEP which imposed inequitable penalties on the West. I know it affected all of Ontario. It affected Kingston, the steel industry in Hamilton, and Algoma Steel in the Hon. Member's riding. It affected all of eastern Ontario.
I have heard the Opposition talk about what we have not done. I heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) tonight set forth in great detail all of the benefits we have brought to this country through-

When interest rates were 22 per cent the farmers were going belly-up by the dozen every day. 1 knew those people. Do not talk to me about farmers getting into trouble. My friends in my community were affected. Your damned interest rates got out of control. You had no control, no voice in your Government to bring them down. 1 hate to hear the Liberals telling me what they did for the farmers when they did not do a damn thing.

April 30, 1987
This Party represents all of Canada. It represents the farm community. We have put up 46 speakers and very few were from the City of Toronto or the City of Montreal. Many were from rural areas.

I come from a rural area so do not talk to me about Whitby. It is part of my constituency. I live in a rural area.
Talking about Whitby, I want to tell the Hon. Member what the Liberals did to the farmers in my riding. I want to tell him what they did to 18,000 acres of prime agricultural land in my riding. They drove farmers off that land because they decided they were going to build an airport in 1971.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext: Shame!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Not only that, they went to Quebec and destroyed 98,000 of the most arable acres in the Province of Quebec. It was about 1 per cent of the total arable land. Yet it was our Party that took 80,000 of those acres and returned them to farming. It is our Party that will return most of the acreage involved in my riding. Do not tell me about my riding and what the Liberals did for farmers. You hurt the service industry, you hurt the co-ops, you hurt everyone. We will get the land back to its original owners.
We have a major problem in the industry because of the critical problem internationally. Today many farmers cannot afford to pay the rent for their land. It is not worth their while to seed that land. I even approached the manager of the airport property and said that possibly he should give it to farmers just to keep the weeds under control. He said that unfortunately, because of over-supply, farmers do not want to invest the money in planting. That is a tragic situation.
What happened? France is a prime example of what happened. TThey have done extremely well and produce abundant amounts of cereal grains. Right after World War II they were a net importer but now they are an exporter. Many other countries we have assisted to become self-sufficient are now net exporters of grain. We have to deal with that. We cannot afford to pay our farmers a subsidy of $320 a tonne. We are not rich enough. It is only those countries with a much larger tax base who can afford it. We have to make do with less. We are a very large country with a very small population.
Farmers have also been faced with a change in eating habits. Not as much grain is consumed today as there was 10 years ago. This is a serious problem and our Government is trying to deal with it and at the same time give some dignity back to the agricultural industry.
The announcement today that we have reduced the freight rate increase to 5 per cent was very important. Under the method set up by the Liberal Party that increase would have been about $11 this year as opposed to the $6 announced today. I was talking to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) before I came in here tonight. After I read a number of pages
of what we had done for agriculture I turned to him and asked, what else are you going to do for the farmer? I sort of smiled and looked at him and said I have never seen such a complete list of assistance for the agricultural community in the eight years I have been here.
I am proud to be a Progressive Conservative. I am proud to be working with this Government. I am proud to work directly with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) of this country who, I have said many times, will go down in history as the greatest Prime Minister this country ever had.

speechtext:
I am proud to be a Canadian. I am proud particularly to be able to speak about western Canada with the same feeling that I speak about my own area. They have suffered. Go back to the dirty thirties, the dirty seventies and the early eighties. They have suffered. I do not know how much more we can do but we must rationalize on an equitable basis.
The Opposition has talked about our removing the moratorium on FCC loans. In 1982 and 1983 we pleaded with them to do something to save these farmers. We put a moratorium on foreclosures and we put a review board in place. Not only that, we provided advance payments for crops. We provided crop and livestock drug assistance. We made a record interim payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. We have done more for the exports of this country than has been done in 20 years of Liberal Governments before us. We increased our sales to Russia, and have sold grain to Egypt and Brazil.
We have had to take numerous initiatives on behalf of the agricultural community because of the neglect of the Liberals while they were in government. The Liberals never cared about the farm community.
Unfortunately, the Member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) is not here, because he is largely responsible for these initiatives. I want to congratulate him for his persistence in our caucus in expressing the concerns and views of western Canadians who are in agriculture. He is a western grain farmer and probably grows more grain than all the farmers in the Opposition combined.
Members opposite rose with a holier than thou attitude to talk about the dreadful things we are doing to farmers. The majority of the 46 Members from our Party who spoke in this debate are farmers or live on farms.
I want to say a few words about the capital gains tax. The capital gains tax exemption was a serious inequity. Someone from Toronto who owned a house worth $ 1 million and sold it for $2 million a year later would have to pay no capital gains tax. However, a farmer in my area who owned a $100,000 farm that became worth $200,000 had to pay capital gains tax. We rectified that terrible inequity.
April 30, 1987

The Opposition has spread fear throughout the country about what our free trade initiative will do to the agricultural community. I can tell the House that we will protect agriculture because we intend to maintain the good agricultural industry in this country.
When I met some 240 dairy farmers at a meeting I told them that while I cannot relieve their fears about what might happen, since they have suffered so much through different periods, I could promise that I would stand up for them and ensure that we would protect the marketing boards that had been put in place.

We cannot afford the subsidies that the Americans give their farmers because we do not have enough money. Therefore, we have developed another method and it is working. Those farmers left that meeting knowing that they have a Government that cares.
I had an opportunity to speak to 80 members of the feather industry. They included broiler chicken producers and egg producers. They were also very concerned, but I tried to allay their fears. I had a final meeting with a small group from the local durum agricultural association. I was somewhat complimented by the response I received when I asked why the meeting was so small. They told me that I had answered most of their questions already.
We have taken major steps on behalf of the agricultural industry and I am proud to be part of this Party and tell farmers in the rural communities in my riding that we have stood up for them and will continue to do so in order that they may become a healthy component of this economy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to participate in the debate. There is absolutely no truth to the rumour that although I represent a rural community I was elected by the farm vote on a promise that I would not speak on agricultural issues. They sent me here to speak on those issues.
1 want to say a few words about the participation in this debate. First, we heard some very knowledgeable speeches from members of the New Democratic caucus who represent the farming community. However, those knowledgeable speeches got off track when we heard from the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy). He is a notable expert in rural items, who once told the House that his riding of Ottawa Centre was a microcosm of Canada. I do not know whether he is farming what he is throwing, but I point out that he is the Member who continually stands in the House to complain about the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption which the NDP has fought since we introduced it. There does not seem to be anyone in the NDP who realizes that the capital gains tax
exemption was implemented immediately for farms because the Conservative Party realizes that the farm represents the pension of farmers when they retire. Day after day, members of the NDP complain about the fact that we have exempted that pension.
We then heard from the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). I was moved when I heard her speech. I realized why she is put on so many travelling committees. Then we heard from the Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) who went through a whole speech without moving an amendment. Subsequently the Member for Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin) made one of his few speeches, while he is still a New Democrat, before he becomes an independent. That is the only Party he has not represented.
Having been somewhat caustic, I want to compliment my good friend, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), who commenced the debate. I have worked with him on the Public Accounts Committee and I commend him for his efforts in this debate, as well as the Members of his Party who represent rural communities. Had it not been for the NDP, this debate would certainly have collapsed because there was very little knowledgeable participation from the Liberals.
That brings me to the Liberal Party. I want to highlight some of the speeches made by their Members. We heard from the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) whose knowledge of the rural community out west is basically from a 30,000 foot level as he flies back and forth between Vancouver and Ottawa. He stayed in Vancouver longer, before he sold his condo. Now that he has sold it, he does not take as many trips and is losing some of that knowledge of the rural community.
We then heard from the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy). He is one of the two members in the western caucus, and he did a good job.
The Hon. Member for St. Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston) spent 20 minutes denying that there were high interest rates during the Liberal depression. We listened to 20 minutes of explanations that simply did not wash.
Having said that, I want to compliment the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster) who briefed his colleagues, and I am sure it was not easy. He hung here in the debate and 1 compliment him on his efforts.
There are two reasons this debate has been welcomed by the Government Party; because we had two things we wanted to get across. First, we have an excellent record to brag about as a Government in our efforts to assist Canadian farmers. We understand the problems. We do not have them all solved yet, not for a minute, but the effort and the steps have been there. Second, the west is finally fully represented on agricultural issues at the table, as a region and in the House. Members from all areas of Canada in our Party fully understand the

April 30, 1987
problems of the western grain producer. We break bread with our colleagues from the west. We sit on committees with them. We participate in the House of Commons and there is absolutely not one Member of Parliament from the Maritimes, Quebec or Ontario in the Progressive Conservative Party who does not have an empathy with our colleagues from the west. We understand fully.
If I had one message I would like the people from the west to take from what I say it is this. The Members of Parliament from the central provinces, Ontario and Quebec, and they are here tonight, understand. There is no learning curve with us. We understand the problem and our Government, from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) down, has the full support of the Members of Parliament in the Progressive Conservative Party from Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces in the work they are doing on this problem.
The work is considerable. Because it has been referred to at length in this debate I will not walk the House through the details of the programs. There is however, a special grains program, there is crop and livestock drought assistance, there are interim pay-outs, the Western Grain Transportation Act amendments and the commodity based mortgages. All of these steps have been taken to help the west.
I would like to dwell on interest rates for a minute. We have worked as a Party to lower interest rates. We have saved farmers millions of dollars. Those steps have been taken. We have the Farm Credit Corporation rates at the lowest levels since 1979. Interest rates have been reduced five times.
With respect to farm debt review boards, legislation has been passed to set up these boards composed of people who have a knowledge of the agricultural community and have the experience in farming and financial matters to try to ease these tensions.
We have the Canadian Rural Transition Program. In my riding, this was referred to from time to time by my constituents, who are farmers. I got the best example a couple of weeks ago. On the seventh concession of Orillia Township in 1956 there were 21 farm families. Now, 31 years later, there are four farm families on that same concession farming the same amount of land. What has happened is that the ability of our farmers-and we should all be proud of this-to expand production and produce has increased faster than anyone's ability to find the markets and to be competitive in them. Being competitive in them is really the problem we are talking about today.
We have been at the forefront in calling for a new set of ground rules for international agricultural trade. The Prime Minister raised it in Tokyo as Canada's number one agenda item. We have been trying to get an informal international agreement on agricultural trade practices during the negotiations of the the new GATT rules. This may take years, but we have been there. We have made all this effort.
We know how our farmers are facing problems because our competitors are just out-subsidizing us. It is just not practical in this world where we have people who are hungry, not to get food to them. It is just not practical that we are competing with the European Economic Market and the United States which subsidize their producers. I do not think anybody in this House, no matter to which Party they belong, thinks that is a very effective way of doing things.
I went to the annual Simco County Federation of Agriculture meeting. Many Members of Parliament and Members of the provincial Legislature attended. A lot of briefs were presented at that meeting from the Cattlemen's Association, the corn producers, the egg marketing board, the maple syrup producers, the milk committee, the pork producers, the sheep producers and the wheat growers. We heard the briefs and we had a back and forth discussion. There was public participation. I was pleased to hear people tell us that they are in general agreement with the efforts of the Government, that they know what we are faced with and they are behind our efforts in trying to do something.
As I suggested earlier, we do not have all the answers and we have not won the battle. There is no question that our Government has made the effort to win the battle. We have a Prime Minister who time and time again is very, very vocal, and who has then followed his vocal comments with efforts to address the concerns of agriculture. We have a first class cabinet Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) from Ontario and his colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer). They work in tandem.
It would be interesting if I were to tell the House just exactly how this ministry works. It works with complete cooperation between the two Ministers, along with the Parliamentary Secretary from the riding of Champlain, Quebec, to give it a Quebec focus. The Ministers have excellent staffs who always have time for Members of Parliament and their problems. They have a concerned Public Service staff backing them up.
The caucus is fully behind all of those people and the Prime Minister in their efforts on the issue. Let me say to the people who are suffering at this time that we do have an understanding of your problems no matter where you live in Canada. Speaking as an Ontario Member of Parliament, especially Ontario, we do have an understanding, and we intend to continue the good fight.
I want to finish my speech by complimenting everybody, the Speakers in the chair, Members at the Table, the pages, the staff, and especially the Hansard staff. With some exceptions, it has been Parliament at its best, and we have truly focused the concern of Canadians on this very important issue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the revised wording. It would be laughable, if the subject were not so difficult for many Canadians, to hear members of the Liberal caucus sitting opposite talking with such feigned concern about agriculture and about the west.
Even the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) got into the act, making a case for everything that he failed to do in the period in which he led a Government that totally failed agriculture and totally failed the West in so many critical areas of economic activity. His speech yesterday can only be treated with a degree of cynicism that it so richly deserves. We do not need to go back to former Prime Minister Trudeau's disparaging and insulting remarks to western farmers, remarks that defined his personal attitude and that of the Liberal Party toward exercising some of the responsibility that they had to the west and to farmers. That Government chose to turn its back on both the west and its farmers, just as it did when its

April 30, 1987
policies brought about interest rates of 22 per cent and higher, which really is the root cause of the difficulties plaguing agriculture and many other segments of our economic society.
Yesterday we heard the Leader of the Opposition complaining bitterly that Farm Credit Corporation rates are averaging 11 per cent. I would like to ask what action came from his Government to help farmers locked into contracts with 16.75 per cent interest. What did the Leader of the Opposition do when it was within his power as Prime Minister to do something to assist those farmers that he is now so zealous in defending? The answer is nothing. Neither he nor the Liberal Government he led did anything. It was the Government of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who, together with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) looked at those terribly high interest rates that Liberal policy had brought about and who took the action to reduce the rate for all those farmers who were locked in at 16.75 per cent interest. That is only one of the many positive actions which the Hon. Minister of Agriculture has brought to bear on the critical pressures which threaten agriculture in Canada.
If time permits I will talk later about the many varied positive actions which the Mulroney Government has taken in support of agriculture and in support of farmers. The point which has to be made is that every one of these supportive actions by the Mulroney Government could have been taken months and years ago by the Liberal Government which preceded the Mulroney Government. The problems existed then. In fact, it was Liberal policy that produced the most damaging of these problems. The problems existed but the Liberals did not have the will to address them. They refused to accept responsibility when they were in office.
[DOT] (mo)
Yesterday the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) said some things that I think should be noted. He said that when the former Liberal Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Whelan, was asked when the Liberal Government would do something for farmers facing disaster as a result of interest rates that went up beyond 22 per cent, the Liberal Minister of Agriculture responded by saying: "soon, soon". The Liberal Government never did provide the relief that farmers sought.

speechtext: Soon never came.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
The "soon, soon," of Mr. Whelan, the former Liberal Minister of Agriculture, was in reality: "never, never". There was no relief from the Liberal Government under Prime Minister Trudeau nor under the Prime Minister who succeeded him.
1 would like to add my voice to that of the Hon. Member for Bow River in evidence that will add to the growing body of cynicism which surrounds the statements made in this debate originating from Liberal benches. Yesterday the Liberal Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) said that "speaking is not good enough and that there is only one Party that can act,
and that is the Government". He said that "only the Government can do something".
The fruit growers in British Columbia shower apples upon the Members of the House of Commons annually. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you profit and benefit from them. Those fruit growers from British Columbia's Okanagan Valley would say that it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member for York Centre could not yesterday have spoken with some retroactive effect. Where was the voice of York Centre when Okanagan farmers were asking the Liberal Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Eugene Whelan, to honour the obligations under the stabilization Act which the Act imposes for commodities designated in it?
When I repeatedly brought to Mr. Whelan's attention the matter of a deficiency payment for Okanagan orchardists, a deficiency payment which would be triggered by the disastrous 1983 prices for soft fruits including peaches, apricots and cherries, the answer I received was "no", even though Mr. Gerald Geen, the President of the fruit growers' association, and I raised it personally with Mr. Whelan. The Liberal Government would not make that payment even though disaster faced many farmers as a result of the disastrous prices that returned only 20 per cent of the cost of production to those farmers I represent. Mr. Whelan said in the House and to me: "We aren't going to pay".
Contrast that with the action taken by the present Minister of Agriculture when this Government took office. The Minister of Agriculture reversed that unworthy decision and made that very substantial payment after the people of Canada had the good sense to put the Progressive Conservative Government in place. By that single action, the people of Canada provided Canadian agriculture a benefit unequalled in the history of Canada. Never has agriculture received so much legislative, policy and Treasury attention from Ottawa.
Let me read from the March 1987 issue of the magazine entitled the British Columbia Orchardist. The President of the British Columbia Fruit Growers' Association, Gerald Geen, who represents some 2,000 farmers concentrated in the Okanagan, Similkameen and Creston Valleys, wrote the following in response to the $4.5 million payment made recently to apple producers in the area:
The really good news is that the federal government has just announced that stabilization payments will be made to Canadian apple growers for their 1983 and 1984 apple crops.
He went on to say the following:
I can tell you that our industry has had very positive support on this matter from the Prime Minister and one of his senior policy advisors who last summer spent two days with me in the Okanagan; Right Hon. Joe Clark, Secretary of State for External Affairs who met with Fred King, Martin Linder and myself last August; Hon. Michael Wilson, Minister of Finance; Hon. Pat Carney, Minister for International Trade; Hon. John Crosbie, Minister of Transportation; Hon. Tom Siddon, Minister of Fisheries and Oceans; Hon. Frank Oberle, Minister of State (Science and Technology), several other key Cabinet Ministers and the entire B.C. Conservative Caucus.
I especially want to recognize the Minister of Agriculture, Hon. John Wise, and his assistant Mr. John Donald, for vigorously supporting our request for stabilization during the last twelve months ... On behalf of our apple growers,
April 30, 1987

I want to thank everyone at the federal government level who has in any way
assisted our industry in getting this payment. Your efforts are very much
appreciated. The forthcoming funds are very much needed by our producers.
I read that into the record because I want to emphasize the fact that despite what is coming from the benches opposite, Canadian farmers know the facts and the facts are that they and their difficulties are receiving more attention from this Government under the Right Hon. Prime Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) than any other Government has provided to agriculture in Canada.
On Tuesday of this week, the Hon. Minister of Agriculture was in the riding I represent, Okanagan-Similkameen, to open officially the new $24 million Agriculture Canada Research Centre. More than 1,500 citizens of the area were there to demonstrate the popular support which the Summer-land Experimental Station as it was called in 1914 when it was established, has earned from farmers in all of British Columbia.
As I have already mentioned, Mr. Speaker, I have often brought with me apples to distribute to Members of Parliament-
An Hon. Mlember: And cherries.

speechtext: And cherries, and apricots, and peaches-

speechtext:
All of the tremendous produce that comes from the Okanagan Valley. One apple that gets great attention here is the Spartan apple, a strain that was developed at the Summerland Experimental Station. It is a beautiful red apple, a cross between a McIntosh and a Newton. I know that it is one of your favourites, Mr. Speaker.
As I say, the Spartan apple was developed at the Summer-land Research Station. You may consider it Agriculture Canada's contribution to your well-being, Mr. Speaker. But that facility is also involved in fruit processing techniques, in controlled atmosphere storage research, and other areas.
I heard the other day about a tremendous new facility that is going up in the Province of Ontario that will keep apples for a full year without deterioration. The Summerland Research Station has been involved in that type of work for 30 years, and such facilities have existed in the Okanagan Valley for 25 years at least. In fact, we have controlled atmosphere storage for something like two million bushels of apples in place in the Okanagan Valley.
The reason the Okanagan is at the forefront of horticultural technology is the Summerland Experimental Station and the efforts that the federal Government has put into research at that facility.
Low volume orchard spraying-something which every environmentalist in Canada should rise up and cheer-also
owes its development to the Summerland Experimental Station of Agriculture Canada, as do the new irrigation techniques that are in use.
The Okanagan area has average annual precipitation of only 10 inches. Without irrigation, nothing could be grown. Water for irrigation is a precious commodity and something which must be used judiciously, and toward that end, the Summer-land Experimental Station has assisted farmers in the Okanagan in developing water saving techniques.
It is important that we point out what Agriculture Canada is doing for farmers in this country, and particularly the degree of attention the Minister of Agriculture has devoted to research in agriculture.
Let me just take a moment to outline for you some of the programs and expenditures this Government, under the direction of the Minister, has been engaged in.
At Vegreville, Alberta, we had an expenditure of $4.57 million for construction and research into soil quality; in Quebec, an experimental farm complex at a cost of $6.1 million; in London, Ontario, $16 million for an office-laboratory complex; at L'Assomption, Quebec, $8.5 million for research facilities to find alternate crops for tobacco growers; at Big River, Saskatchewan, $1.5 million for expansion of the Provincial Forest Nursery; again in Saskatchewan, $577 million for the expansion of a livestock centre; at the Lacombe Research Station, Alberta, $210,000 for library facilities and a conference room; at St-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Quebec, $16 million for an office-laboratory complex; at Lethbridge, Alberta, $22.3 million on the Animal Disease Research Institute; at Guelph, Ontario, $2.7 million for a new animal pathology laboratory; at St. Hyacinthe, Quebec, $17 million for a pathology laboratory; and in Nepean, Ontario, $33.6 million for an Animal Research Center office-laboratory complex.
When you add to those expenditures the $24 million that has been spent at the Summerland Experimental Station, total expenditures amount to some $150 million. The expenditures of Agriculture Canada on research funding are projected to be $240 million for 1986-87.
To my mind there has been a degree of confusion brought about by the Opposition as to the effect of the lifting of this moratorium. I think it needs to be made clear that the moratorium that was in place is one that applied only to contracts with the Farm Credit Corporation. It did not apply in respect of loans or mortgages held by private sector lending institutions.
The moratorium is unsustainable forever. There is probably no time at which it could be lifted without someone being affected. It is for that reason that it was put into place in the first place.
The Government has now put into place farm debt review boards and the Rural Transition Program, both of which will be effective in easing the problems associated with the lifting

April 30, 1987
of the moratorium. The moratorium itself was not designed to eliminate these problems; rather, it merely provided some breathing space.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is drawing to a close. I wanted to talk a little more about Spartan apples. Given the time constraints, I shall just have to bring you one and demonstrate in that way what it is I am talking about.
