subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a deepening crisis has been developing on Canadian farms over the past two years. Nowhere is this more evident or more serious that in the grain economy of western Canada.
We are, unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, engaged in the world today in a form of trade war that is particularly vicious and one in which Canada is, in one sense, the main victim and, in another sense, has no alternative but to participate.
The export subsidy war between the European Economic Community and the United States has caused prices for Canadian grains to plummet. Prices dropped 20 per cent last year, and a further 18 per cent drop for the 1987-88 crop year was announced by the Canadian Wheat Board last week.
Who among us, Mr. Speaker, could face a cumulative reduction in our incomes over a two-year period of something in the order of 40 per cent? I say that, of course, in the context of a small business operation, which most Canadian grain farms are, and in the context of having fixed costs, many of which have risen dramatically over the years leading up to the
drop in revenues. We are all aware of the rising tide in interest rates that engulfed farms in western Canada in the early 1980s; we are all aware of the rising costs of energy, fertilization and labour for farming operations. Yet, while these costs were rising, farmers, for the last two crop years, have faced what can only be described as reductions on a disastrous scale.
On Monday last, with perhaps the worst timing possible, with farmers already under severe stress, the Government announced that on Tuesday, the very next day, the Farm Credit Corporation would once again be permitted to foreclose on family farms. The moratorium that had been in place for 18 months was being lifted.
I should point out that the Farm Credit Corporation is, after all, seen very much as the bellwether and leader in terms of farm lending. Everyone in this House knows what happens when one bank raises its mortgage rates. When this happens all the other banks follow suit. I think it can be anticipated, and the Government must surely expect no other consequence, that other lenders to farmers will take this as a signal that it is again open season on farm foreclosures.
The Government has refused to make a commitment to a deficiency payment program in the forthcoming crop year. It says that those sorts of announcements will come at the appropriate time. That time is now. Farmers are traditionally, and I believe never more than today, plain-spoken people who understand the facts and know what is going on. In plain talk, a deficiency payment program is a subsidy. Some people would call it a hand-out and farmers would much rather make their income on a market system which provides them with a price return for their commodities than accept a subsidy on the production of those crops.
What we are calling for, and not because this Party has any ideological commitment to subsidies, not because we believe that the farm economy and the grain war can be sustained indefinitely in the face of what has been happening, but simply because this Party understands that it is a case of survival for western grain farmers and the western grain industry, is a commitment to provide Canadian grain farmers with at least a guarantee that the total receipts for crops this year will equal those of the last crop year.
In doing so it is obvious, I think, that we ourselves and those others who support such a move are not taking this on as some sort of welfare commitment, but are very seriously addressing the short-term remedy for the Canadian grain farming situation, without which short-term remedy we will never have the opportunity to bring in the long-term solutions which, of course, can be the only solutions for the grain economy.
As Oscar Wilde observed, in the long run we are all dead, but Canadian farmers may not survive the short run. They are very willing to absorb the impact of inflation and the increase in other price factors if only they could have a guarantee from the Government on the revenue return to the farmers.
April 30, 1987

We are not bringing this motion forward in some spirit of partisan and unreserved condemnation of the Government's total approach to the farm economy because we do understand that there have been some worth-while initiatives introduced and some worthwhile accomplishments. We know that the Government is working hard on the international front. Any Canadian Government would, because the anarchy, the discounting and the marketing manoeuvres that are being carried on at the moment in the world grain market can only lead to further chaos if measures are not taken to restrain them.
We know that the Government understands also that the grain export economy is, if you like, to a large degree the mirror image of the agricultural situation in the Third World and in less developed parts of the Second World. We know, after all, that Canadian grain should never be sold or distributed in such a way as to affect the viability of the Third World farmer because, without the opportunity for the Third World farmer to produce her crop and sell her crop for a cash return, and also to use her crop to nourish her family, those who took that opportunity away would be guilty of a crime against humanity which would have the most profoundly sincere consequences in the Third World.
This Party does not say that the Government has totally failed to assist the farm sector in recent months. We question very much the Rural Transition Program. We know that something useful at least has been accomplished through the debt review boards and we know that the Government has consulted with farm organizations, although often the effects of having listened are more evident in the breach than in the materialization. I return again to the fact that government assistance has not been adequate and will not be adequate without new announcements to ensure the short-term survival of the western grain economy in order for it to be able to take advantage of the opportunities which still exist to be taken advantage of in western Canada.
The alternatives to a deficiency payment program, the alternatives to other adjustment measures, are indeed no alternatives. Without an announcement from the Government we will be looking at widespread bankruptcy. We would be looking not simply at economic dislocation, not simply at unemployment which, after all, is something which, regrettable though it is, many of us have some experience with and which we as a society have measures both to combat and to ease the short-term difficulties therein entailed, but at something as serious as bankruptcy and unemployment. The seriousness is doubled by the very fact that it means the end of a way of life for anyone in western Canada who is forced off his farm by the lack of assistance forthcoming from the Government.
We know that stress increases on individuals in direct proportion to the number and magnitude of changes that they have to undergo in their lives. If we allow the western grain farmer to be subjected to the stress of bankruptcy, unemployment and relocation all at once, we will see people who are stressed beyond belief, stressed beyond the comprehension of
you, me, or any of us, and perhaps stressed beyond their limits to sustain themselves in the face of that sort of trial.
We would be looking not only at the disappearance in the less prosperous parts of grain producing western Canada of the farms, but also at the disappearance of the entire rural community. That includes bank branches, lawyers, doctors and the co-ops and credit unions which built western Canada and enabled farmers to build up farm economies in the first place. Perhaps even more serious than those consequences, it would bring about, of course, the complete absence of soil stewardship.
Sometimes when I travel from the farm areas of my riding I travel through farming areas of Manitoba. I am often impressed by the scale of those operations and, in some way, a little envious for my own farmers who must contend with a much smaller market, who are generally much more diversified than farming only a single commodity, whether it be grain or potatoes, and who have themselves been facing many, many trials over the past few years which the provincial Government has been somewhat reluctant to assist them with and which, unfortunately, because they are not grain farmers, federal programs have also not touched on very much either. My farmers are in a serious condition but they understand that because the average western farmer does not have access to alternative employment opportunities, does not have access to the wood lots which are available to northwestern Ontario farmers. It is the western grain farmer who is in the worst situation.
In talking of soil stewardship, let me say that last week-end was a fairly windy one in western Canada. As I drove down the highway I could see topsoil blowing off at a time of the year when it would normally be nicely fixed in place even if it had been tilled. The fact is that when there is an agricultural depression, the future prospects of the agricultural economy are drastically diminished by the farmers' inability to conserve his soil.
The Government has provided some assistance, but on the other hand, it has allowed the input cost to farmers to rise. As a result of the announcement of the discontinuance of the moratorium perhaps during the worst time of the year, in spring, we face a very serious situation.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian farmers are saddled with a $25 billion debt. We know-and they know-that the interest rates set by the Liberal Government are too high and that farmers simply cannot survive.

Let me deal with the long run solutions for the farm economy, because without alternative markets for those crops there will be farmers who will go out of production. Some months ago I had the pleasure to participate in the Energy Committee's investigation of fuel alcohol. I was struck by the

April 30, 1987
strong desire of some sectors of Canadian agriculture to link their grain surplus problem with the country's energy situation, particularly in respect of gasoline supply.
There have been corporate announcements of imminent petrochemical solutions to gasoline lead octane problems, but I believe from the evidence I have seen that there are biochemical and biomechanical solutions available that could utilize grain production in western Canada as a feedstock. This could strengthen the price of grain that is sold for food and thus enable our farmers to dig themselves out of the hole in which they find themselves.
Will the Government let our mostly foreign-owned oil refining industry turn its back on Canadian farmers, or will the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), who has a grain ethanol plant producing in his riding, take some action to ensure that the octane requirements of Canada's future production streams are met in a way that provides an economic opportunity and future for Canadian farmers?
Fuel ethanol has been available in Canada for six years. It will be one year ago tomorrow that the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources produced a report that favoured a 5 per cent to 3 per cent blend of ethanol and methanol, not only in order to reduce Canada's reliance on imported additives, but also to help farmers of western Canada with a new crop market. Nothing has been done. We understand that some low-level studies have been conducted within the Canadian Wheat Board, but the fact is that the Government must take action because it knows a solution is available and that there are remedies to help the western farmers with another market for their grains.
The fact is that the Government has sold out the farm economy indirectly to the multinational oil interests. Everyone should realize that there is no free market in petroleum production within Canada. There is no free market in refined gasolines. By making the policy decision that the so-called free market would decide, the Government is on the verge of cutting off a major economic opportunity for Canadian farmers and giving it, instead, to the multinational oil companies. Furthermore, this is in a form that will create very few jobs and will essentially keep that centralized control so much favoured by the multinationals.
We are told that there are imminent investments in the MTBE plant of $275 million each for a plant in western Canada and a plant in eastern Canada, creating 100 jobs each. That is the sort of solution to Canada's octane shortage that this country simply cannot afford because when the remedies are technically available in a new and developing technology that still has its economy of scale and has its efficiency and effectiveness developments before it, we would be very poor Canadians if we were to sell such an opportunity to the already excessively dominated multinational oil industry.
Supply concerns of the 1970s in the United States prompted federal and state tax incentives, and a large independent
refining industry controlling half of U.S. capacity, which is something that does not exist here, co-operated with the move to introduce ethanol into the fuel stream. Canadian production today is the same as it was in 1981, unfortunately, when Mohawk Oil recommissioned a 7.2 million litre a year distillery in Minnedosa and began selling that 10 per cent blend. Why is that 10 per cent blend not available right across the country? Why are Canadian farmers being denied the possibility of $200 million, or $400 million or $500 million a year in additional revenue, even just in the short term, with the 5 per cent-3 per cent and 10 per cent ethanol blends that would be marketed and commercialized virtually immediately?
Recent bipartisan moves in the United States Congress and administration may soon mandate oxygenated fuels, ethanol and methanol to help meet the 1987 Clean Air Act standards. That policy is supported by 46 United States Senators, Republican and Democrat, and by Vice-President Bush, who of course has aspirations to the presidency himself.
Whether or not that happens, North American oil refiners have to fill an emerging octane gap, estimated at possibly over $10 billion a year, with lead replacers of their choice and not necessarily the public's choice.
Canadian Government and parliamentary support for proethanol forces in this country as well as world-wide could help tip the scales in favour of the biochemical option for lead removal and to reduce other emissions. Ethanol is a fuel that is well known and presents very few environmental risks. Of course, it has great economic potential.
You are signalling that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I could have talked for much longer and I hope to have a further opportunity to talk on the possibilities and the potential that ethanol has for Canadian farmers, particularly Canadian grain farmers. More jobs will be created throughout Canada, more Canadian farmers will be able to keep farming and be profitable. International success in ethanol production could help strengthen world grain prices and we could keep the Canadian western grain economy going, if the Government had but the vision to use its legislative powers toward that end.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I acknowledge the vital import of the agricultural producers' great contribution towards feeding Canadians, as well as their right to earn a decent living and to get a fair price for their products, I must admit that the intricacies of agricultural production, particularly wheat, fall somewhat beyond the scope of my expertise. As you would know, Mr. Speaker, I feel more at home when dealing with communications and cultural matters. CBC listeners can often hear programs concerning farmers, and I can assure you that the day-to-day problems of the farm community are often explored not only on these programs but also in the course of educational and regional programs. A current topic has been the 18 per cent drop in the price of wheat and the definite
April 30, 1987

possibility that agricultural producers may very well lose both their farms and their homes.
Mr. Speaker, you also know that I used to be the critic on the status of women, and we were made vividly aware of the very serious situation of Mrs. Irene Murdoch and the discrimination she experienced when the court ruling did not give her any recognition for all the work she had done, day in and day out, seven days a week. Since then there has been some improvement in the situation of women who happen to be full-fledged partners in the agricultural community.
I believe that we should pay homage to couples, both men and women, and their children who work very hard on farms throughout Canada.
Until now, Mr. Speaker, as a woman living in urban surroundings I was hesitant to join in this emergency debate on the agricultural crisis in Western Canada. But after listening to my colleagues in the House, even though I am not all that familiar with agricultural affairs I can still readily appreciate the human drama being played in Canadian rural homes, their sentiments of fear, anxiety and frustration.
I have often travelled through the countryside with my family to admire the scenery and the wild flowers, to pick up daisies, blueberries, strawberries and raspberries, to buy fresh and tasty farm products, to marvel at the sight of wide expanses of wheat and corn fields. Particularly in the fall, I never get tired of looking at the fairy-tale colours of the trees.
However it never occurred to me that a house-for-sale sign might indeed hide a human drama due to this Government's inadequate farm support policy. Certainly this insensitive policy of the Conservative Government cannot be the result of laziness on the part of farmers, the lack of motivation, the long hours of work, a reduced budget. Quite the contrary, farmers are so anxious and so proud to preserve the heritage which in many cases was left to them by their ancestors that they do not think twice about toiling under very harsh conditions and making do with aid programs which fall far short and might even be described as being totally unacceptable.
Monday's announcement by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) that the Farm Credit Corporation of Canada would lift the moratorium declared on September, 1985, with respect to foreclosures on bankrupt farms has created utter distress for hundreds of owners of small and medium-size farms, leading them to despair, family violence and, in some cases, suicide.
It has become quite evident through the course of this urgent debate that a long-term vision of society is absolutely critical in order to arrive at the short-term remedial steps required at this time. If we as Canadians value the family farm, its stability, its place in the grand design of our society, then the necessary fiscal measures must be taken to enable farmers to survive this crisis.
On the international stage the grain subsidy situation is being fully addressed and increased efforts are being made to restore sanity in international grain markets. However, my Leader and my colleagues have tried to make the Government understand that just citing figures and comparing them to those of last year or the year before, boasting about how much more the Government has invested in the West's economy than the Liberals did, are not answers to the family farm crisis. They bring no solace to the individual farmer and the crisis in his family life. The way to demonstrate leadership is not to say: You did not do it and we are doing something. The way to demonstrate leadership is to come up with a plan of action.
We acknowledge that $1 billion was pumped into the agricultural economy last year. I will not go into the way it was offered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as a sort of little lollipop dangled in front of the voters in the middle of a provincial election. It was a needed support. However, because that is true it does not mean other similar steps do not have an ongoing and important place in the plans and policies and political vision of the Government. Obviously it is a Government with no vision and certainly no heart. Farm families are paying a heavy price while the Government dallies and promises schemes for diversification of the economy.
Monday's announcement of lower initial grain prices for 1987-88 indicates that the price of wheat will be down by 18 per cent and that of barley by 25 per cent. When those announcements were made the Government should have given some indication of how it intends to react to this new crisis. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma, has given this House the benefit of his wise counsel, deep commitment to and knowledge of this field. I do not pretend to have that knowledge but why can the Government not listen to our experts? It could take some direction given that it is completely lacking in any ideas of its own.
The Government has boasted of improved federal-provincial relations. If that is true, why does it not sit down with the provinces and co-operatively develop a plan to keep families on the farm in a productive capacity? Why does it not see them through this short-term crisis until it can bring forward that White Paper we have been waiting and waiting for, which obviously has no content, no concept and no political vision? Let the Government at least support the family farm which is such an important part of our heritage and our institutions. Rural family farms are revered institutions in our society. Rural communities and related industries are all in jeopardy. It is not just the farmer who is affected; it is the manufacturer of the equipment the farmer uses and the supplier of seeds and everything else needed in the ongoing operation of a farm.
The reason I am speaking in this debate is that the crisis has far-reaching social and economic implications, not just for the West but for the total economy. As I said, one cannot remain apart. We cannot live in glorious and ignorant isolation from the problems of all Canadians. We are a grand and widespread country. We have regional differences, but we are expected to

April 30, 1987
address them. That is our social contract and that is what the Government has failed to do.
I think it is important that all Canadians, Francophone and Anglophone in every part of this country, pay attention to this situation. Because you live in one of the metropolitan centres across this land does not mean you can be insensitive to this crisis. We know man cannot live by bread alone, but we also know that bread is the staff of life, and that is particularly true for the western farmer.
If you have listened to some of the root causes of the problem we are addressing, as I have over these last many hours of debate, they sound like the plagues which afflicted the Egyptians: drought, grasshoppers, dust, wind, and locusts. Then we have the heavy subsidization of the U.S. and EEC farmer. We have the astronomical drop in prices, the third straight year of decline, which could mean the total return to producers will be 40 per cent lower for wheat, 45 per cent lower for oats, and barley payments below the 1984 per tonne payment. Flax seed and canola prices are lower by 34 per cent and 32 per cent respectively. One can sense the tremendous tragedy taking place and it is easy to understand the frustration and fear for survival which is being echoed behind the doors of each one of our family farms. It becomes obvious that the responsible, dedicated producers, individual farmers carrying on a family tradition or fulfilling a private dream, watch helplessly as forces beyond their control choke life out of their land and choke and close their visions of the future.
What does this requiem for the family farm mean in human terms? Let us consider what one of the studies that was done and reported has to say about this matter. I am reading to you, Mr. Speaker, from the Western Report of January 12, 1987, in which there appears an article entitled: "Farmers Under Stress". There is an interesting quotation from Pliny the Elder who stated:
The agricultural population-produces the bravest men, the most valiant soldiers and a class of citizens the least given of all to evil designs.
I hope that that continues to be the motto of this sector of our society. I suggest, as the article states, that:
Blissful, wholesome farm life, replete with golden wheat fields and rosy-cheeked dairy maidens, is the stuff of prose and poetry. In reality, being a farmer has become so trying that two University of Brandon psychologists say it is now more stressful than being a police officer or a multinational corporate executive.
Last winter, Drs. James and Lilly Walker set out to ask 1,200 farmers what effect the poor economy was having on them. Last month the pair released the resultant report, Characteristics and Correlates of Stress Among Canadian Farm Families, at a University of Brandon conference called "Hungry for Answers-the Farm Community in Crisis." Growing food is one of Canada's most stressful occupations, they concluded. Declares the duo: "This stress is chronic and dangerous."
The study revealed that stress symptoms such as headaches, marriage problems and irritability were three or four times more prevalent in the average farmer than in an RCMP officer three days after being involved in a shooting. What's more, the stress on the policeman is "transitory," say the authors, a "one-time event." But for farmers, the stress just goes on and on.
The Walkers went on to give some additional notes of the methodology that they used in setting up the 79-question survey which included queries about the weather, social problems like spousal neglect, workload and general worry. The article continues:
Stress levels were partly measured by awarding points to such frequently troubling things as insufficient cash flow, debt load and rising expenses. Says Dr. James Walker: "Farmers create a lot of their own stress by being worried about the weather and prices."
That is enough for them to worry about without having to worry about poor government policy and inadequate government planning.
The great question which must be asked is the following. What should the Government do? We know that during the course of the last election campaign the Tories presented a series of 20 from-the-heart type promises. I would like to mention just three or four of them. One of the 20 was to allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds so that farmers will have access to reasonably-priced funds. Has anyone heard of the Government creating agri-bonds? I think not. Another promise was to revise Section 31 of the Income Tax Act to reflect the principles of equity. There have certainly been no principles of equity mentioned in this situation. Another promise was to re-establish a long-term dairy policy. The Government cannot even bring about a shortterm policy of crisis intervention, how can it even think in terms of the long term? Another promise was to expand agricultural research and development by providing greater assistance for agricultural colleges, more funding for research and development, and amending tax policy to encourage private sector investment. What has the Government done in this respect? It has closed down research facilities.
One last point I would like to bring to the attention of the House is the Prime Minister's promise to allocate the necessary funding to assist producers in refinancing their loans at current prevailing rates. What the Government has really done is to send a message to the banks to foreclose, instead of having all the banks, as well as the Federal Business Development Bank and the Farm Credit Corporation, support the worker. I have not even mentioned the fact that the Government has abolished Canagrex, a fine Crown corporation created by Mr. Eugene Whelan to market Canadian agricultural products abroad.
The Prime Minister is on his way out west. If he is going to be visiting Red Deer and Lethbridge, Alberta, North Batt-leford, Moose Jaw and Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, and Winnipeg, Manitoba between Wednesday and Friday of next week, I would like to ask him to deliver the following message on his trip. I suggest he use his marvelous hyperbole in a constructive way at that time. First, let him reinstate the FCC moratorium on farm foreclosures and introduce a proper farm debt restructuring program. Second, let him announce a deficiency program for this year's crop. Third, let him announce the long-promised western economic diversification strategy.
April 30, 1987

During this debate four Ministers of the Crown have spoken, including the Prime Minister. But not one of them gave any commitment for specific assistance. I suggest the Prime Minister has a glorious opportunity, and we know how he loves photo opportunities, to announce at least those three constructive policies. If he does, I think that perhaps some of the stress, strain and family discomfort and dislocation which has been expressed in the debate over the last two days might well be alleviated. Let him show some leadership.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lawrence I. O'Neil (Cape Breton Highlands-Canso):
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29   AGRICULTURE CANADIAN GRAINS CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the issues and problems facing the agricultural industry in Canada. Many Members of the House may not be fully aware that we in Atlantic Canada have a very important agricultural industry, including an important agricultural industry in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia we have problems in our agricultural sector. In Atlantic Canada we have the same or similar problems to those about which other Members have spoken in respect of western Canada. I know from speaking to members of my caucus from Ontario and Quebec that farmers in both those provinces have serious problems as well. From time to time in caucus we have heard strong and aggressive voices concerning the agricultural industry. Members of our caucus from all provinces bring forward, in an aggressive way, the problems that are facing the agriculture industry in Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick-all the Provinces of Canada. Of course, the motion before us deals specifically with western Canada.
We know what the problem is. However, that is not the issue. The issue is what is being done to address the problem. In this respect I am proud to stand here today to speak on just what our Government has done to address the problems facing the agriculture industry from the East Coast to the West Coast. The commitments that were made and honoured are well known by those in the agriculture industry.
Farmers are convinced that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) and the whole Progressive Conservative caucus are strong allies of their industry. For example, they know that 14 of 16 campaign promises in the Prince Albert statement have been addressed. Farmers know that 414 initiatives having a total value of $6 billion have been implemented by the Government. They know that this is a record after only two and a half years of this Government being in office. They know the mess that was left after 20 years of Government by the Liberal Party. They know that for every 1 per cent drop in interest rates there is a savings to the Canadian farmers of $120 million.
The Canadian farmer knows all about this. He has full confidence in the policies being pursued by our Government. It is ironic that food remains our best buy as consumers. It is ironic that we pay more for a litre of pop than we do for a litre of milk. That is typical of the situation that faces our farms.
.S'. O. 29
The farming community faces the situation of rising costs and decreasing revenue. It is a serious problem, Mr. Speaker.
I am going to outline through you, Mr. Speaker, to other Members of the House and to the Canadian public what has been done in two and a half short years to address some of these problems to rebuild the strength of the Canadian agricultural industry. I am going to start by referring to the Atlantic livestock feed initiative. This policy brought in by our Government and an agreement signed just two or three weeks ago between the federal and provincial Governments is an attempt by our Government to establish feed grain selfsufficiency in Nova Scotia and in all of Atlantic Canada. Under this policy, our Government has committed itself to maintaining for a period of time freight rate assistance on grain that moves into Nova Scotia, grain that is important to the beef industry and other livestock industries in Nova Scotia. We have done more than simply continue a subsidy in keeping with our philosophy of developing the regions. We have put in place a series of incentives that will help the Nova Scotia farmer grow his own grain so we will not have to import grain from outside our province. Let us look at what was done on the same issue by the previous Government. I will tell you what that Government did. The Liberal Government did nothing over the last 10 or 15 years when the feed freight assistance rate was declining. There was no serious attempt to address this problem of the agricultural community of Nova Scotia. We have been in office but two and a half years and we have responded and put in place a program after consultation with the industry, a program which is welcomed and a program that is good for the economy of Nova Scotia, not just the agricultural sector of that economy.
What about the question of the financial plight of the farmers in this difficult time? What have we done to assist and put in place an equitable forum where their debt situation can be discussed? We have established farm debt review boards. Legislation has been passed to set up farm debt review boards composed of people with knowledge and experience in farming and financial matters. This process has enabled many farmers to remain on the land. It provides an opportunity for independent third party review to the farm community. It assists in setting up voluntary arrangements between a farmer and his creditors to help ensure the survival of the farm business. Surely that is a constructive response to the financial problems facing farmers, giving them an opportunity to have their case presented in an open and a fair way.
What else is there, Mr. Speaker? The reality is that there are farmers who, in the end, want to leave the farm. They want to undergo a transition to another kind of employment. We have responded to this reality and established the Canadian Rural Transition Program. It is designed to help families who have to leave farming because of financial difficulties to make

the transition to new employment and another way of life. The federal Government will provide financial assistance for farmers' transition, relocation, job search and retraining. Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you know, those who come from Cape Breton are renowned across Canada and in the House for the eloquence of their rhetoric and the honesty with which they present their points of view. No matter from what side of the House we come, we are often impressed with the clear and compelling way in which they present their cases.
Just moments ago, we heard from the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil), the last of the speakers on the government side. It was unfortunate that we heard from him last and I would hope that the character of that speech would encourage others to present themselves because it has left an awful taste in all of our mouths. This is so because someone who represents Cape Breton has presented a case which is based on such utter and complete falsehood as was the allegation that it was the New Democrats who supported the Bank Act when in fact it was the New Democrats with one lone Tory, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who opposed that Bank Act. I rise now to say that if we are to defend a particular point of view, we must do so truthfully or we do harm to the argument we are trying to present.
I am very, very proud of the fact that the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) initiated this very significant debate in the House of Commons. I know that he is a fit representative of the New Democratic Party because this Party is a Party that has its roots on the farm and in the west. However, it also has its roots among the labourers of the city. Because of the initiative of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert and my Party, the concerns of the farm will be clearly dramatized to those of us who live in the city.
I have heard speaker after speaker during the course of this debate suggest that those of us who come from the city should not be involved in this debate because our ignorance would contribute nothing to the expansion of knowledge or information or the solution of the problem that exists in our agricultural sphere. Among that category of Members of Parliament, I may be regarded as an example of urban rot, but I stand here proud to participate in this debate because I think it is about time the people of the city had dramatized for them the situation on the farm. I am sure they share with members of my Party the absolutely compelling point of view that just as we must seek justice and economic security for the people of the city, we must make those people understand that their security, prosperity and justice depends upon economic security on the farm.
When I, as others in the city, eat my shredded wheat, my corn flakes or my meat and drink my milk, I must recognize that all of those commodities are produced as a result of blood, sweat and tears. There is no one who does not understand that

April 30, 1987
the commitment to the land is something that can only be maintained with a great deal of hard work. I do not think there is anyone who does not know that those who work on the farm rise early and work late. They develop callouses upon their hands in an effort to produce from the land.
There are not too many among us who understand, however, that when we talk about blood, that blood truly exists. There is a higher rate of accidental death on the farm than there is in other areas of labour. As well, of the unnatural causes of death on the farm, one-third are suicides, so great is the stress. When we recognize that in that which we eat there are tears as well, it is another assertion that the stress on the farm has become overwhelming. Why should it not be overwhelming? We realize that in the last crop year, prices were cut by 21 per cent, and this year they will be cut by 19 per cent. I think it is incumbent upon every worker, every business person, every professional in this country to look at their own situation and imagine taking a 40 per cent cut in their salaries or wages. They would then begin to understand the situation in which the farmer finds himself.
When one reflects upon the fact that the dire circumstances in the farming community are made worse by the announcement that effective tomorrow the moratorium on FCC loans will end, we begin to gain a comprehension of the existing situation. How many Canadians recognize that the price of grain, as a result of cuts last year and this decision, is no different from what it was in 1976 and 1977? Yet the cost of doing business has tripled. We then expect the farmer to survive.
I understand, but perhaps others here do not, that there exists in the international market-place a severe set of circumstances which make competition extremely difficult. The EEC is subsidizing its farmers to the tune of about $70 billion a year. The U.S. is subsidizing its farmers to the tune of around $22 billion a year. World prices are thereby reduced. This is something which is not under the ready control of the Government, but we encourage it to persist in its efforts to reach international agreements under GATT which would provide a solution to the problem. However, it is no contribution to the plight of the farmer for the Government to decide that the moratorium on FCC loans will end tomorrow.
I know the Government is claiming that there are only a small number of farmers affected. I have heard both the number 6,000 and the number 600. 1 have heard that it only involves 50 farmers a month. However, if one opens up The Toronto Star this morning-I will readily admit as a microbiologist and biochemist that I do not have the information readily available to me so I must depend upon information supplied by a number of sources-he will find that the assistant manager of the FCC office in Edmonton points out that 10,000 prairie farmers are $227 million in arrears on FCC loans. He says that technically they are open to foreclosure. If one looks at the individual provinces, one finds that 21 per cent
of FCC accounts in Alberta and 24 per cent of FCC accounts in Saskatchewan are in arrears. The situation is so severe that one should not be surprised that there are 8 per cent or 25,000 fewer farmers this year than last.
When the Government blithely terminates the moratorium, one must look around to see to whom the Government looks for advice. I watched television last night and saw the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) claim that all significant farm organizations said the moratorium should be removed. When one examines that statement, as the NDP readily does on all occasions, and checks the facts, we find that the National Farmers Union, the three prairie Wheat Pools, and other farm organizations flatly deny that any such statements were made on their behalf. That they would support the lifting of the moratorium as claimed by the Minister of Agriculture is flatly untrue.
What kind of advice is the Minister of Agriculture following when he chooses to lift the moratorium in the hasty fashion in which he did and without putting in place the necessary steps to ensure the survival of our farm community? If one examines the submission of The Canadian Bankers' Association to the Standing Committee on Agriculture and looks at its recommendations, one finds that its fifth recommendation was that there should be no consideration given to debt moratorium or compromise. It is not to the farmers in trouble that the Government is listening. It is listening to the bankers. That of course is in line with a long, long tradition.
If one examines the other recommendations of the bankers, one confirms the source of the advice and direction the Government receives and according to which it acts. The banks recommended that government transition programs involving relocation, retraining and support be implemented. Get them off the farms. The second recommendation was that farm financial review boards should be restricted to an advisory capacity with consideration to be given to the powers of direct lending or provision of loan guarantees to existing lenders or future lending operations as deemed possible. That is certainly being implemented because in Ontario we find that of 425 cases before the review board, 193 have been completed and only two have signed agreements.
Whose advice is the Government following? Whose pleas is it listening to? It said there should be a great deal of circumspection about the introduction of such programs as agribonds. When one considers that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Government promised the implementation of an agri-bond program and it is yet to be heard from, one confirms the source of advice for the Government and its approach to the problems of farmers.
We understand that the problems in agriculture are complicated. However, it is a sorry state of affairs when we can ensure that arms suppliers are well paid and profits are high, when trillions of dollars are spent on arms which are often given away, yet in Canada the farmers are going to food-banks and thousands starve across the seas. It must be evident that it does not need a great genius to find a solution that
April 30, 1987

would feed the world and make sure our farmers are fed. However, that is not going to be done by a Government that announces so much negative action, as it has over the last two weeks, while refusing to commit itself to the minimum contribution to an improvement of the lot of the farmer, that being an announcement for the next crop year of deficiency payments at least as high as they were last year.
I hope this debate initiated by the NDP will lead not to continuing partisan conflict in the House but to a creative culmination of an effort to ensure that in Canada we will maintain our farms and our farmland.
It must be clear to those of us in the city that if the farmers suffer and farms disappear, the city person will not be very far behind. That should be the message to all Canadians insisting that justice be accorded to the farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is seldom we have debates like the one we are having now in the House of Commons. Canadians who are watching the proceedings, especially those who live in our major cities and urban areas and are not terribly familiar with the problems of the agricultural industry, are problably wondering what is going on.
The main reason why the Official Opposition is firmly resolved to make every effort to focus the attention of the Government and the public in general on this issue is that we have today a crisis situation, a serious and tragic one, which affects all grain producers in Canada, and especially our western farmers.
Why do we have this crisis? The answer is quite simple, Mr. Speaker. Last year, as a result of decisions made by this Government, the price paid to farmers for their grain went down 20 per cent. And as if that were not enough to jeopardize the viability of farming operations, a few days ago the Government and the Canadian Wheat Board announced that prices for the 1987 crop year would go down another 18 per cent. Last year it was 20 per cent and this year 18 per cent. While prices paid to farm producers went down 20 per cent and 18 per cent in two years, input costs have continued to rise, including the costs of various kinds of energy and the cost of chemical fertilizers and pesticides. Production costs are going up while prices are going down, so that grain producers across the country-in fact most grain producers happen to be in western Canada-are facing bankruptcy.
To give some indication of what the drop in prices paid to producers represents, the Leader of our Party, when he spoke in this debate yesterday morning, pointed out that in 1984-85, No. 1 wheat was $170 a tonne. In 1986-87, the price was down to $130 a tonne and this year, the Wheat Board announced that the price for No. 1 wheat would go down further to $110 a tonne. The producer who sees the price per tonne drop from
$170 to $110 over such a short period is under considerable financial pressure.
The price of other grains such as barley, for instance, has gone down as well. Mr. Turner told the House about these major price variations. In 1984-85, producers were getting $125 a tonne for No. 1 barley. In 1986-87, the price was down to $80 a tonne.
We heard a few days ago that the price for this year's crop is down to $60 a tonne, which means that in two years, the price of No. 1 barley has dropped from $125 to $60, less than half, so that our grain producers are facing a major crisis. The lower prices they get for their crops this year will make it increasingly difficult for farmers to finance their long- and short-term loans. It puts families, in an industry where most operations are still based on the family farm, under severe financial pressure and physical and moral stress. These farmers do not know how long they will be able to survive, to operate their farms and not only that, to stay in their homes. As though it were not enough to have to worry about the price of grain, farm producers have now been informed that the Government has decided to let the Farm Credit Corporation lift the moratorium on foreclosures.
In 1985, the Government had decided to put a moratorium on the foreclosures that would otherwise have resulted from decisions by the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation. Last week, the Minister responsible announced the moratorium would be lifted, so that we have a situation where in a short period of time, farmers first heard that the Canadian Wheat Board, obviously with the Government's blessing, had reduced prices for their crops, and then that the Government had lifted this moratorium. Less income will make a bad financial situation even worse and, since the Farm Credit Corporation will now be able to seize farms and farm equipment, it only adds to the pressure and puts farmers and grain producers in a practically untenable situation.
Mr. Speaker, the decision to end the moratorium affects not only western producers but also producers in Quebec and other regions. This morning, in La Presse, there was a long article by reporter Pierre Gingras describing how a number of Quebec producers might be affected by the Government's decision to end the moratorium on foreclosures on farms whose owners are in arrears on loan payments to the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation. Here is what he wrote: "Over the next few months, once the moratorium has been lifted, about one hundred Quebec farm producers will be getting Farm Credit Corporation of Canada foreclosure notices preventing them from declaring bankruptcy with respect to farms financed through FCC". He indicates as well that the FCC has 74,000 customers, including 7,500 in Quebec.
This decision obviously affects all producers, and this question does not concern only western producers, but Quebec farmers as well.
As a matter of fact, if we look at the overall agricultural situation we can see that western producers have to cope with

April 30, 1987
falling commodity prices, but eastern producers in general- including those of Quebec since we are part of the eastern region-are hard hit by other economic factors, more especially by the decisions of this Government or its lack of political courage to seek solutions to the extremely serious problems facing our producers.
We have just gone through a spring period and once again all sugar bush owners were able to see for themselves the ravages caused by acid rain. I should think that in recent weeks most parliamentarians have received letters from Quebec's Union des producteurs agricoles indicating losses incurred by farmers who run maple sugar operations, losses which can be directly traced back to acid rains playing havoc with our maple forests. As can be expected, they want the Government to take a tougher and more direct approach in its discussions with the United States in an attempt to find a solution to the acid rain problem.
The second stressing situation for both eastern and western producers is that, in view of the free trade negotiations with the United States, they wonder what is going to happen to the marketing boards which regulate production. Of course this concerns our industrial and whole milk producers, our poultry producers and our egg producers because all these commodities now fall under marketing board regulations. These marketing boards may be put on the table in the negotiations with the United States. Several of my colleagues and I had an opportunity to tour the western provinces, and we also met with Maritime, Ontario and Quebec agricultural producers. We got the same message from coast to coast: Ask this Government not to put marketing boards on the negotiation table. Everywhere people told us that giving up the marketing boards would mean a large number of farm producers would disappear, and with them, a rural way of life that has been a part of our society for so many years. Farmers are in a very good position to compare the situation we have now under the marketing boards with the way things were handled previously, when milk, egg and poultry producers were subject to broad market swings, to dumping by the United States and other countries, all of which put them under extreme financial pressure. They do not want to go back to those times.
In this debate, the Liberals are asking for three things. Our Party Leader, Mr. Turner, made this very clear in his excellent speech yesterday, it was repeated by our Party's agriculture critic, and perhaps it would be appropriate for me to repeat our Party's demands at this point. The Liberals are asking for reinstatement of the moratorium on farm foreclosures by the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation. The Liberals want the Government to continue the moratorium so as to avoid putting additional pressure on producers already faced with two consecutive reductions, 20 per cent and 18 per cent, in the price of grain.
Second, we are asking the Government, now that farmers are about to seed their 1987 crop, to let grain producers know what kind of price they can expect for their grain at the end of the 1987 crop year, in other words, to announce immediately a
deficiency payment program for this year's production, not last year's but the production for 1987 which farmers are seeding at this very moment.
Third, we ask the Government to deliver on the promises it has been making for the past two and a half years, and I am referring to the promised Western Economic Diversification Strategy.
Mr. Speaker, this debate may seem inordinately long. I know this has exasperated some people, but it is the only way we in the Opposition can show grain producers, both western grain producers and those in the rest of the country, that we are doing our duty, that we are concerned about their situation and that we are acting responsibly by pressuring the Government to take action. We are not only talking about farm foreclosures but about a whole way of life that is being destroyed as a result of this Government's failure to act.
For three days the House has been debating an issue of fundamental importance to every Canadian. It is the survival of our family farms.
No matter where one lives, whether it be in the Cities of Vancouver, Edmonton, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax, or St. John's, every Canadian must be seriously concerned about the crisis facing rural Canada today.
To be objective, part of the problem facing rural Canada is caused by international forces such as the U.S. Farm Bill, with its huge subsidies, that was enacted by the United States to counteract the farm subsidies of the European Common Market. These subsidies must be vigorously opposed by the Canadian Government at every available opportunity. However, many of the problems facing our farmers are made in Canada and are directly the result of the Government's action or inaction.
Surely the Government realizes that one of the greatest crises in Canadian farm history is not going to be resolved by the Canadian Wheat Board cutting not only last year's price of wheat by some 20 per cent, but also cutting this year's price of wheat by 18 per cent.
As if this situation was not bad enough, the Government announced this week that it is lifting the ban on farm foreclosures by the Farm Credit Corporation. At the very time when farmers desperately require stability in their industry, and at the crucial seeding time of the year, the Government decides to choose this time to undermine further the confidence of the farming community by reintroducing foreclosures of our family farms. Moreover, the Government has compounded this deplorable situation by refusing to give a commitment of a deficiency payment for the new crop year this year to our farmers, at the very time when they have to make a decision on whether or not to seed. Surely, even the Government realizes that farmers have a right to know today what return they may reasonably plan to expect on their investment.
April 30, 1987

Not only has the price of wheat been going down but also decisions by competitors have been creating more problems. Unfortunately, I do not have enough time to read a letter sent by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) concerning the American Government's decision on the sale of barley to Saudi Arabia. That will create additional problems for our farmers.
There are other problems in western Canada, one of which concerns the sugar-beet industry, particularly in Manitoba. In 1985, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) indicated that he would announce a sugar beet policy and that the federal Government would cover debts going beyond 1987. Neither of these commitments have been met. Instead, the Conservative Government in Ottawa continues to haggle with the NDP Government in Manitoba over developing a support program for the sugar-beet farmers of Manitoba. Meanwhile, a whole industry is on the verge of collapse.
If agreement is not reached shortly on this important matter, the Manitoba Sugar Company will be forced to close down, which will put a $90 million industry out of business, wipe out 300 to 400 farmers, and cost up to 500 jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to get involved in the debate and to make a couple of points with respect to the debate. I think

April 30, 1987
people who know western agriculture such as the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and many of my colleagues on this side of the House who come from western Canada, realize there are a number of facts we have to get back on the table and see where we go from there.
The first point which has to be made is that western Canadian farmers understand the root causes of the pricing situation in the world today with respect to grains. We know the reductions which have taken place. I think it is important for all of us to know what we are competing with. The Liberal Party said previously, for instance, and the spokesman for the Party with respect to financial matters made the same point again with respect to the barley sale to Saudi Arabia by the United States, that Canada's share of international grain sales is going down. That is not the case. It is quite the opposite. In fact, it appears very clearly today that the sales through the Canadian Wheat Board, Canada's portion of international grain sales, is going up. That is the first point to be made.
The second point we have to make is the pricing policy. I want to note very clearly that we are competing very well in terms of sales. We are competing very well in terms of quality, and we are competing very well in terms of traditional and new markets. What we, as Canadians, are competing against is national treasuries. We are competing, for example, against the treasuries of the European Community. The European Community has made a decision, post-war, that Europe would become self-sufficient in food regardless of the cost to the treasury. That is the first point which has to be made. No one in this House is to blame and no one in Canada is to blame.
I would suggest that no one who understands the international grain market in Canada wants that situation to continue, least of all the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board. That is the first point to be made.
The second point is that we are competing with the United States Farm Bill which was a response by the United States primarily, not totally, against the action of the EEC. The point now is that the United States is spending about $25 billion U.S. in support of grains. That is projected to go to $30 billion U.S. next year, at least that is the estimate. So the question for us then clearly becomes what can the Canadian Government, the Canadian people, do not only to maintain markets, which we have been doing, but also to sustain the efforts of our Canadian grain producers?
I think it is best if we take a look at what some farm leaders are saying. I have been hearing a lot of rhetoric around the House today. I think if we look at what was said by the former Chairman of the United Grain Growers, Mac Runciman, who is a respected person in the grains business, he really describes the contribution of a number of Members on this issue. He said that he used to say when he was Chairman that the grain business was 14 per cent protein, and those of us from the grain belt know what that means, and 86 percent politics, "And the bad news is that over the past number of years-", and I would add during this debate, "-that the protein
content of our business is falling fast and the political content is going up", and that is not helping our grain producers. I say that with respect because I think we have to get to some first principles.
The first point the Liberal Party now makes is that we have not done anything. Then when they are challenged in the debate they say: "Well, maybe you have done something but you haven't done enough". That is the point they make. When I take a look at graphs, and this source is Agriculture Canada, and I take a look at federal support of agriculture in western Canada, I see that in 1983 it looks like approximately $250 million. In 1984 it had gone to about $1.2 billion, and I can go to 1987 to the forecast of over $3 billion.
